notes.explains: The plan is to trade off the bad light-squared bishop, and the reflex is just to do it now — but look one move further first. Trade immediately and it opens a check, with the queen landing to fork your king and the piece that recaptured. So the queen steps to d7 first: it covers the a4 check-square and keeps the bishop on c8 defended for its coming trip. One quiet move, and the fork never exists.
notes.teaches: A plan to trade off your worst piece can fail on a single check — before playing the trade, look at the square the enemy queen would check from once the recapture lands. One quiet preparing move is the difference between a good plan and a lost piece.

notes.explains: Where should the knight go? Let the pawn you want to push decide. The natural square in front of the f-pawn would quietly kill the plan of ever running it — so the knight comes to e2 instead. It still holds d4 and c3 and covers f4, but now the f-pawn is unobstructed behind it. Castle, then let that pawn charge at the base of the enemy chain.
notes.teaches: Where a knight goes should be decided by which PAWN you mean to advance later — the natural central square sits in front of the f-pawn and quietly cancels its charge, while the square beside it does the same defensive work and leaves the pawn free.

notes.explains: It is tempting to grab in the centre with a capture on e5 here — but don't, and here is exactly why. The bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 to the king, and that knight cannot legally move at all. So take on e5 and you simply drop a pawn: Black snaps e4 and nothing recaptures, because the only guard is frozen. Instead push the d-pawn past — it grabs space and kicks the knight on c6 to a new square.
notes.teaches: Before making a capture in the centre, check whether the piece you are counting on to recapture is pinned — a bishop pinning a knight to the king removes that knight from every calculation, and captures that looked safe stop being safe.

forkOf.lineName: Four Knights Game / Scotch Four Knights: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Immediate Fianchetto
notes.explains: Both kings are tucked away and the bishop sits home on g2 on the long diagonal. This whole scheme is built around that bishop — one setup that answers a dozen defences — and that consistency is exactly why it has been among White's best tries for decades. Black has a real menu of replies from here, and none of them is refuted; they are simply different games.
notes.teaches: A setup that stays popular for decades usually earned it structurally, not fashionably — when one scheme answers several defences at once, that consistency IS the argument for it.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Immediate Fianchetto
notes.explains: Two squares for this knight, and the difference is a whole tempo. On c6 it would stand right in front of White's d-pawn, so the push to d5 arrives hitting it and White gains time — so we choose d7 instead, where that same advance hits nothing. The knight still does its real job from here: it guards e5 and readies the central pawn strike the whole setup is built around. The oldest and easiest of these systems to learn, and a thoroughly practical way to play it.
notes.teaches: Between two developing squares for the same knight, prefer the one the opponent's pawn break cannot hit — denying a tempo is worth more than the extra square the other move covers.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Fianchetto Variation, Immediate Fianchetto
notes.explains: The bishop went out to g5 to pin, and has come straight back to c1. It is a club favourite and it is a mistake: the knight it pinned was defended, so taking on f6 won nothing — which means the bishop only committed itself to a square a pawn can kick for free. Two moves spent, nothing gained, and it is the same position with Black to move.
notes.teaches: Before pinning, check whether the capture would actually win something — a pin against a defended piece threatens nothing, so the opponent can simply ask the bishop where it means to live.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Najdorf Variation, Opocensky Variation
notes.explains: Some moves choose a move; this one chooses a structure. Push the pawn two squares and you grab space but hand over a square for good — play it to e6 instead and the centre stays fluid, nothing conceded. On e6 it covers d5 and f5, the two squares a knight would kill to reach in front of this structure. Pick it knowingly: everything for the next twenty moves flows from here.
notes.teaches: Some moves are a choice of MOVE and some are a choice of STRUCTURE — pick knowingly, because everything you do for the next twenty moves follows from it. To the sixth rank keeps the centre flexible and the light squares guarded; a square further seizes space and concedes one square for good.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Greco Gambit, Traditional Line
notes.explains: The pawn hits the bishop and the reflex is to drop it back down the diagonal — but a retreat is a move spent for nothing, and it hands White the centre. Look for a check first. The bishop steps sideways to b4 with check, so the reply is forced, and that free tempo is exactly what makes the counter-strike in the centre possible next move. A retreat costs a move; a check earns one.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advance attacks your bishop, the instinct is to slink back — and a retreat hands the centre over for nothing. Look for a check first: the same bishop steps sideways with tempo instead of backwards without one.

notes.explains: White hits e5 at once instead of building up behind it. It looks like giving the centre back — but count what gets freed, not what gets given: the pawn comes off, the closed character goes with it, and White's knight is already out on f3 while Black's pieces are not. There are quieter roads to the same structure, delaying the recapture or preparing it with the c-pawn, but taking straight back is the main one.
notes.teaches: Trading a centre pawn is not losing the centre if it opens lines for the pieces already out — count what gets FREED, not what gets given.

notes.explains: The knight recaptures in the centre and immediately touches the knight on c6. This is the pure version — no gambit, no quiet pawn recapture — and everything from here is about that knight on d4. It sits on the best square on the board, but be honest about it: it is also the piece every black developing move will point at.
notes.teaches: A centralised knight is only strong while it cannot be chased — recapturing into the middle is a gain of space and an invitation at the same time.

notes.explains: Two moves share the main line here, both aimed at the knight on d4: the bishop to c5 and the knight to f6. The knight leads to the chaos, the positions both sides must know move for move — but sharpness you can't recall at the board isn't sharpness, it's risk. The bishop to c5 is the manageable road: it asks the same question of d4 without demanding a memorised maze in return.
notes.teaches: Between two sound replies, the one that needs less memorised theory is the better practical choice — sharpness you cannot recall at the board is not sharpness, it is risk.

forkOf.lineName: Scotch Game / Scotch: Mieses Variation 4...Nf6 (e5 Push)

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3 to hold the knight on d4 — but it does more than defend. It lines up opposite the bishop on c5 and sets a real threat: take on c6 first, the knight lands hitting the queen, and after the recapture the bishops come off on c5 for free. Black has to answer that before doing anything else.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, look first for the defence that also creates a threat — adding a defender that lines up a favourable trade wins the argument twice.

forkOf.lineName: Scotch Game / Scotch: Kasparov's Nb3 Line (4...Bc5 5.Nb3)

notes.explains: The queen steps to f6 and the threat evaporates: the knight can still take on c6, but it no longer arrives hitting a queen. And the queen isn't only dodging — it joins the pressure on d4 down the diagonal and quietly eyes f2, a detail that pays off in two moves' time. One move, three jobs.
notes.teaches: Step out of a fork before it happens rather than after — the best square is the one that dodges the threat and joins the attack on the piece that made it.

notes.explains: The little pawn to c3 puts a third guard on d4 and takes b4 away from Black's pieces in the same move. It is the main line because the knight on d4 is what the whole position is arguing about: hold it and White keeps his shape, lose it and the game is about nothing else. Solve the pressure first, then develop.
notes.teaches: A pawn that adds a defender to a contested piece is worth more than a developing move that ignores it — solve the pressure, then develop.

notes.explains: The knight develops to e7, not f6, keeping the f-file clear for the queen. And taking on c6 now is simply bad for White: Black doesn't recapture — Black takes the bishop on e3 first, threatening mate on f2, which is the whole reason the queen went to f6. White must take back on e3 with the f-pawn, and only then does Black take on c6, with White's structure in ruins.
notes.teaches: An in-between capture beats a recapture when it comes with a bigger threat — before taking back, look for the move that must be answered first.

notes.explains: The bishop goes to c4, the popular choice, aimed at f7 — but popular isn't automatically safe. Black's plan doesn't change, the pieces keep coming out, and now the bishop is a target: a black knight jumping into the centre hits it, and that centralising leap is the move reckoned to give Black the simplest equal game.
notes.teaches: The most popular developing square is not automatically the safest — a bishop aimed at f7 is also a bishop with no retreat when a knight arrives in the centre.

notes.explains: Black castles, and one thing quietly flips: taking on c6 is no longer bad for White. The in-between capture on e3 stops working, because now the knight on c6 can take on e7 with check, and a check must be answered first. So Black would simply recapture with the queen instead — still a fine position, just not the free structural damage that was on offer one move ago.
notes.teaches: A tactic that depends on an in-between move dies the moment the opponent's reply comes with check — re-check your resources after every king move, including your own.

notes.explains: You're a piece down and you want the knockout immediately — but it isn't there yet. The modest pawn to d3 holds the pawn on e4, opens the diagonal for the last minor piece, and the bishop on c4 is already safe. Nothing is threatened and nothing needs to be: you make the position solid before you make it sharp, because the compensation is time and time only pays once your pieces are on the board.
notes.teaches: A piece down, the temptation is to hunt the refutation right now — but there usually isn't one yet. The moves that make a sacrifice work are the boring ones, because the compensation is TIME, and time is only worth something once the pieces that spend it are out.

notes.explains: When you're behind on material, an opponent who throws the queen out early to threaten mate is doing your work for you. Castle: the king reaches safety, the rook lands on f1 defending the f2-square the queen was eyeing, and the queen that came out to threaten now has to spend a move retreating. Answer an early queen with development, never with panic.
notes.teaches: An opponent who throws the queen out early to threaten mate is doing your work for you when you are behind on material — castle, and the same move that reaches safety also brings a rook to the defence and forces the queen to retreat.

notes.explains: Against an early queen sortie, don't hunt the queen — develop at the centre. The knight to c6 covers d4 and puts a second piece out, while White's queen has already moved three times and holds nothing. Chase it directly and you'd burn your own tempo; this keeps every move useful, and the queen still has to find somewhere to stand.
notes.teaches: Against an early queen sortie, develop at the centre rather than hunting the queen — every piece that comes out with a job keeps the queen short of safe squares by itself.

notes.explains: The best central push is the one that arrives hitting something. The pawn to d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and claims the centre in the same move, so the bishop has to spend a move retreating and the centre gets built for free. Look for this whenever an enemy piece sits on a diagonal a pawn can reach.
notes.teaches: The best central pawn move is the one that arrives hitting something — when a single push both builds the centre and gains a move, it is nearly always the move.

notes.opening: Alekhine Defense: Four Pawns Attack, Main Line
notes.explains: Develop in the order that keeps an answer ready for the opponent's most annoying jump. A knight landing beside your queenside pawns is only a problem while the rook behind them sits at home — so the knight comes to c3, holding d5 and b5 and clearing the rook's path to the c-file if that knight ever hops in. It answers a move that hasn't been played yet.
notes.teaches: Develop in the order that keeps an answer ready for the opponent's most annoying jump — a knight coming beside your queenside pawns is only a problem while the rook behind them is still at home.

notes.explains: A rook's-pawn step that makes a bishop declare itself is almost free — either it takes, handing you the pair and a recapture toward the centre, or it retreats and you've won the square. The pawn to h3 puts the question to the bishop on g4: whichever it chooses, the square it is standing on stops being available to it, and nothing in your camp is weakened by the move.
notes.teaches: A rook's-pawn step that makes a bishop declare itself is worth playing almost without calculation — either it takes, handing you the pair and a recapture toward the centre, or it retreats and you have won the square for free.

notes.explains: When the enemy queen comes out early, develop at it. The knight to c3 hits the queen sitting in the middle of the board — Black knew this was coming, since recapturing with the queen always concedes it — so the question is not whether the queen gets chased but where it goes, because that choice decides which of several quite different games follows.
notes.teaches: When the enemy queen comes out early, develop AT it — a knight that gains time on the queen has paid for its own move.

notes.explains: A queen retreat is a plan, not an apology. The queen steps to d6 rather than the older squares, keeping an eye on d4 while staying off the file White's rook will eventually own. This treatment rose to prominence recently and now has a book of its own — entirely legitimate. What it does not do is change White's job: develop the pieces, take the centre, play a normal game.
notes.teaches: A queen retreat is a plan, not an admission — judge the square by what it eyes and what it stays out of the way of, not by the fact that the piece moved twice.

notes.explains: Take the centre even though the square is already under fire. The pawn to d4 holds e5, and note it arrives already attacked — the queen on d6 looks straight down at it — so White is not building at leisure, and every developing move from here has to keep that pawn in mind. That is the whole shape of the line: nothing forcing, nothing clever, just a race between White's space and Black's pressure on the point that space rests on.
notes.teaches: Occupy the centre even when the square is already under fire — a pawn that will need defending is still worth more than the space you never took.

notes.explains: When one pawn is the target of everything, pick the developing square that also guards it. The knight to f3 adds a defender to the pawn the queen has eyed since it retreated. Nothing exotic from here — the plan is exactly what it looks like: finish developing, keep the centre held, and take the small edge that space and the extra tempo have already bought.
notes.teaches: When one pawn is the target of everything, prefer the developing square that also guards it — solving the pressure while developing is the cheapest defence there is.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Sämisch Variation, Closed Variation
notes.explains: The modest f-pawn is the spine of the whole setup: it bolts the centre shut so everything that follows — the bishop out, the queen behind it, castling long, the pawn storm — happens behind a wall. The pawn on f3 defends the pawn on e4, and with pawns alone holding the centre the pieces are freed from guard duty for attacking posts. The fianchettoed bishop across the board now stares into a wall that never needs a defender.
notes.teaches: The modest f-pawn move is the spine of this whole setup — it bolts the centre shut so that everything that follows happens behind a wall. Judge it by what it enables, not by what it looks like.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Sämisch Variation, Closed Variation
notes.explains: Whether you can accept a pawn offer depends on your structure, not your nerve. A setup with nothing loose behind it can open the centre and grab material safely — count your weak pieces and pawn holes first, and when the count is zero, take. The knight on b5 attacks the pawn on d6 and the pawn on a7; nothing at home hangs, the centre is bolted and development is finished, so the grab is just good bookkeeping.
notes.teaches: Whether you can accept a pawn offer depends on your structure, not your nerve — a setup with no weaknesses behind it can open the centre and grab material without exposing anything. Count your loose pieces and pawn holes first; when the count says none, take.

notes.explains: The rule against an early queen is really a rule against a queen that can be chased — so count what could chase her first. The queen recaptures on d4 in the middle of the board, holding the pawn on e4 and the knight on c3 and looking down at g7. The advance that would normally hit her would weaken the very square in front of it, so she is not going anywhere. Rules describe positions; check whether yours is one of them.
notes.teaches: The rule against an early queen is really a rule against a queen that can be CHASED — count what could attack her before deciding. If the pawn breaks that would hit her are unavailable or weakening, the centre is the best square on the board.

notes.explains: The knight simply develops to f3. If Black grabs it, you might flinch at the doubled c-pawns — but don't: those c3 and d4 pawns brace the centre, and White keeps the strong light-squared bishop. Placing that bishop on d3 first is exactly what makes this calm reply work.
notes.teaches: Do not reflexively avoid a doubled pawn — when the trade that doubles you also hands you the bishop pair and a pawn duo supporting your centre, welcome it. Judge the exchange by what you end up with, not by the tidy pawns you give up.

notes.explains: The pawn to e5 grabs central space and, crucially, attacks the knight on f6, so Black has to stop and move it. That is a free tempo: White gets room for a kingside build-up while the opponent spends a move tucking the knight away.
notes.teaches: Advance a central pawn when the push also gains time by hitting a piece — space seized with tempo, rather than as a slow lunge, gives you a free move to get on with your plan while the opponent scrambles.

notes.explains: The pawn to a3 pokes the bishop on b4 and forces a choice, and both answers help White: take on c3 and hand over the bishop pair with a supported centre, or drop back with a lasting headache. Ask the question — Black shoulders the answer either way.
notes.teaches: When an enemy bishop pins your knight and nothing forces your hand, a rook-pawn poke makes it commit — either it captures, handing you the bishop pair, or it retreats with a lasting awkwardness.

notes.explains: Here is the catch. With c5, Black threatens to shove the pawn to c4 next, hitting the bishop on d3 which would have nowhere safe to go. It is the standard trap in this structure — White has to deal with the idea now, before getting on with the attack.
notes.teaches: In a cramped, closed structure watch for a pawn thrust that cages your own developed bishop — the space you gained can become a trap, so spot the pawn advance that hits a bishop with no retreat before it lands.

notes.explains: The queen goes to e3, and it works on two fronts: it guards the d4-pawn, and it sidesteps the bishop-to-b5 try that Black would meet with a6, forcing off White's prized light-squared bishop. The attacker stays on the board — that is the move that matters here.
notes.teaches: Answer a threat with the move that does two jobs at once — and never trade the piece your attack depends on. A quiet queen move that guards the point and preserves your key attacker beats a developing move that invites its exchange.

notes.explains: The queen swings to f4, on its way to g4 or g3 to bear down on g7 and the king. And the route costs nothing: from those squares it keeps one eye on the centre, so the attacking plan gains its ground without giving anything back.
notes.teaches: Reroute your queen toward the enemy king by way of a stepping-stone square — when the plan is a kingside attack, the queen's journey to its attacking post is worth the tempo, especially when the route keeps defending the centre for free.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit
notes.explains: Read the opponent's prep from which reply they pick. The knight jumps into d5 and offers the pawn — the gambit proper. Black's best is the knight to b4, which the engines like and the books recommend, so a player who finds it is telling you they know this line. The answer that keeps it interesting is to take on f6 straight away. And one thing to get right after: if Black recaptures with the queen, do not grab the pawn on d4 — the queens come off with a check to follow, the knight drops in on c2 forking king and rook, and the whole gambit turns into a lost ending.
notes.teaches: Read the opponent's preparation from which reply they choose — a move that only appears in books tells you the next ten moves will be theory, so switch from testing them to testing the position.

notes.explains: Judge a defensive pawn move by what it costs, not whether it's safe. The pawn to d6 holds e5 and that is all it does: it brings no piece out, and it shuts in the bishop on f8 that a moment ago had the whole diagonal to choose from. Solid is not the same as good — two concessions in one move is exactly the sort of thing an opponent is entitled to punish, and there is a standard way to do it.
notes.teaches: Judge a defensive pawn move by what it costs, not by whether it is safe — a move that neither develops a piece nor frees one has conceded two things at once, and both are exploitable.

notes.explains: Against an opponent behind in development, open the position. The pawn strikes at e5 at once, and the logic is mechanical rather than clever: they have spent a move without developing and blocked a bishop, so you make those facts matter by opening lines while they are still true. Wait, and they untangle for free.
notes.teaches: Against an opponent who is behind in development, open the position — every line you open is worth more to the side with more pieces looking down it.

notes.explains: The knight takes back in the middle, covering f5 and b5, and there is no hurry to move it anywhere. If it gets traded, taking back with the queen is perfectly comfortable here — the piece that would normally chase a queen off that square has to come out first, and it has not. So White simply keeps developing and lets the position stay open.
notes.teaches: A centralised knight that cannot be chased does not need to move again — develop the rest of the army and let the opponent decide whether trading it off helps them.

notes.explains: The bishop checked and has now stepped back, having achieved one thing: a black piece stands on d7, wedged between the queen and the pawn on d5. So the queen can no longer take that pawn back — only the knight can. White has spent two moves with the same bishop and still comes out ahead, because the interposition is permanent and the retreat costs nothing.
notes.teaches: A check is worth playing when the only ways to answer it all cost the defender something, even if you intend to retreat straight afterwards — forcing a piece onto a square where it blocks its own side's plans buys a concession quiet development never would.
notes.structural: the interposition is permanent — its checkable claim belongs to Bd7, not to the retreat it is anchored on

notes.explains: Black takes, and the pawn on d4 will not survive — but which White piece removes it matters. The knight recapture is the one that leads to the sharp open positions this whole line is played for; taking with the queen instead is a different game, quieter and with the queen already committed. Both are legal here, and Black does not get to choose.
notes.teaches: A capture with two possible recaptures is a fork in the road, not a formality — wait to see which piece takes back before deciding what game you are in.

notes.explains: The knight takes back in the middle of the board and now covers b5 and e6, the two squares Black's setup cares about most. This is the real open position — the one with a genuine mass of theory behind it, where White has something like ten separate playable schemes from a couple of moves away. Nobody learns all of it at once, and nobody needs to.
notes.teaches: A knight recapturing into the centre is worth more than the material it restores — it takes the squares the opponent's queenside expansion needs. Notice which squares before you plan around them.

notes.explains: The knight comes out and leans on e4. It is the move Black wants in every version of this position, so there is no reason to spend a thought on it: it develops, it asks a question, and it leaves the choice of system to White. The huge branching comes next, and it comes on White's move.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has many playable setups and you have one useful move, play the useful move — developing with a hit costs nothing and makes them commit first.

notes.explains: A check is worth playing when every legal answer costs something — look at what each reply does to the defender's own pieces. Blocking on d7 with the bishop is the natural-looking answer, and it quietly costs Black the recapture: the bishop now stands between the queen on d8 and the pawn on d5, so the queen can no longer reach it and only the knight can win the pawn back. It also takes d7 from the knight on b8, which now has to settle for c6 or a6.
notes.teaches: A check is worth playing when every legal answer to it costs something — look at what each reply does to the defender's own pieces before judging the check as slow. The value is not in the check, it is in the awkward square the opponent has to commit to.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The knight comes to c3, guarding e4, and right now the game could still become several different openings — a quiet knight game, a sharp f-pawn advance, or the lines with both knights out. Nothing is settled yet, which is the point: whatever Black has prepared, it is not yet clear it even applies.
notes.teaches: Develop with a move that keeps several openings available — the less your third move commits to, the more of the opponent's preparation is wasted.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: Black brings the knight out and immediately leans on e4. It is defended, so nothing is won — but from here on every White move has to keep that pawn covered, and that is a constraint White will feel for the next several moves.
notes.teaches: Meet a developing move with a developing move that carries a threat — attacking the pawn the opponent just defended forces them to keep defending it.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The second knight comes out to hit e5, and the position is a mirror image of itself. Neither side has done anything special; both have simply put the knights where knights go. The real game starts with the first pawn break, and it is White's turn to choose one.
notes.teaches: In a symmetrical position, the extra move is only an advantage if it can be turned into a threat — mirror until the opponent commits, then look for the break.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: White cracks the symmetry with the pawn to d4, hitting e5. This turns the knight game into an open one — the pawns come off in the centre, the position opens, and both sides play with pieces rather than pawn chains. From this side of the board it is a comparatively rare choice, which is itself worth something.
notes.teaches: A pawn break in a symmetrical position is a decision to change the pawn structure while you still have the move — break when the resulting position suits your pieces, not because you are tired of mirroring.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: Black takes, and the pawn that lands on d4 is looking straight at the knight on c3. White has to deal with that, which means recapturing right away rather than slipping in a useful move first. Small thing, but it is why this structure resolves so quickly.
notes.teaches: When you capture toward the centre, look at what the pawn attacks on arrival — a recapture forced by your pawn's new target is a tempo you did not have to ask for.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The knight recaptures in the centre, touching the knight on c6, and Black chooses where the dark-squared bishop goes. The move in most books is the pin on b4, leading to the well-charted lines where White trades on c6 and develops the bishop to d3. The bishop to c5 is the other road — second most popular, entirely reputable, and steering into a different pawn structure altogether.
notes.teaches: The most-recommended move is not the only good one — a second-most-popular move that steers into structures you understand better is worth more than a main line you half remember.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: White has traded on c6 and now develops the bishop to d3, where it supports the pawn on e4. That pawn is the pressure point of the whole structure: Black's doubled c-pawns are the price paid for a pair of long-range pieces and a target to aim at. A different bishop square looks more aggressive and leaves e4 short of help — which is exactly the kind of thing that decides these positions.
notes.teaches: When one pawn is the target of everything, develop the piece that covers it — choosing a developing square that also defends beats choosing the square that only looks active.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The pawn goes to d5 and hits e4. This is the point of the bishop having gone to b4 rather than c5: with the pin, almost everyone strikes with the d-pawn two squares, opening the position immediately and using the doubled pawns as central mass. The other bishop square quietly changes the plan to the modest one-square advance and a slower game. Same opening, two different structures, decided four moves earlier.
notes.teaches: An early bishop move is really a choice of pawn break three moves later — ask which pawn advance the bishop's square makes natural before you play it.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the f7 diagonal instead of the quiet pawn move — which would have allowed a trade on f3 followed by a capture in the centre. Not every position needs the theoretically best try: development is finished on c4, a square whose value does not depend on a calculation, eyeing f7 and holding d5.
notes.teaches: When a natural-looking move lets the opponent trade into your centre with tempo, prefer the developing move whose consequences you can see to the end — a sound piece on a good square beats a sharper move whose compensation you would be hunting for afterwards.

notes.explains: The whole point of these first moves is one comparison: the same locked centre, but with the light-squared bishop outside the chain instead of buried behind it. So bring it out first, every time, and only then close the chain. The bishop to f5 is already working — it holds e4, the square in front of the chain where the opponent would love to post a piece, and the pawn can go to e6 behind it next. Same pawns, bishop on the right side of them: the good version.
notes.teaches: The whole point of this defence's first moves is one comparison: the same locked centre with the light-squared bishop outside the chain instead of behind it. Bring the bishop out first, every time, and only then close the chain.

notes.explains: Against a pawn chain the plan is no secret: attack the base. The pawn strikes at c5, hitting the pawn on d4 — the base of the chain that runs up to e5 — and it lands best now that the minor pieces have settled. The pawn asks the question, and the pieces developed on the previous moves are aimed at exactly this fight.
notes.teaches: Against a pawn chain, the plan is not a secret: attack the base. The c-pawn's strike at the centre is the main idea of the whole structure, and it lands best once your minor pieces have settled.

notes.explains: The knight has recaptured on f5, stepping from the rim into the fight, and every pawn in front of the king still stands where it started. The queen on b6 keeps leaning on the pawns on b2 and c5 meanwhile — pressure held, structure intact, one piece better than before the trade.
notes.teaches: When a trade is offered on a square your knight can reach, prefer the recapture that improves a piece over the one that moves a pawn. The knight that retakes arrives on an active square with the pawn shield untouched — same trade, and one version develops you.
notes.structural: the recapture chosen to activate a piece and keep the pawn shield — same trade, better version

notes.opening: Neo-Grünfeld Defense: Classical Variation, Modern Defense
notes.explains: Both sides have finished the same quiet development, and this is the move that decides which game gets played. The pawn arriving on d5 covers c4 and e4 together, so the natural pawn breaks are answered before they are even played. The modest alternative one square shorter leaves both of those squares free and invites a bigger centre instead.
notes.teaches: When a setup gives you a free choice of central pawn move, pick the one that takes squares away from the opponent rather than the one that only makes room for you — a pawn on the fourth rank of the centre contests two squares at once, usually the two the other side wanted.

notes.explains: The pawn to e4 completes the broad centre, holding d5 and f5 and shutting the long diagonal the bishop on g7 was just aimed down. Black is not trying to stop this — the whole design is to let the centre be built and then hit it, either in the middle with a pawn to e5 or on the wing with a pawn to c5. What White has taken in space, White now has to hold.
notes.teaches: Building the widest possible centre is a commitment, not a free gain — it takes squares now and hands the opponent a fixed target to strike at later.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d6 rather than two squares, contesting e5 and holding the point the whole plan turns on. It looks modest and it is the move that makes the position work: the centre stays flexible, the bishop keeps its diagonal, and the pawn strike in the middle is now available whenever Black wants it. Committing further this early would tell White which plan is coming.
notes.teaches: A one-square pawn move that looks passive is often the one that makes the break possible — ask what it prepares, not what it occupies.

notes.explains: The knight arrives on f3, adding a guard to d4 and contesting e5 — the exact square Black wants to strike at. This is the most-played arrangement, and White's problem from here is a pleasant one: the space is real, but so is the fact that a broad centre needs defending, and Black's pieces are all pointed at it.
notes.teaches: With a big centre, develop the pieces that hold it — every developing move that also guards the centre is a move you will not have to spend defending later.

notes.explains: The knight comes out to f3 and contests e5 without committing the e-pawn. This is the quiet road, and it is the one engines tend to like best at high depth: rather than build the broad centre Black is preparing to hit, White copies Black's own approach — flank bishop, modest centre — and leaves the counter-attack nothing to bite on.
notes.teaches: Against a setup built to counter-attack a big centre, consider not building one — mirroring the opponent's structure removes the target their whole plan needs.

notes.explains: The pawn to g3 prepares the bishop's home on the long diagonal, directly opposite the one Black has already fianchettoed. This is the version reckoned objectively strongest and the one the engine reaches for at depth. There is no big centre to attack, so both sides play for the light squares and for the moment the diagonal opens — a slower game, and a harder one to prepare against precisely because it refuses the argument the defence was built to have.
notes.teaches: Two bishops on the same long diagonal is not a stalemate of ideas — it is a fight for who gets to open it, and the side with the extra tempo usually decides.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The pawn has stepped to f6 to push the bishop off the diagonal — and the bishop drops back to e3, where it hits the pawn on c5 and covers d4. The pawn move that chased it cannot be taken back, and the squares it gave up are exactly the ones the bishop now works on. The retreat cost nothing.
notes.teaches: A bishop chased by a pawn should retreat onto a diagonal that already has a target — if the pawn move that drove you away also weakened a square you can now hit, the retreat has cost nothing and the weakness is permanent.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps to h6 and offers itself for the bishop on g7, the only piece holding the dark squares near the king. It is defended by the queen behind it, so the offer is real. Declining leaves the bishop sitting on the king's doorstep; accepting hands over the very squares the fianchetto was built to hold.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed king, put your bishop where it offers a trade the defender cannot sensibly refuse — once the guard of the dark squares comes off, every square around the king a pawn does not cover belongs to the attacker, and the pawns there can never cover them again.

notes.explains: The pawn goes to d5 and hits c4, and with it the game stops being about occupying the middle and starts being about pressuring it. This is a demanding way to play — it is rarely seen below master level, and the reason is not that it is unsound but that it asks for a great deal of memorisation and a set of ideas unlike anything else. Nobody stumbles into playing it well.
notes.teaches: Striking in the centre with a pawn you intend to trade off is not a contradiction — giving up the centre in order to attack it is a complete system of ideas, not a concession.

notes.explains: The knight takes back on d5 and immediately leans on the knight at c3. Black has no pawn in the centre at all now and is not troubled by that: the whole plan is to let White build the big pawn centre and then take it apart. White's natural reply is to kick this knight with the e-pawn, and that is exactly what Black is inviting.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the piece that keeps making threats — a knight landing in the centre where it attacks a defender is worth more than the pawn structure it declined to build.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e4, hitting the knight and giving White the broad centre outright. This is the natural move and the main one. What it also does is accept the terms: the pawns on d4 and e4 are the thing Black has been building against since move three, and every black piece from here will be aimed at them.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers you the centre, take it — but know you are accepting a target, not a gift. The pawns are strong exactly as long as they can be defended.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the long diagonal and looks straight at d4. White has the ideal-looking pawn centre with a pawn on c3 holding it up, and it is still reckoned one of the soundest ways for Black to play. The plan from here is unambiguous: push the c-pawn to c5, bring the knight to c6, and if the knight comes to f3, pin it with the bishop to g4. Black hands over the centre and then throws everything at it as fast as possible — which is why an unprepared White player gets into as much trouble here as an unprepared Black one.
notes.teaches: A fianchettoed bishop pointed at a doubled-pawn centre is the whole plan in one piece — judge such a centre by whether it can advance, not by how imposing it looks.

notes.explains: The bishop to e2 covers g4, which is the square Black's light-squared bishop would love to reach once a knight lands on f3. It is the first move of a specific scheme: bishop here, castle, and then the other bishop out to g5. This is the version where Black has given up the centre completely — allowing three and potentially four white pawns across it — and intends to attack it with pieces instead.
notes.teaches: A modest bishop development can be the first move of a named system — ask what it takes away (here, the pin the opponent most wants) before calling it quiet.

notes.explains: Black tucks the king away on the side the play will eventually happen. That sounds dangerous and it usually is not: the centre in this structure tends to lock, and once it locks neither side can open lines against a king quickly. What follows is the defining pattern of the whole opening — both sides attack, on opposite wings, at their own pace.
notes.teaches: Castling toward the side you intend to attack on is normal here, not reckless — in a closed centre the king is safe behind its own pawns precisely because nothing can be opened quickly.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on e5 and hits d4 — the most popular way to play the position, and the branch point. White can trade, hold the tension, or push past. In practice the push is what almost always comes, and it settles the character of the game for the next thirty moves.
notes.teaches: A central strike does not have to win anything to be right — it forces the opponent to choose the structure, and knowing which structure follows each choice is most of the preparation.

notes.explains: White has pushed past and the centre is shut: pawns facing each other with nothing to capture. This is the position the whole classical line is heading for, and it has a flavour all its own. Neither side can make progress in the middle, so play goes to the flanks — White expands on the queenside where the space is, Black throws the kingside pawns at the white king. Both attacks are real and the game is usually decided by which one lands first.
notes.teaches: When the centre locks, stop looking for play there and find your wing — a blocked centre does not mean a quiet game, it means both sides get to attack without being interrupted.

notes.explains: This is the traditional way: hit c5 straight away rather than developing first. The two orders usually reach the same middlegames, and the difference is what Black is allowed in the meantime — which is the whole reason a modern repertoire prefers bringing the knight out before committing the d-pawn. At club level the old order is a serious practical weapon, because the theory that neutralises it is theory most opponents have never seen.
notes.teaches: Two move orders that reach the same structures are still two different move orders — compare them by what the opponent gets to do in between, not by where the pieces end up.

forkOf.lineName: Sicilian: Alapin / Alapin: Stoltz Attack (4.Nf3 before d4)

notes.explains: Black takes, and the pawn on d4 is now looking at c3. Recapturing with the c-pawn is the point of this move order: it answers the threat and, in doing so, takes the pawn off c3 entirely, so the grab on that square stops existing. Develop the knight first instead and Black keeps the option of taking on c3, which is a different game with a pawn in the balance.
notes.teaches: When two recaptures look the same, count the options each one leaves the opponent — taking with the pawn here removes a whole line from their side of the board.

notes.explains: The knight comes out to c6 and on the way props up the pawn Black won on d4. White will take it back with the c-pawn anyway, but the order matters: Black gets a piece out for free while the recapture is being arranged. Notice what the delayed recapture allowed — with a pawn still on c3, taking there was on the table, and that option is the whole difference between the two move orders.
notes.teaches: Develop toward the material you are holding — a gambit pawn you cannot defend is a tempo already spent, but one your developing move happens to guard is a real question for the other side.

notes.explains: White has taken back on d4 and Black answers by hitting the advanced pawn on e5. This is the shape the whole line has been heading for: an isolated pawn on d4 that hands White squares and initiative, against a solid black position that will trade pieces and lean on it. Neither side is worse — the argument is over whether that pawn is a spearhead or a target.
notes.teaches: Handing a gambit pawn back at the right moment is not a concession — give it back to hit the pawn that is cramping you and you have bought the time to finish developing.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to c4 and asks the knight on d5 to make up its mind. The knight has been sitting in the middle since move three and this is the first move that actually challenges it. Dropping back to b6 is the popular reply; taking on e5 is the other one, and it is the move that steers towards an equal game.
notes.teaches: Aim a developing move at the piece that is doing the most work — development that also asks a question is worth two moves.

notes.explains: The knight steps back to b6 and hits the bishop. It is worth knowing why the usual sacrifice does not work in this exact position: take on f7, the king takes back, push the pawn to e6 with check — and the king simply returns to g8. White has nothing left that can touch the pawn there, and the bishop that has not moved all game can even remove it. The sacrifice fails precisely because Black is undeveloped, which is not how these things usually go.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing on f7, ask what happens after the king walks back — a sacrifice that needs a follow-up piece is refuted by the opponent having one more defender than you have attackers, even a defender that has never moved.

notes.explains: Instead of dropping the bishop back where it came from, it steps across to b5 and pins the knight on c6 against the king. The move that chased it has been answered with a move that asks its own question, so the tempo Black spent kicking the bishop has come straight back. This is the position where the very old theory begins, and it runs a long way.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is kicked, look for the retreat that attacks something — stepping sideways with a threat costs the opponent the tempo they thought they had won.

forkOf.lineName: Sicilian: Alapin / Alapin: 2...Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nf3 (Alt Move Order)

notes.explains: Black takes on e5, getting rid of the advanced pawn that has been holding d6 and f6 since move three. The pawn that lands on e5 now leans on d4 in turn. White will recapture with the knight and the position opens up: fewer pawns, more piece play, and an isolated pawn on d4 that is both a weakness and a source of squares.
notes.teaches: Trade off the pawn that is taking your squares, even when it opens lines for the opponent — space you cannot use is worth less than squares you can.

notes.explains: The bishop comes out to d7 and props up the pinned knight on c6. That is the whole job: the knight is what attacks the piece sitting on e5, and it can only do that work while something is holding it. Note the bishop does not hit the piece on b5 — its own knight stands in the way — so this is support, not counter-attack. Everything from here has been played thousands of times; it is the backbone of the old main line.
notes.teaches: A pinned piece needs a second defender before it needs sympathy — develop toward the pin; the move that unpins and develops in one is usually the only move worth playing.

notes.explains: The queen takes back on d7 rather than the king or a knight, and from there it holds the knight on c6 — which matters, because that knight is about to become the single most important piece in the position. Two pairs of minor pieces have come off, the position is simplifying, and Black is close to being fully out.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the piece that ends up doing something — a queen that lands defending a loose piece is not a queen that came out too early.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to e6, taking d5 away from White's pieces for good and opening the way for the dark-squared bishop. It looks passive and it is not: the knight that just came to c3 would love to sit on d5, and this quietly says no. Black is one move from being completely developed.
notes.teaches: A small pawn move that takes a central square away is worth more than it looks — deny the outpost before the piece arrives, not after.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e7 and Black is about to finish developing, so this is the moment. The queen belongs on g4, hitting g7 through the bishop and e6 in front of it. But the order matters more than the idea. Swinging the other bishop out to h6 straight away is a blunder: Black replies by taking the isolated pawn with the queen, where the knight on c6 defends it, the queen covers g7 from there, and White's own queen is left hanging. Take the knight on c6 first. Then the same queen grab simply loses the queen, the bishop arrives on h6 with real force, and the black bishop is forced to f6 where the knight comes to e4 and hits it again.
notes.teaches: Check the order before the idea — if the move you want to play hangs something, look for the capture that removes the defender first, because the attacking move is still there next turn.

notes.explains: A move order can be worth more than the move it delays. Black has shut the king's bishop in with the d-pawn, and White has developed the light-squared bishop and the queen's knight before touching the centre. The central push is still coming and usually transposes to the same structures — but held back, it arrives when the pieces are already placed to meet the reply, and a defender off familiar ground is worth a tempo by itself.
notes.teaches: A move order can be worth more than the move it delays — playing the natural central break a little later, after the pieces are out, keeps the same position available while denying the opponent the setup they have prepared against.
notes.structural: a move-order judgement: the same position reached with the pieces already placed

notes.explains: Black has castled and it all looks routine, but taking on e4 here works: after the recapture the d-pawn comes forward and attacks the knight on e4 and the bishop on c4 together. Dropping the bishop to d3 keeps the bishop pair and the material is level — what is gone is the centre. Trading the e4 pawn for the pawn on d6 is a poor bargain, because it frees the very bishop Black's opening had shut in.
notes.teaches: Whenever a bishop sits on c4 and a pawn on e4 with a knight able to reach it, check for the centre fork trick before you castle — it is not usually winning, but it solves the defender's problems, and the cost is paid in structure, not material.
notes.structural: names a resource to check for before castling, not a claim about castling

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: A pawn taken from you is not a pawn you must take back at once. Both obvious recaptures on d4 invite the queen's knight to c6, hitting the piece that just landed there and developing at the same time — so placing the bishop on d3 instead ignores the pawn for now, gets on with the kingside, and trusts that d4 is weak enough to collect in due course. Recovering material on the opponent's schedule is how a lead in development gets spent for nothing.
notes.teaches: A pawn taken from you is not a pawn you must take back immediately — when every natural recapture can be hit with tempo, the move that wins the pawn is the one you play later, after the pieces are out.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The pawn on e5 covers both f6 and d6, so the king's knight and the dark-squared bishop lose their natural developing squares, and Black's position is cut in two with the queenside pieces struggling to join the kingside. That is why White is content to leave d4 alone for the moment: the clamp is worth more than the pawn.
notes.teaches: One advanced pawn can do the work of a piece when it takes away the squares the opponent's pieces most want — judge such a pawn by what it denies rather than by whether it is defended, and be correspondingly unwilling to part with it.
notes.structural: what the e5 pawn denies — a property of the structure, not of the move played

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The pawn chain is fixed and White has castled. Three tries come into consideration: the knight to e7, heading for f5 or g6 behind the chain; the bishop out to c5 where it eyes the centre immediately; or the pawn to f6, striking at the head of the chain before the pieces are settled.
notes.teaches: With the centre locked and the king still to be tucked away, the choice is which piece the position needs first — a knight behind its pawns keeps every option, an active bishop commits it, a break at the head of the chain changes the structure at once. They are not the same game.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: Black challenges the e5 pawn directly, and the reply is the bishop to b5 — pinning the knight on c6 against the king, since d7 is empty. That takes the sting out of capturing on e5, because recapturing with the knight then hits c6 a second time, from the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: A move that is wrong early can be exactly right once the position has changed — striking at a cramping pawn with the f-pawn loosens the squares around your own king, so before you play it, ask which enemy piece is waiting to use them.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b4 to swap itself for the knight on c3 — but ask what it actually costs. Develop the other bishop to d3, and if the exchange comes, recapture with the c-pawn: that is the point — it takes the central squares, opens a path for the queen along the c-file, and leaves White the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Being pinned against nothing is not a threat — when a bishop comes out to trade itself for a knight, ask what it actually costs you. Doubled pawns are only a weakness if they cannot be used, and a pair of bishops plus open lines is usually the better half of that bargain.

notes.explains: The knight has landed on e5, and from here the choice is between castling and bringing the queen's knight to d7. The difference matters: the knight on d7 can offer a trade on e5 and change the structure before White's kingside pawns get going, while castling leaves the centre alone and lets the storm start at once.
notes.teaches: A knight planted in the centre is often preparation for a pawn advance elsewhere, not an end in itself — whether that advance works usually turns on move order, because if the opponent can challenge the knight first, the whole plan arrives a move too late.

notes.explains: The advance of the g-pawn drives the bishop, and after it steps to g6 the h-pawn comes too, threatening to push again. Every square the bishop can then reach is covered by a white pawn, so it can only come off for a pawn — which is why the alternative here was the quieter bishop to d3, inviting the trade on White's terms instead.
notes.teaches: Pawns hunt bishops — when your king is castled on the side an enemy pawn storm is coming, count the squares your loose bishop can retreat to and check whether pawns cover them. A bishop with only defended squares to run to is still lost if every one of them can be taken by a pawn.

notes.explains: The centre has just been clarified and both sides look alike. Developing the queen's knight to c6 is the natural move and is the inaccuracy here, because the knight can be harried from b5; the small pawn move to a6 takes the square away first, and it is that line that holds the balance.
notes.teaches: In a symmetrical-looking position the most natural developing move and the move that actually equalises are frequently not the same — where a knight would be hit by a knight jumping to b5, a quiet pawn move that takes that square away can be worth more than a tempo of development.

notes.explains: The pawn hits e4, and unlike a bare central strike this one comes with support behind it. White has to make a decision: push past it, hold the tension, or trade. Each leads to a different opening, and Black is comfortable in all three, which is why this defence has a reputation for soundness rather than sharpness.
notes.teaches: A central pawn that arrives already defended asks a question the opponent must answer — compare it to the same pawn arriving loose, and the difference is who gets to choose what happens next.

notes.explains: White takes, which is the most straightforward of the replies and the one that settles the pawn structure at once. The pawn on d5 is attacked and will be recaptured; what matters is that the centre is now symmetrical and the game will be decided by piece placement rather than by a pawn break neither side has made yet.
notes.teaches: Resolving the tension immediately is a choice for a clear structure over a complicated one — it is not passive if the structure it produces has plans in it.

notes.explains: Black takes back with the c-pawn and the structure is settled: mirrored pawns, an open c-file, and no immediate targets. Every viable black setup from here is organised around one piece — the light-squared bishop, which is now hemmed in behind its own pawn on d5 and needs a route out before it is shut in for good.
notes.teaches: After a symmetrical trade, the position is decided by which pieces have good squares — find the piece with the fewest and build the setup around it.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the diagonal toward the black king and the setup that follows is a familiar one — the c-pawn one square, then the other bishop out to f4, a solid formation reminiscent of an entirely different opening. The point for Black is the move order. Bringing the queen's knight out first is what most players do on sight, but the sounder route is the other knight, keeping the option of getting the light-squared bishop out before it is locked in. White's small pawn move to h3 is exactly the move that shuts that route down, and once it is played Black has to switch to a different plan altogether.
notes.teaches: Develop in the order that keeps your worst piece's route open — the natural knight move is not automatically the right one when it costs your problem piece its only good square.

notes.explains: The bishop comes straight out to g5 and pins nothing — it simply attacks the knight on f6 before White has committed the c-pawn. This is one of a family of sidelines that avoid the main theoretical roads entirely, and it has been overtaken in popularity by its quieter cousin, where the bishop takes a safer diagonal and never invites what happens next. The reason is on Black's reply.
notes.teaches: An early bishop sortie that skips the usual second pawn move is a system, not an oversight — meet it on its own terms rather than reaching for the move that answers the main line.

notes.explains: Rather than defending the knight or moving it back, it jumps to e4 and hits the bishop that just came out. This is the standard answer and the one worth learning, though it is not the only good one — players comfortable with the structures after a modest pawn to e6 do well with that instead. White now has to decide where the bishop lives, and the choice is real: there are three defensible squares and they lead to different games.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, look at the squares in FRONT of it before the squares behind — a knight that jumps forward and attacks the attacker turns a threat into a question.

notes.explains: The bishop drops to f4, where it still eyes c7 and holds e5, and this is the main line. The alternatives are worth knowing: stepping back along the same diagonal to h4 keeps the bishop on the board but achieves little, and there is a sharper flank push popularised by English players that is a genuine sideline rather than a mistake. Of the three, this is the one that keeps the bishop useful.
notes.teaches: Between retreats, prefer the one that keeps the piece doing something — a bishop that steps back onto a working diagonal has lost a tempo; one that steps back to safety has lost the piece's purpose too.

notes.explains: Black has propped the centre with the d-pawn before taking, and only now grabs on f4 — the second most popular way to handle the offer. The pawn on f4 is the whole point of the argument from here: Black is a pawn up and White has an open file and a lead in development to show for it.
notes.teaches: You can accept a gambit a move late — slipping in a solid pawn move first costs nothing if the offer will still be there, and it means taking on your terms rather than theirs.

notes.explains: The pawn to g5 props up the one on f4, and it has to: giving the pawn back makes the whole line pointless, because everything Black conceded — the open file, the loosened kingside — was the price of keeping it. It looks careless to push pawns in front of the king like this, and it is the move.
notes.teaches: If you accept a gambit, commit to holding the material — taking a pawn and then handing it straight back leaves you with the worse position and nothing to show for the moves.

notes.explains: The pawn hits g5 and this is the main line and a sacrifice line at once — the knight is being offered. After Black pushes past with the g-pawn there is a jump into g5 that a strong grandmaster has played and that is probably unsound; the real move is to put the knight all the way back to g1. It looks absurd and it is precise: the pawn chain around f4 has been loosened enough that White can afford a move going backwards, because the knight is coming out again at that pawn and Black cannot hold it.
notes.teaches: A retreat to the back rank is not always a lost tempo — when the retreat is what lets you attack the pawn you have been undermining, going backwards is the move that goes forwards.

notes.explains: The pawn on c3 takes d4 in hand, ready to hit the bishop on c5 and shut its diagonal for good, while the quiet bishop development already stands guard in front of the king. The attacking setup across the board has no target left — the counterplay ended before it began.
notes.teaches: The antidote to a piece-activity gambit is not to refute it move by move but to switch off its one dangerous piece — blunt the diagonal into your king's position, and with that bishop talking to nobody the gambiteer is simply a pawn down with pretty pieces.

notes.explains: The queen has gone to a1, the very square the a-pawn promotes on, with the pawn already on a3. The one defensive idea — a rook racing to the back rank to fight for that square — arrives too late at a square that is no longer for sale.
notes.teaches: When a passed pawn nears the end of the board, look at the whole board and ask one question: what can still stop the promotion? The strongest technique is often to seize the promotion square itself with a heavy piece — nothing can contest a square you already occupy, and the pawn walks home behind you.
notes.structural: promotion secured by occupying the queening square with the queen before the pawn asks for it

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Averbakh Variation, Flexible Defense
notes.explains: The bishop lands on g5 pinning the knight on f6 against the queen behind it. The central pawn push this setup exists to play is still legal, and it now runs into the pin rather than into a defence.
notes.teaches: The best developing moves do a second job the opponent notices only when they try their plan — pinning the knight that would support the central break does not forbid the break, it makes it cost a pawn and an ending. Ask of every developing square: which of their ideas does this quietly discourage?

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Sämisch Variation, Bobotsov-Korchnoi-Petrosian Variation
notes.explains: The pawn to f3 does two jobs. It puts a second guard on e4, which the bishop on g7 has been staring at down the long diagonal since it came out, and it prepares to push the g-pawn and roll the kingside pawns at the castled king. The cost is real and permanent: the knight on g1 can no longer come to f3, so it has to take the slower route through e2.
notes.teaches: A modest pawn move that props up the centre is often also the first move of a pawn storm — ask what it enables as well as what it defends, and what square it takes away from your own pieces.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Sämisch Variation, Bobotsov-Korchnoi-Petrosian Variation
notes.explains: Black castles, which is automatic here — every reasonable system against this setup starts the same way. The choice comes next, and there are three: the flank break with the c-pawn two squares, which is the line reckoned objectively best; the queenside expansion with the knight to c6, then the a-pawn, the rook, and the b-pawn; and the old central strike with the e-pawn, which is the traditional way to play this defence and is perfectly viable despite its reputation. White, meanwhile, will develop the dark-squared bishop or bring the knight round to e2, and those two often transpose into one another.
notes.teaches: Castle before choosing a plan when several plans are all playable — the king move is common to all of them, so it costs nothing and buys a move of information about what the opponent commits to.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The bishop steps to d7 in anticipation of a pawn move that has not been played, and it takes d7 away from the knight on b8 at the same time. Nothing has been gained yet and one option has been spent.
notes.teaches: Playing a move because you assume what the opponent will do next is how a piece ends up on a square chosen by a plan that never happens — wait one move, because the same bishop has several futures depending on which setup appears, and this square also blocks the knight that wanted it.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: McDonnell Attack, Tal Gambit
notes.explains: The bishop has been given up for the pawn on f7 and the king has taken. White now brings the knight out to f3, the only developing move with tempo available, covering e5 and g5 and holding the back rank. From here the attack has one piece out and a bishop invested — the material is not coming back unless the defender helps.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice on f7 has dragged your king out and there is no follow-up check, the refutation is development, not evasion — count the attacker's pieces, and if only one is out, every move you spend bringing a piece toward the king is worth more than the pawn you are up.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to g4 onto the knight on f3, which both develops toward the queenside plan and provokes a reply. The other queenside piece follows next move, and the king goes long behind them. A bishop that pins on its way out buys the tempo that makes the plan work.
notes.teaches: Decide which way the king is going BEFORE choosing developing squares, then bring out the pieces on that wing first — castling long is only fast if the queenside is already clear, and each developing move should also ask a question.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Averbakh Variation, Geller Defense
notes.explains: The pawn steps to g5 and attacks the knight on f6 and the pawn on h6 in the same move. One of them must give: the knight retreats or the pawns trade, and either answer opens lines on the side of the board where all the storming pawns already point.
notes.teaches: In a locked centre the pawn storm is the argument, and its best moves hit two things at once — a pawn advance that attacks a piece and a pawn together forces a concession whichever way it is answered, and every trade it causes opens another line toward the king.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Averbakh Variation, Geller Defense
notes.explains: Castling long brings the rook from a1 — the one piece that had no job — into the game while the king steps to safety, and the kingside tension stays exactly as it was: unresolved, on the opponent's clock. Whoever takes first there opens lines for the side that was ready.
notes.teaches: In a tense position with many captures available, two disciplines pay together: let the opponent be the one who takes — you only recapture, keeping every file that opens working for you — and ask which of your pieces is missing in action. The move that signs in the last absent piece usually outranks every capture on the board.
notes.structural: the last absent piece signed in before any capture — tension held so the opener pays for the opening

notes.explains: Two paths diverge here. Capturing on b2 wins a pawn, but the rook then comes to b1 attacking the queen, and at that moment the only black piece off the back rank besides the queen is the fianchettoed bishop. Advancing in the centre with the d-pawn instead keeps the pieces at home for now but leaves nothing loose.
notes.teaches: Taking the pawn on b2 with the queen is a decision about time, not about material — the rook that swings to b1 arrives with a threat and gains the move it would otherwise have spent developing, so the side that grabbed the pawn ends up defending in a position where nothing else is out.

notes.explains: White has given up a bishop to open lines against the uncastled king, and the black queen sits on a2 with almost nothing else developed. Three tries come into consideration: the knight check, castling, and a quiet queen move — the difference between them is whether they hurry the queen along or shut her escape route first.
notes.teaches: When an enemy queen has raided deep into your position, the move that wins is rarely the check that chases her — look instead for the quiet move that removes her last route home. A queen with plenty of squares and no way back is a piece you can hunt at leisure.

notes.explains: White has supported the e4 pawn with the f-pawn rather than a piece, so the centre will not disappear on its own. Four continuations branch from here — capturing on e4, developing the queen to b6, bringing the knight round via h6, and striking with the e-pawn — and they lead to genuinely different games rather than transposing.
notes.teaches: Against a big pawn centre propped up by f3, the choice is between resolving the tension at once and keeping it — releasing it hands the opponent a clear structure to play against; keeping it means accepting a cramped position for a while in exchange for keeping options.

notes.explains: Once a bishop sits on a long diagonal, develop around it. The natural square for the king's knight would block that diagonal for the whole game — so the knight goes to e2 instead, covering d4 and f4 and supporting its partner on c3, with the long diagonal untouched behind it.
notes.teaches: Once a bishop has been placed on a long diagonal, every later developing move is judged by whether it stands in the bishop's way — the natural square for the king's knight blocks that diagonal for the rest of the game; the square beside it does the same central work and leaves the line open.

notes.explains: The other knight takes back on c3, holding the queen behind it and covering d5, b5 and e4, and the queenside pawns stay whole. Either pawn recapture would have doubled them for no return.
notes.teaches: When a bishop takes a knight and two pawns plus a piece can all recapture, the pawn recaptures usually feel forced and the piece recapture is the one that keeps everything — ruin your own structure to open a file deliberately, not by reflex, and when the structure is what your plan needs, take with the piece.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps to f4 and looks straight down at the pawn on c7 while covering e5, the square in the middle that both sides want for a knight. It also holds h2, which matters later once the pawns start moving on that wing. Nothing is committed in the centre yet, and the piece that would have been trapped is already out.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchetto, get the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before you build it — once the modest e-pawn move goes in, that bishop has no way out, so develop it first on the diagonal where it already has a target.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The centre is closed enough that the game will be decided on a wing, and the pawn goes to h4 covering g5. Black must either let it come to h5 or stop it with the h-pawn, and both replies loosen something around the king. Nothing is threatened for several moves; the point is that the shelter is now a little worse whatever happens.
notes.teaches: A rook's pawn pushed at a fianchettoed king is not an attack yet — it is a question the defender has to answer with a pawn move of their own, and whichever answer comes, a pawn in front of the castled king will have moved.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The knight comes to e5 in the centre, where it hits the pawns on c6, f7 and g6 at the same time. It cannot be taken by a pawn and it cannot be chased by one either, so the only way to remove it is a trade — and every trade there opens a line toward the king the pawns have already been loosened around.
notes.teaches: An outpost is worth more the more it touches — before planting a knight in the middle, count the pawns it will hit. A knight attacking three at once cannot simply be ignored, and driving it away usually costs the defender a concession somewhere else.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The pawn goes to f3 and covers e4 and g4, the two squares from which a black knight could come and challenge the outpost. Nothing is attacked and nothing is developed. What has changed is that the knight on e5 now has no way of being asked to leave, so every plan built around it stays available.
notes.teaches: When a knight is doing all the work in the centre, spend a move making sure it cannot be dislodged — a modest pawn move that covers the two squares an enemy knight would jump to is what turns a good square into a permanent one.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The knight has been exchanged and the bishop takes back on e5. From there it hits the knight on f6, which is the piece defending the fianchetto, and it holds the pawn on d4 behind it. The square that was strong for the knight is strong for the bishop as well — and the bishop stares straight at the king.
notes.teaches: When your outpost knight gets traded, recapture with the piece that inherits the square — a bishop that lands on the long diagonal facing a fianchettoed king has taken over the job, and it arrives hitting a piece, so the defender does not get the quiet move the exchange was supposed to win.

notes.opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
notes.explains: The bishop is heading for g7 and the long diagonal. Three continuations come into consideration: developing the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain while it still can get out, mirroring with a fianchetto of your own, or bringing the queen's knight out and leaving the pawns uncommitted for one more move.
notes.teaches: Against a kingside fianchetto the third move decides which structure you are playing for, and all three tries here are sound — the bishop out early claims the dark squares, the fianchetto answers the opponent on their own terms, the knight out keeps the centre pawns free. Pick the structure you know.

notes.explains: The bishop on b7 aims down the long diagonal at the pawn on e4. Putting the bishop on d3 defends that pawn and the one on c2 behind it, so the whole idea of the setup opposite has nothing to work on. The bishop is modestly placed and it is the move that makes the big centre permanent.
notes.teaches: When the opponent fianchettoes on the queenside, their bishop's only target is your centre pawn — develop the bishop that defends it rather than the one that looks more active. A centre that cannot be undermined leaves the fianchettoed bishop staring at a wall for the rest of the game.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5, hitting the knight on f6 and covering d6. The knight has no comfortable square and the pawn now blocks the long diagonal the bishop on b7 was placed for. One move gains space, gains a tempo, and shuts the opponent's best piece out of the game.
notes.teaches: Space gained with tempo is the cheapest kind — when the centre pawn can advance hitting a knight, look at what the pawn covers once it has moved; if it also takes the square that knight would retreat to, the diagonal you were worried about closes at the same time.

notes.explains: Both knights are developed and the g-pawn steps forward to put the bishop on the long diagonal rather than on the usual c4 or b5 square. Nothing is committed yet in the centre: the plan waits to see which setup Black chooses, because the pawn structure Black picks decides where White's pieces belong.
notes.teaches: A fianchetto is unusual in the open game, and that is most of its value at club level: the positions are sound but unfamiliar, so the opponent is out of book while nothing has been risked. It is reachable through more than one move order, which makes it hard to sidestep.
notes.structural: why an unusual-but-sound setup is worth playing at club level

notes.explains: Both sides have developed symmetrically and nothing is resolved. One try takes on the centre at once. The other steps the g-pawn forward so the bishop can take the long diagonal, keeping the centre closed and asking the opponent to think rather than recite.
notes.teaches: With four knights out and the centre untouched, the fourth move picks the whole character of the game — the central push opens lines and heads for the studied positions; the fianchetto is unusual in an open game, and that is most of its value at club level: sound, and unfamiliar to the person opposite.

notes.explains: The pawn to c5 hits d4 and asks it to make up its mind.
