Trading gives Black comfortable play, holding the tension is playable, and pushing past is the critical answer — and each of the three is a different opening. Black is choosing a fight over the centre rather than an occupation of it.
notes.teaches: Hitting a central pawn with a wing pawn invites it to advance past you — that is the trade: you concede space in return for a target you can chew on for the rest of the game.

notes.explains: The pawn goes past to d5, taking c6 and e6 — the two squares Black's knight and light-squared bishop would most like. This is the critical continuation. Black now has a real choice about how to undermine that pawn, and one of those choices is to offer a pawn on the queenside to open lines against it.
notes.teaches: Advancing a central pawn past its neighbour buys squares and costs flexibility — it is right when the squares it takes are the ones the opponent's pieces need.

notes.explains: The pawn to b5 hits c4 and offers itself. The point is not the pawn: taking it opens the a- and b-files, and Black's rooks and the bishop on the long diagonal will press down them for the rest of the game — often long into an endgame, and often a pawn down without minding. Taking is what the books recommend and is entirely topical. There is also an old and little-known knight retreat to d2, which meets the capture on c4 by striking in the centre instead — almost reversing the gambit, offering a pawn back, and regaining it. It has teeth precisely because nobody has seen it.
notes.teaches: When a gambit offers a pawn to open two files, taking it is not automatically the test — a rare declining move that hands the pawn straight back on your own terms can leave the gambiteer with nothing to show for the structure.

notes.explains: The pawn's capture on c5 has cleared the d-file from top to bottom: the queen on d5 now looks straight down at the queen on d1 with nothing between them. The pawn can be regained at leisure — the open file and the exposed first rank are the real change on the board.
notes.teaches: When the centre pawn finally captures, look down the file it just left — the capture that wins a pawn can open the line your queen was already standing on, and a file opened onto their back rank matters more than the pawn that opened it.

notes.explains: The queen checks from a5 down the open diagonal to the king on e1. There is no comfortable answer: blocking invites the queen trade, and the recapture pulls the king into the middle of the board with pieces still on. Every later idea gains a move against a king that has to watch its step.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is still in the centre, a queen check that can only be answered by a block is a lever — the block invites the trade, and the recapture drags the king to a working square of your choosing, so the endgame starts with their king already misplaced.

notes.explains: The pawn takes the second central square and holds e5. Black has deliberately not put a pawn alongside it, which is the whole design of this defence: concede the middle, develop behind it, and then undermine it from a distance. White gets the space and the obligation that comes with it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent declines to contest the centre with pawns, take it — and understand you are being invited. The space is real; so is the fact that it will be shot at.

notes.explains: The knight came out first and only now does the pawn step to g6, taking f5 and preparing the bishop's home on the long diagonal. That order is what makes this the defence it is. Its close cousin plays the flank pawn on move one instead and often puts off the knight entirely, going for a queenside pawn advance first — the two transpose constantly, and the move the opponent is withholding tells you which one you are really in.
notes.teaches: Two defences can reach the same position and still be different openings, because the difference is which moves they DELAY — watch what the opponent has not played yet.

notes.explains: The f-pawn joins the centre and White now has three abreast, holding e5 twice over. For several decades this has been regarded as the most principled way to fight for an advantage here — not necessarily the strongest move, but the most aggressive one, and it carries an enormous amount of theory behind it. The pawns look overwhelming and that is exactly what Black is playing against.
notes.teaches: The most principled try and the objectively best move are not always the same move — choose the aggressive one for what it demands of the opponent, and know you are choosing a theory load.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the long diagonal and, for the moment, holds its own knight on f6 rather than hitting anything. That is the point: the pressure down the diagonal only becomes real once the knight steps aside, and Black will look to arrange that at a moment when it costs White something. Everything in this structure runs on that delayed threat.
notes.teaches: A fianchettoed bishop aimed at the centre is not yet attacking it if a piece of your own stands in the way — the plan is to move the blocker with tempo, and until then the pressure is potential, not real.

notes.explains: Instead of shoring up the queenside knight, the other knight comes out and hits e4. This is the high-level answer to the bishop, and it has a reputation for steering toward simplified positions early. That reputation is only half deserved — the endgames it produces are far from lifeless, and White has several genuinely different ways to meet it rather than heading for them.
notes.teaches: When the opponent puts pressure on your position, look for a developing move that ignores it and creates pressure of its own — counter-attack in the centre usually beats a defensive shuffle.

notes.explains: White tucks the king away rather than propping up the attacked pawn. Taking it is entirely playable for Black — this is the main road — but it hands White the initiative and a series of tempo moves against the knight that grabs it. The alternative is a quieter one-square pawn move by Black, which is passive but a perfectly legitimate old defence rather than a mistake.
notes.teaches: Offering a pawn you can regain is a way of asking the opponent to commit — castling instead of defending is the move when the capture costs them time and leaves you a lead in development.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The bishop steps to e3 backing up the knight on d4, so the pressure down the diagonal has nothing to win. Both sides now have a bishop staring at a defended piece, which is a standoff the better-developed side is happy with.
notes.teaches: When a bishop comes out to stare at the knight sitting in the middle, the answer is to reinforce that knight rather than to move it — a defended centre piece cannot be traded profitably, and the defending bishop lands on a square where it will be useful for the rest of the game anyway.

notes.explains: The knight develops to c6 and takes the d4 square in hand, and with the bishop already pinning the defender on f3, the jump into d4 is a real threat the opponent has to answer at once. The developing move set the agenda.
notes.teaches: The best developing move is the one that arrives carrying a threat — a knight that comes out eyeing the central jump forces your opponent to spend their next move on your plans instead of their own.

notes.explains: The knight swings to h5 and takes both f4 and g3 in hand — the two dark squares the doubled pawns no longer guard. The factory starts running on the side of the board where the opponent's king lives, one hop ahead of their regrouping.
notes.teaches: When the pawn cover in front of their king has been damaged, do not wait — get the wheels turning on that wing before they reorganise. A knight hopping toward the weakened squares stakes the claim, and every piece that follows finds the squares already prepared.

notes.explains: One passed pawn stands on d3 and another on h3, a whole board apart, and the enemy king on one side cannot reach the other in time. The plan is the pawns' own legs — each step by one forces the king to abandon the other.
notes.teaches: Two passed pawns on opposite sides of the board beat a lone king even when neither pawn has support — the king cannot stand in two doorways at once. Count the squares before agreeing to any trade that leaves this race: if the pawns are far enough apart, the position that looks thin is simply winning.
notes.structural: two distant passers against a king judged by counting, not hope — the king cannot hold both doorways

notes.opening: Grünfeld Defense: Exchange Variation, Nadanian Attack
notes.explains: The knight has stepped to a4 and the capture on c3 is off the table — the centralised knight has nothing to take and no favourable trade to anchor its plans on. The pawn can come to e4 next with the centre intact, which is exactly the picture this defence exists to prevent.
notes.teaches: This defence's whole machine runs on one trade: the knight takes on c3, the pawn chain forms, and the c-pawn's strike attacks it — deny the trade and the machine has no fuel, so a knight move to the rim that disallows the capture forces a different game entirely.

notes.opening: Grünfeld Defense: Exchange Variation, Nadanian Attack
notes.explains: The king steps to c1 out of the check, and in doing so it defends the pawn on b2 — the pawn a blocking piece would have abandoned to a capture with check. Nothing hangs, the extra material stays, and the attack has run out of forcing moves.
notes.teaches: When a check can be met by blocking or by a king step, count what each answer leaves loose before choosing — a block that abandons a pawn with check is not a developing move, it is a blunder in stages, and the quiet king step that keeps everything defended is precise, not passive.

notes.explains: Pushing to e5 is a little trick: White wants to drag you into a locked chain with the e-pawn shoved past, on their terms. Don't be sucked in — we will happily play that structure, but a better version of it, with the light-squared bishop developed outside the chain first.
notes.teaches: Recognise when a move is trying to move-order you — to steer the game into a structure you don't play by transposition. The counter is not to panic into their version but to reach a better version of it on your own terms.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to g4, pinning the knight on f3 to the queen and leaning on the e5-pawn that knight is defending. This is the whole point: the bishop is already outside the chain, and it is the most testing version of the structure — a favourable one, not the cramped one White wanted.
notes.teaches: If you are handed a structure you would normally avoid, take its most active version — pinning the piece that defends the opponent's advanced pawn puts that pawn under immediate pressure and poses the sharpest question.

notes.explains: The queen goes to c7, and it is quietly doing three jobs: it leans on the e5-pawn down the diagonal, it sits far enough back to dodge any tempo-hit, and it prepares e6. It also lines up a clean recapture on c6 if the bishop trades itself off — one square, plenty of work.
notes.teaches: When placing your queen, choose the square that does the most jobs at the least risk — one that eyes the key pawn, stays clear of tempo-gaining attacks, and prepares your next move beats a more forward but exposed post.

notes.explains: And here is why the queen went to c7: when White trades on c6, the queen takes back, not a pawn. The structure stays clean and healthy, and Black comes out of the swap solid and comfortable with nothing to fix.
notes.teaches: A queen move can be quiet preparation for a trade you already see coming — positioning it so the queen, not a pawn, recaptures keeps your structure intact when the opponent swaps on your knight.

notes.explains: There are tactics to dig into here — but you don't have to. Black plays the simple e6, reaching a comfortable, solid structure with the bishop already outside the chain. It is a judgment call made on understanding, not on a long calculation, and it is plenty good.
notes.teaches: Not every position demands deep calculation — when a tactical try and a calm move both work, sound structural understanding lets you play the calm one on judgment and save your clock.

notes.explains: The knight develops to e7 — a modest-looking hop, but it is on its way to f5 where it will press the centre, and it clears the path for the dark-squared bishop too. The plan is the journey, not the square it starts on.
notes.teaches: Develop a knight toward its best future square even when the first hop looks modest — in these locked structures the knight's journey to the strong central-edge post is standard, and the destination justifies the detour.

notes.explains: And there it lands — the knight to f5, pressing the pawn on d4 and gripping the dark squares. With the bishop outside the chain and the knight on its dream square, it is Black who is a shade better now and setting the agenda. The one White tried to cramp is doing the pressing.
notes.teaches: The thematic knight jump to the fifth rank turns a solid, cramped structure into an edge — landing on the square that hits the base of the enemy centre is how the defender becomes the side doing the pressing.

notes.explains: The pawn on h3 covers g4, so the bishop's arrival there now runs into a defended square — it can still come, but it gets asked the question immediately and on your terms. With that settled, castling short is safe and the plans with the pawns can begin.
notes.teaches: In quiet openings the annoying pin against your king's knight is half your opponent's plan, and the rook-pawn's one-square step is the standing answer — play it before castling short, so the bishop's visit costs a tempo instead of creating a nagging problem.

notes.explains: The pawn on h6 attacks the knight on g5. The square c6 is empty, so the capture on d5 hit nothing and gained no time. The knight on g5 must retreat, and a full move is gone from the raid.
notes.teaches: A famous attacking pattern is a set of conditions, not a move to copy — the knight's raid works in its home position because a specific piece stands on a specific square, and removing that piece makes the same raid lose a tempo at every step.

notes.explains: You could grab space in the centre now — but Black castles instead and keeps the real weapon in hand. The moment White plays c3, the central break comes as a pawn sacrifice for a fierce attack. King safety first, the sacrifice second, and only when White has walked into it.
notes.teaches: The point of a system can be a pawn sacrifice you have not made yet — get castled and ready, and hold the freeing break in reserve until the opponent commits to the setup that invites it.

notes.explains: Rather than play the move that invites the whole prepared attack, White plays a4, leaning on the b5-pawn and steering clear of the memorised lines. It refuses the theory fight and hands the question back to Black — the most testing modern way to duck the system.
notes.teaches: When you fear an opponent's deep preparation, sidestep it rather than walk in — a quiet flank thrust that leans on their pawn chain avoids the memorised attack and asks a fresh question.

notes.explains: You could sit and defend the b-pawn — but pushing it to b4 is cleaner. It takes the tension away and clears the path to swing the rook off the a-file to b8 and fianchetto the bishop to b7. The chain stays whole and every piece gets active.
notes.teaches: When a flank pawn pokes your chain, advancing past it is often cleaner than defending it — pushing keeps the tension off and frees your pieces to develop behind the pawn.

notes.explains: White strikes with d4 instead of the usual quiet c3. The reflex is to snap it off — but that would be the mistake: taking on d4 lets White shove the e-pawn forward with tempo. Black should hold the centre together rather than grab.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break can test the opponent more sharply than the routine supporting move — but do not capture on reflex; opening the centre for the opponent can cost more than the pawn is worth.

notes.explains: So instead of grabbing, the pawn to d6 defends the e5-pawn and holds the centre together. It is the quiet, accurate reply — no tension released, no space handed over, and Black stands perfectly fine.
notes.teaches: When your centre pawn is attacked and capturing is unsafe, support it — the modest defensive pawn move keeps the structure intact and refuses the opponent the space grab a careless capture would hand them.

notes.explains: The pawn to a6 takes b5 in hand, which is the square the queenside advance needs after a capture in the centre. Nothing is threatened yet, and the capture is now supported before it happens.
notes.teaches: A rook's-pawn move in a quiet opening is rarely aimless — read it as the announcement of a two-move plan. It usually prepares to take a pawn and HOLD it with the advance behind it, and knowing that one move early lets you defend the pawn before it is grabbed rather than chase it afterwards.

notes.explains: The knight arriving on f6 hits the pawn on e4, so the choice is not between developing and attacking — the move does both. That matters most against a set-up that has not committed its centre yet, because the question has to be answered before anything else gets built.
notes.teaches: Given two developing moves, prefer the one that asks a question — a piece that comes out attacking something forces a reply, so you get the tempo to finish developing instead of spending it answering.

notes.explains: Pushing the pawn to e5 hits the knight, and the two pawns covering f6 do not rescue it: taking on f6 would win a piece for a pawn and the recapture only gets the pawn back. So the knight cannot simply sit there, which is exactly what the push is asking. The answer has to be a move that creates a threat of its own rather than a quiet retreat.
notes.teaches: When a pawn attacks a piece, counting defenders is the wrong calculation — the pawn is worth less than anything it hits, so the trade is good for the attacker no matter how many times the square is guarded. The piece has to move, or find a bigger answer elsewhere.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The bishop on g5 attacks the knight on f6 and pins it against the queen behind it. The knight can neither move nor be comfortably unpinned, so the kingside squares it was guarding are already half-abandoned while the attack is still choosing its plan.
notes.teaches: After the centre opens, the enemy king's knight is the piece holding the position together, and the bishop's pin against the queen freezes it — every attacking idea that follows gains a move because the defender's best piece is spoken for.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The king tucks into the corner, off the diagonal that runs through the centre toward g1 — the line the enemy bishop would love once the pawns advance and the position opens. The attacking setup continues next move, now without a single tactical string attached to it.
notes.teaches: Before committing to the pawn storm, spend one move stepping the king off the diagonal your opponent's pieces want — prophylaxis is cheapest when nothing is happening yet, because the check or the hit that would have interrupted your attack at its critical moment simply never exists.
notes.structural: the king stepped off the working diagonal before the storm — prophylaxis paid while it costs nothing

notes.explains: The bishop returns to its original square after the trade it came out for was declined, guarding the base pawn on e6 exactly as it did before it left. Two moves have gone into a piece that is now where it began, while the other side developed both times.
notes.teaches: A piece that goes out, is asked a question, and comes home has spent two moves to arrive where it started — that is the real cost of an early sortie, paid in a currency that cannot be earned back. Count the moves, not the squares, when deciding whether a plan is worth starting.

notes.explains: The knight has come to c6 hitting the queen, and instead of retreating she steps sideways to a4, where she hits that same knight back and eyes the pawn on a7. She also holds the pawns on c2 and e4 from there. The move that was supposed to gain time has instead put the knight on a square where it is the piece being asked questions.
notes.teaches: Bringing the queen out early is only bad when she has to move again — look for the square where the move that chases her has already been made, and from there she is out, doing something, with no tempo left for the opponent to win.

notes.explains: The pawn goes to c3 covering b4 and d4, which are the two squares a bishop or knight would use to come at the queen with tempo. It also blunts the fianchettoed bishop's diagonal. Nothing is developed by the move and the position becomes much harder to play against, because the loose piece stops being loose.
notes.teaches: When your queen is out and slightly exposed, the pawn move that covers the squares an enemy piece would use to attack her is worth more than another developing move — count where the attack could come from, then take those squares away. A queen nobody can hit is simply a developed piece.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to f4 covering the dark squares in the middle. Black can step the knight back and invite the bishop to return, or castle and get on with the game. Both are playable and they lead to completely different results, so this is the moment to know which one you want.
notes.teaches: When a bishop lands on a square the opponent can challenge by shuffling a knight, the position is offering a repetition — taking it is a legitimate result and refusing it is a decision, but decide, rather than drifting into the same squares three times without noticing what you agreed to.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The queen took back in the centre and now the pawn takes the square it was standing over, hitting c5 on the way. White has the ideal setup — a broad centre backed by the pawn on c3 — and has not spent a move that was not also useful. Recapturing with the queen is not careless: the chase is short and Black develops during it. This exact position has been reached thousands of times and is deep theory on both sides.
notes.teaches: When the enemy queen sits on a square your pawn wants, take the square — a developing move that also gains time on the queen is the cheapest tempo in the opening.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight comes out to f6, the main move by a distance. It contests e4, it takes part in the fight for the centre, and it prepares to castle so the queen is not the only thing keeping the position together. Everything up to here is theory; the branching starts one move from now.
notes.teaches: When the queen is exposed, develop a piece that shares its duties — the knight that covers the squares the queen is standing on is worth more than the knight that only looks active.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight comes to f3, adding a guard to d4 as it develops. This is where Black stands at a real crossroads — four different moves here are all worth serious attention, and they lead to genuinely different games rather than transpositions of one another.
notes.teaches: With a broad centre, develop the pieces that hold it — a knight that both comes out and defends the pawn it stands behind never has to be recalled.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The pawn steps to e6, which looks like the least ambitious move on the board and is not. The intuitive alternative, bringing the queen's knight out, leaves the dark-squared bishop shut in with nothing to do; this clears its diagonal instead. Developing the light-squared bishop outside the chain is the other serious try. White's answer is the knight round to a3, heading for b5 where it hits c7 and forks the king and rook if allowed, so Black spends a move guarding that square — the queen stepping home or the other knight coming to a6.
notes.teaches: Between two developing moves, prefer the one that unlocks a piece with no other route — the natural knight move is worse than it looks when it leaves a bishop behind its own pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop takes on c3, removing the knight that was contesting the centre and leaving the recapture to damage the queenside pawns. The advance that would claim the middle now has one fewer supporter, and the doubled pawns left behind cannot help with it either.
notes.teaches: Giving up the bishop pair is a price, not a mistake, when what you buy is a permanent say over one central square — the knight being traded is a defender of that square, and once it is gone the pawn advance the whole opening is built on becomes hard to arrange.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to g4 with the kings castled on opposite sides, taking f5 and h5 in hand, and the next step of the same pawn asks the knight on f6 to leave. That knight is the kingside's gatekeeper — everything the storm wants to do afterwards begins with making it move.
notes.teaches: With the kings on opposite wings, the pawn storm is not a mood — it has two precise jobs: it pries open files for the rooks, and before that it evicts the knight in front of the castled king, the gatekeeper whose departure makes every later sacrifice work. Aim the pawns at that knight first.

notes.explains: Castling long against a short-castled king splits the board into two attacking zones: the pawns in front of each king are free to charge, because they shelter nobody on their own side. The position stops being about equality and starts being about speed.
notes.teaches: When you need to unbalance a position — because the material or the position says a draw is a loss — the simplest formula is to castle the opposite side from your opponent: both sides get pawn storms that do not weaken their own king, and the better attacker wins rather than the better memoriser.
notes.structural: opposite-side castling chosen deliberately to turn the game into a race both sides must run

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Smith-Morra Declined
notes.explains: The queen has to choose a square, and the pawn on b2 is hanging. It can be left: the knight that takes it is out of play, and the attack continues with the knight coming to g5 regardless. What matters far more is the pawn on e5, which is the reason the bishop on g7 has nothing to look at — the queen belongs where it keeps that pawn and the attacking pieces together.
notes.teaches: When you are attacking, sort your pawns by what they are doing rather than by whether they can be taken — a pawn that shuts an enemy piece out of the game is part of the attack and must not be traded away, while a pawn on the far side that no piece is using can simply be allowed to fall.

notes.explains: The pawn to e6 declines the offer and props up the centre with a pawn rather than a piece. It is the soundest way to meet the gambit and the one to learn first, because the structures it produces turn up across half the queen's-pawn openings. The price is immediate and permanent: the bishop on c8, which a moment ago had five squares, now has none. Every plan from here is partly about getting it out.
notes.teaches: A defence worth learning first is one whose ideas transfer everywhere else — accept its single structural cost knowingly, because solving that problem IS the opening.

notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 and joins the c-pawn in pressing on d5. Nothing is threatened yet — d5 is defended — but the count on that square is what the next several moves are about, and White is building it first.
notes.teaches: Develop toward the square the pawns are arguing over — a knight that adds an attacker to the contested centre square makes every later trade there happen on your terms.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to g5 and pins the knight on f6 against the queen. That knight is one of the defenders of d5, so the pin is really another attacker on the centre — the count has shifted without a single capture. Black has to answer this before getting on with development.
notes.teaches: A pin on a defender is worth more than an attack on the thing defended — pin first, then increase the pressure on what the pinned piece was holding.

notes.explains: The knight to d7 adds a defender to f6 and appears to leave the centre pawn hanging. It is one of the oldest traps in the game and people still walk into it: take twice in the middle and the knight on f6 falls with the pin — except it does not, because taking the knight lets Black take back and, when the queen is snapped off, a bishop check on b4 forces the only legal reply and wins the piece straight back. Black ends a knight for a pawn ahead. The sound move is the modest pawn to e3, which unpins nothing and threatens nothing and is simply correct.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing what looks like a free pawn, ask why it was offered — a capture that opens a line toward YOUR uncastled king is the shape of a trap, not a windfall.

notes.explains: The bishop stepped in to break the pin and the king is now tucked away — both moves Black wants in every version of this position, so neither needed a decision. What does need one is the light-squared bishop still sitting behind the pawn on e6. There are several respectable ways to solve it, including simply making a home for it on the long diagonal, and that choice is what separates the systems here.
notes.teaches: Order the opening moves by which ones you would play in every plan — break the pin and get the king safe first; the piece you genuinely have to think about can wait.

notes.explains: The rook slides to c1 on a file that is still closed — and closed by its own knight on c3, so nothing is attacked and nothing is defended yet. That is the point. The c-pawn will eventually be captured or pushed and the knight will eventually move, and when they do the rook is already sitting on the file looking at whatever Black has left there. A standard preparatory move that costs nothing and asks nothing.
notes.teaches: Put a rook on the file you expect to open, even when your own pieces still block it — the move is not measured by what it attacks today but by what it will see when the file clears.

notes.explains: The bishop has taken on f6, which is the whole point of putting it on g5. Both recaptures are legal. Taking with the e-pawn keeps the pawns tidy but leaves the queen's bishop staring at its own pawn. Taking with the g-pawn doubles them on f7 and f6, opens the g-file, and leaves Black with the pair of bishops, since White has just given the dark-squared one away.
notes.teaches: When a bishop takes your knight, the recapture is a choice about what you want the position to look like for the next thirty moves, not a reflex — taking with the g-pawn accepts doubled pawns and looks ugly, and in return opens a file, keeps both bishops on open diagonals and leaves the e-pawn free. Doubled pawns that are not weak are simply pawns.

notes.explains: White has closed the position in with the modest e-pawn, and Black's doubled f-pawns are not going anywhere. That makes the c-pawn advance the move the position wants: it strikes at the base of White's centre while the two bishops still have open diagonals to work along.
notes.teaches: A pawn structure tells you which break to look for before any calculation begins — with a solid centre pawn and no dark-squared bishop opposing you, the lever against the queenside is the one that opens lines for the pieces you kept. Read the structure, then find the move it asks for.
notes.structural: reads the structure to find the break; one move, so no fork

notes.explains: Black has hit the bishop with the knight and White, instead of retreating it, has pushed the h-pawn. Nothing is hanging and nothing is forced; the position is double-edged and both sides still have everything to play for. Advancing the d-pawn to stake out the centre is the natural, unhurried reply.
notes.teaches: An early rook's-pawn thrust is unsettling rather than refuting — meet it by asking what it actually does (usually it defends the bishop's retreat square or prepares to open a file) instead of treating strangeness as danger. Being surprised is not the same as being worse.

notes.explains: The bishop steps into d5, hitting the rook in the corner on a8 and the pawn on f7 on the same move. The pawn that just advanced is what cleared the diagonal, and nothing covers d5 any more.
notes.teaches: Before advancing a pawn on the wing, check every long diagonal that already points into your position — a pawn move that chases a knight is worthless if the square it vacates lets a bishop through to two targets at once.

notes.explains: The bishop collects the rook in the corner. Counting up, the side that spent its moves on the queenside pawns is now the exchange and a pawn down with most of its army still on the back rank.
notes.teaches: In a tactical flurry the side with more pieces out usually comes out ahead, and that is not luck — it is arithmetic: every extra developed piece is another defender, another attacker, another resource in the calculation.

notes.explains: Taking on e6 hits the bishop that the check forced onto d7 and the pawn on f7 together. The bishop is standing where it cannot help, so nothing recaptures on comfortable terms.
notes.teaches: When a piece has been forced onto a square by a check, look at what it stopped guarding before assuming the position is balanced — a blocker interposed under duress often stands in front of the very pawn it used to defend, and the capture that looks like it invites a recapture is simply a free pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop is heading for g7 and wants the long diagonal opened. Two tries come into consideration: resolve the centre now, or hold the clamp with the modest pawn move and make the opponent find a way in. Neither is a mistake; they are different bargains, and the closed version is quieter and much harder to play against.
notes.teaches: With pawns already on c4 and e4 there are two honest plans, and they lead to different games — pushing the d-pawn two squares opens the centre and hands the fianchettoed bishop its long diagonal; playing it one square keeps everything closed and leaves that bishop biting on granite.

notes.explains: The pawn goes only to d3, where it defends the pawns on c4 and e4 at the same time. Both of those are the clamp — between them they cover the squares in the middle that the opponent's pieces want. Nothing has been grabbed and nothing can be attacked, which is exactly the point.
notes.teaches: A pawn advanced one square instead of two can be the move that makes a whole structure work — judge it by what it holds rather than by the ground it takes, because a single pawn propping up both wings of your centre means neither can be undermined, and a clamp that cannot be broken is worth more than space you have to defend.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3, hitting the pawn on c5 and covering d4. That square in the middle is the one the fianchettoed bishop is aimed at through the whole game, and it is now held by a piece that cannot easily be driven away. The centre stays closed and the dark squares stop being available.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has fianchettoed, the fight is for the dark squares that bishop wants to use — develop the bishop that contests them, and prefer the square where it both holds the central outpost and asks a question of a pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop has been exchanged on f3 and the other bishop takes back. From f3 it holds the pawn on e4, which is half the clamp, and covers g2 and the queen behind it. The knight that guarded those squares is gone and nothing has been loosened, so the trade costs nothing in a position that will not open.
notes.teaches: Giving up a knight for a bishop is not automatically a concession when the position is closed — what matters is whether the recapturing piece takes over the jobs the knight was doing.

notes.explains: The knight has come to e7 and the bishop steps to g5, looking at it with the queen standing behind on d8. The knight still has four legal squares and every one of them loses the queen, so in practice it cannot move at all. The bishop covers f6 and h6 from the same square, which are the squares in front of the fianchetto — so the piece is doing the pinning and the restraining together.
notes.teaches: A piece is pinned in the way that matters whenever every square it can legally reach costs you something behind it — do not look only for pins against the king; a bishop dropped on the diagonal in front of the queen fixes the piece in between just as firmly.

notes.explains: The pawn on a6 attacks the knight on b5, and the pawn move a moment ago took c3 away as its retreat — the knight's comfortable road home is gone, and its remaining choices either misplace it or wreck the pawns around it. One little pawn move, played at exactly the right time.
notes.teaches: Timing in the opening is often about a square that just disappeared — the moment a pawn move takes away a piece's retreat square, the move that attacks that piece is promoted from routine to urgent.

notes.explains: The queen has recaptured on d4 and stands in the middle of the board, centralised by the trade her opponent initiated. The sequence was invited, not avoided: each capture pulled a defender away and the recapture was the developing move.
notes.teaches: Trading on your own terms means arranging that your opponent is the one who captures first, so every recapture improves your pieces instead of theirs — the material stays level; the activity does not.
notes.structural: a level trade sequence steered so every recapture activates the recapturing side

notes.explains: The knight has been placed on c6 rather than behind the c-pawn, and the pawn advances to d5 hitting it and the pawn on e6 at the same time. The knight has to jump somewhere awkward or the centre gets opened on terms the developed side chooses. This is the cost of that knight placement, and it arrives the moment the centre is ready.
notes.teaches: When a knight is developed in front of its own c-pawn, the centre push arrives hitting the knight and a pawn together — before advancing, check whether the defender can answer both, because if one reply saves the knight and a different one saves the pawn, the push wins something whatever they choose.

notes.opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
notes.explains: The bishop develops to d3 and attacks the pawn on h7 down a completely open diagonal — the advanced e-pawn stands out of its way on e5, not in it. The chain is propped by the c-pawn behind it, and every piece is on the square the setup always gives it.
notes.teaches: This setup's pieces have standard posts, and the light-squared bishop's is the diagonal aimed at the enemy king's home — take it before the king castles into it. The modest knight development earlier is what makes the whole scheme work.

notes.opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
notes.explains: The pawn goes to a4 and takes b5 away, so the queenside pawns opposite have no lever to advance with — their storm needs that square and it is gone. The kingside plans can now be prepared without a clock ticking on the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: When your play is on one wing, spend a single pawn move to freeze the other — the rook-pawn's advance takes away the square the enemy pawns need to start rolling, and the counterplay that would have arrived in five moves never arrives at all.

notes.explains: With the pawns locked on d5 and e5, the white centre rests on d4, and the pawn arriving on c5 hits exactly that square. The head of the chain on e5 cannot be attacked profitably while it is defended from behind, so play goes after the pawn holding it up instead.
notes.teaches: A pawn chain is attacked at its base, not at its head — the front pawn is defended by the one behind it, so hitting the rear pawn is the move that asks a real question. Take the base away and everything in front of it is loose.

notes.explains: Before this the base on d4 was held only by the queen, which is a defender you would rather not commit so early. The modest pawn move gives d4 a second guard that nothing can harass, so the centre holds and the pieces stay free to develop where they want to go.
notes.teaches: When the base of your chain is attacked, add a pawn defender before you add a piece one — a pawn holds the square without being driven off, while a piece tied to defence has to keep standing there and can be chased.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight on b5 threatens to jump into c7, forking the king and the rook in the corner, so the square has to be covered. Bringing the bishop to d6 does cover it, and looks natural because it develops at the same time — but the bishop on c4 then hits the queen on d5 and White gains the move. The knight to a6 covers c7 just as well and asks nothing of the queen.
notes.teaches: When a knight arrives on b5 and eyes c7, that square wants a knight to guard it rather than a bishop — the question is not simply whether a move defends, but whether the defender then becomes a target itself.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The knight has stepped to a3 and is heading for c4, where it would press on b6 and d6. Three replies deal with it: a pawn to a6 preparing to gain space on the queenside, releasing the tension in the centre at once, and developing the queen's knight. The first keeps the most options, because once the white knight reaches c4 the queen's knight comes to d7 to cover b6 while developing, and the b-pawn then evicts the knight and opens the long diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: A knight travelling to the edge is usually going somewhere better, and the reply that keeps most in hand is one that guards the squares it wants while a piece comes into play — answer a manoeuvre with a manoeuvre; answer it with pawn moves alone and your pieces stay home.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The queen can win the pawn on g2 from here, but the bishop then comes to f3 and every white piece arrives with a threat while the queen looks for somewhere to stand. Advancing the e-pawn instead offers the queen trade and keeps everything sound, leaving White only a small pull.
notes.teaches: The pawn on g2 is the most expensive free pawn in the opening — taking it drags the queen to the edge of the board and away from everything she was doing, and the bill arrives as lost time rather than lost material.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: Two checks are available and only one works. The bishop check on b5 is the eye-catching one, and it is met by interposing the knight on c6. Taking on f7 instead forces the king out, and after the recapture the knight springs to g5 with check: the king has three squares, and the queen on e4 is undefended after every one of them.
notes.teaches: With the enemy queen sitting in the centre and the king still on its starting square, look for the check that wins the queen after the king moves — not the one that looks most like mate. The showy check is usually the one that can simply be blocked; the blunt capture is the one that sets up the fork.

notes.explains: The bishop develops to c4 and defends the pawn on d5 — the extra pawn the whole line revolves around. As long as it stands there, the opponent's pieces are tied to regaining it, which means every developing move that holds it is a move that also cramps them.
notes.teaches: In the structures that come from this pawn grab, the question is always the square in front of the queen's pawn — the shortest way to judge these positions is to ask who controls that square. Hold what you have won with pieces, not more pawn moves, and make the opponent prove the pawn comes back.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Exchange Variation, Gligoric Variation
notes.explains: Taking with the d-pawn doubles the c-pawns and clears the d-file in front of the queen, with d5 and b5 both covered by the new pawn. The bishop pair is gone, and in return every piece has somewhere to go.
notes.teaches: When a capture can be answered by either pawn, the doubled pawn is not the deciding factor — the file is. Taking toward the centre opens a line for the queen and the rook behind it, and that open file is what makes the damaged structure playable. Structure is a means; activity is the end.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Exchange Variation, Gligoric Variation
notes.explains: The pawn to f6 defends the pawn on e5, which was the only thing hanging. The knight this move would normally block no longer exists, so nothing is being shut in, and the move that holds your centre for free is simply the best one.
notes.teaches: "Never block your own knight with the f-pawn" is a good rule and it is a rule, not a law — it holds because the move usually costs development and weakens the king, and where the knight has already been traded off and the king has a safe square anyway, both reasons are gone.

notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 and attacks the pawn on e4, which nothing guards. So the pawn returns and the position that remains is the point of the whole idea: lines are open, development is ahead, and the side that grabbed the pawn has spent two moves on it. Declining to hurry the recapture is also possible, because the pawn is not going anywhere.
notes.teaches: A gambit is only a real sacrifice if the pawn cannot be recovered — check whether the captured pawn has a defender before treating the material as won. A pawn sitting undefended on an open file is a loan, not a gift.

notes.explains: The bishop arriving on c4 joins the knight in hitting f7, and the only piece covering that square is the king. That is the arithmetic the opening has been working towards since the f-pawn left, and it arrives while the defending side still has pieces on their starting squares.
notes.teaches: Count attackers and defenders on the weak square before calculating anything concrete — when a square next to the king is hit twice and guarded only by the king itself, the tactics are usually already there.

notes.explains: The pawn to d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4 together. The bishop's diagonal is now a wall of its own making, and it has to retreat before anything else happens.
notes.teaches: A bishop developed early to the square that eyes f7 is committed before it knows what the centre will look like — the answer is the central pawn break played with TEMPO: it hits the bishop and the centre pawn in one move, so the piece that came out first is the piece that has to move twice.

notes.explains: The pawn to e3 props up the pawn on d4 and covers the square behind the bishop on f4. Nothing is committed, and the setup is now the same against every reply the position allows.
notes.teaches: A system opening earns its keep by having one setup that answers several replies — get the bishop outside the pawn chain FIRST, then close the box behind it, so whichever of the three or four standard replies appears, the same structure meets it.

notes.explains: The pawn to d3 supports the e4-pawn and completes the modest central footing this system is built on, and it can come before or after castling with no real difference. The pieces arrive at the same harmonious picture whichever route you take.
notes.teaches: In a quiet fianchetto setup the exact move order rarely matters, and that is a freedom worth using — when the same handful of moves can be played in almost any sequence, choose the order that keeps the most options open and commits to nothing the opponent can pounce on. Learn the setup as a picture to reach, not a march to memorize.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b5 and attacks the knight on c6, and that knight is the piece holding the pawn in the middle. The long diagonal from the other bishop is already trained on the same pawn from behind.
notes.teaches: An opening that concedes the centre wins it back by PRESSURE, and pressure is applied to the defenders, not to the pawn itself — find the piece holding the enemy centre together and put a question to that piece, and the pawn you are really after starts falling the moment its guard has to move.

notes.explains: The pawn to f4 hits the pawn on e5 head-on and covers g5. The knight move that looks equally natural allows a pawn chain in front of it, after which the centre can no longer be pressured at all.
notes.teaches: A piece attacking a pawn can be answered by defending it; a PAWN attacking a pawn cannot, because nothing wants to trade down into it — when the natural knight move would let the opponent build a chain and settle the centre for good, use the pawn instead.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Four Pawns Attack
notes.explains: The pawn steps to e5 attacking the pawns on d4 and f4 at once, with the fianchettoed bishop already looking down the long diagonal at the same square. Whatever the centre does about it, it stops being a wall — and a centre that has to make a decision is not a centre that is squeezing you.
notes.teaches: The bigger the pawn centre, the more of it is loose — a wall of pawns supports itself only where the pawns are, and striking at the point where two of them touch forces a resolution while your pieces are already aimed at it. Castle first, then hit.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Modern Bishop's Opening
notes.explains: With the bishop already posted on c4 and the modest d3 supporting the centre, the knight steps to f3 and reaches exactly the quiet, familiar centre that a more common move order arrives at from the other side. The knight eyes the e5-pawn and the position settles into well-known paths.
notes.teaches: Two different opening sequences that arrive at the same position are the same game, and an unfamiliar first move is nothing to fear once you see it landing in a structure you already understand — learn positions and plans, not move-order trivia. Recognising the transposition turns a strange start into familiar ground.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on e5 covering d6 and f6, so the knight has no way back to the natural square in front of its king and the dark squares in front of Black stay sealed. The centre pawns are still standing side by side, which is the entire point of the system.
notes.teaches: With two ways to recapture, the choice is a choice of position, not of bookkeeping — take with the wing pawn and the big centre survives intact and the file behind it opens for the rook; take with the centre pawn and the middle thins out exactly where the whole plan lives.

notes.explains: The knight that just came out attacks d4, and d4 is the pawn holding e5 in place. The bishop to e3 adds a second defender to d4, so the front of the centre stays supported without putting a pinnable piece in front of it.
notes.teaches: When a pawn comes under fire, look at what is HOLDING it before you look at the pawn — a big centre is a chain, and pressure on the front pawn is answered by reinforcing the one underneath, while the natural knight move steps onto a square where it can be pinned to the very pawn it is meant to hold.

notes.explains: From e2 the bishop covers the knight on f3, so the pin against it no longer threatens to win anything, and the same bishop is holding the pawn on c4 that the forward square would have left loose.
notes.teaches: The active-looking square for a bishop is often the one that invites the pin; the modest square behind it is the one that answers it — a pin only bites when the pinned piece is undefended, so put a defender on it in advance and the pin becomes a question with an easy answer.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 hitting the knight on c6 and the pawn on e6 together. The knight has to move and the pawn has to be dealt with, and only one of those can be attended to first.
notes.teaches: A space-gaining push is worth playing the moment it comes with a question attached — one pawn move that attacks a developed piece and strikes a defended pawn at the same time forces the answer to be found immediately, and answers found under pressure are the ones that go wrong.

notes.explains: The bishop now stands on b6, bearing down on the pawn on c7 behind it and on the pawn out on a5. The knight that hopped to the rim has won nothing yet, and it is now a piece behind.
notes.teaches: When a piece jumps to an aggressive square, check what it LEFT before you answer where it went — a knight arriving with threats is only frightening if the piece it abandoned is still safe, and once the abandoned one is taken, the aggressive one has to justify itself alone.

notes.explains: Black takes in the centre, which is simply what is played here. White now decides how to get the pawn back, and the choice names the opening: recapture with the knight for the straightforward version, or leave the pawn alone and develop toward f7 for the gambit. Nothing has been risked yet.
notes.teaches: Take a central pawn when the recapture is not automatic — the opponent's choice of HOW to regain it is the real fork in the road, so let them commit first.

notes.explains: White leaves the pawn on d4 alone and develops at the f7 diagonal instead — the gambit. Black has two main approaches from here. One brings the knight out to f6, which invites the pawn advance and the central counter-push that follows it. The other blocks the diagonal with the bishop and keeps the extra pawn for now. Both are respectable; they are simply different games.
notes.teaches: Against a gambit that ignores the pawn, pick a defence by which structure you want, not by which move looks bravest — both replies here are sound and they lead to different games.

notes.explains: White has offered the c-pawn as well and Black declines by developing. Taking it is the mistake: whatever modern analysis says about the resulting position, in practice it hands White a huge lead in development with lines opening straight at the black king, and the extra pawn never gets to matter. Bringing the knight out and hitting e4 keeps the position sound and leaves White to prove the gambit.
notes.teaches: A second pawn offered in a gambit is usually a trap for the greedy — when the capture opens lines toward your uncastled king, count the development, not the material.

notes.explains: The pawns have traded so that the wing majorities point in opposite directions — the queenside pawns outnumber their counterparts and will advance there, while the opponent's extra kingside pawn does the same on the other wing. The imbalance is the plan: push where you are the majority.
notes.teaches: When two recaptures are both sound, prefer the one that creates a structure with a plan built in — recapturing to leave majorities on opposite wings gives each side a clear job, and the whole middlegame plays itself by plan rather than by move-to-move invention.
notes.structural: the recapture chosen for the structure it leaves — opposite majorities, each side owning one wing

notes.explains: The pawn comes to c4 and covers b5 and d5. The central break to d5 is the move this defence uses to free itself, and it is now met by a pawn rather than a piece. Nothing is attacked; the position becomes one where the defender has space to hold and no lever to open it with.
notes.teaches: The way to take a freeing pawn break off the board is to cover its landing square with a pawn of your own — a second pawn on the fourth rank looks like a slow space-grab and is really prophylaxis: the break the defender's whole setup is built around simply stops existing.

forkOf.lineName: Sicilian: Dragon / Accelerated Dragon: Maróczy with ...Qb6

notes.explains: The knights have come off in the centre and the queen takes back. From d4 she hits the knight on f6 and the pawns on a7 and d7, while holding the pawns of the clamp behind her. The exchange that was supposed to relieve the cramped side has instead put the queen on the strongest square on the board.
notes.teaches: Trading knights in a clamped position helps the side with less space, so recapture with the piece that makes the trade cost something — a queen that lands hitting a knight and two pawns at once means the simplification the defender wanted has handed over three tempi instead.

notes.opening: Pirc Defense: Austrian Attack, Weiss Variation
notes.explains: The knight develops to f3, guarding the d4-pawn and covering e5 so the wide row of central pawns stays firmly in hand. The defence has conceded the middle deliberately, and every piece brought up to hold it makes that concession harder to justify.
notes.teaches: A broad pawn centre is a genuine asset, not an overextension, so long as you can hold it — and against a defence that hands you the middle on purpose, the way to punish that choice is to take the space and keep it defended.

notes.opening: Pirc Defense: Austrian Attack, Weiss Variation
notes.explains: The bishop goes to d3 rather than the more natural-looking square a file over, and from d3 it defends the e4-pawn so the knight cannot simply be taken. The active square would have invited a central pawn break that strikes two pieces at once; the modest square sidesteps it and keeps the centre solid.
notes.teaches: The most natural developing square is not always the safe one — when an active post walks the piece into a central break that hits two of your men at once, the quieter square that defends your centre is worth more than the extra aggression.

forkOf.lineName: Pirc Defence / Austrian Attack with e5 c5

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit
notes.explains: Black is a pawn up on d4 and the knight on c6 is what holds it. Two bishop developments come into consideration: one to d3, intending to swing round afterwards, and one straight to b5, which attacks the guard at once — once that knight is dealt with, both the knight and the queen are ready to collect on d4.
notes.teaches: To win back a gambit pawn, attack the piece defending it rather than the pawn itself — counting defenders first tells you which piece to harass, and a bishop that pins or hits the guard does more than a piece aimed at the pawn ever will.

forkOf.lineName: Four Knights Game / Belgrade Gambit: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nd5

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop has been traded for the knight and the pawn recaptures toward the centre. From c6 that pawn covers b5 and d5 — the outpost square in the middle and the square on the wing where a bishop or knight would otherwise sit and annoy. The pawns look untidy on the c-file and the position is perfectly sound, because the squares that matter are held.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are only weak when they cover nothing — before recapturing, look at which squares each pawn would hold from its new file, because a doubled pawn that takes away the two squares the opponent's pieces most want has already paid for the cosmetic damage.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps only to d3 rather than to d4. It props up the pawn on e4 so the centre cannot be undermined, and covers c4 so no piece drops in there. The position stays closed while the pieces come out — which is exactly what the side without the bishop pair wants.
notes.teaches: When you have given up the bishop pair, do not rush to open the position — the modest one-square pawn move keeps the centre closed enough that the two bishops have nothing to aim at, and time spent making the position solid is time the opponent cannot spend making it sharp.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The bishop has been traded on f3 and the queen takes back. From f3 she hits the knight on f6 immediately, so the recapture comes with a question attached rather than as a pause. She also stands behind the pawns on d3, e4, g2 and h3, which means there is no square from which she can be harassed.
notes.teaches: When two pieces can recapture, take with the one that lands doing something — a queen that arrives hitting a piece has gained the move the recapture would normally cost, and if she also sits behind her own pawns she is safe from being chased off again.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: The centre is locked with pawns on e4 and e5 and neither side can force it open there. The pawn goes to a4 and covers b5, which is the square the queenside pawn break needs. With that square held, the position has no natural way to be opened, and the game becomes about who can improve their worst piece.
notes.teaches: In a closed position the pawn breaks are the only way in, so the strongest prophylactic move is often the one that takes a break square away before the break is prepared — a pawn spent on the wing costs nothing here, and the plan it stops was the opponent's only one.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Nyezhmetdinov-Rossolimo Attack, Fianchetto Variation
notes.explains: With the pawns fixed, the knight on c3 has nothing left to do there. Dropping back to e2 keeps it covering d4, the one central square either side could use as an outpost, and opens the route toward the kingside where the position is not yet decided. Retreating is not passive when the square behind is a crossroads.
notes.teaches: In a locked position a knight that has run out of squares should retreat toward a route rather than stand still — judge the retreat by where it can go next and by what it holds on the way, because a knight stepping back while still covering the key central square has lost nothing at all.

notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 holding the pawn on e4 and covering d5 and b5. Both centre files are settled, the knight in the middle is supported, and Black's position is sound and short of space. The advantage is that every one of your pieces has a square and one of theirs does not.
notes.teaches: A defence that props the centre pawn with the d-pawn instead of a piece concedes space without losing anything — so there is nothing to refute, only something to collect. Strike in the middle, recapture with a piece, and finish developing.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 attacking the pawn on d5 and taking b5 in hand, and b5 is the first step of the route toward the outpost it is really heading for. The block it causes on the c-file is real, and it is being paid for with a plan rather than ignored.
notes.teaches: General rules about where a knight belongs are worth following until you can name a concrete route that beats them — a knight developed to the square the rule forbids is justified the moment you can say which two squares it is travelling to and what it does when it arrives.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: The knight hits the queen on b6 and touches the pawn on c5 at the same time. The queen has to move, and whatever it does, the knight's next step lands on the square in front of it.
notes.teaches: A queen posted on b6 and a knight on c3 make a standing pattern worth memorising: the knight steps to a4 with tempo, and the square it is really going to is c5. Learn the pairing rather than recalculating it — the knight looks misplaced on the edge for exactly one move, which is the move the queen spends moving.

notes.explains: The pawn push has been taken and the bishop recaptures on c4, back on the diagonal pointing at f7. The centre pawns have come off, so nothing blocks it any more, and the king opposite has not yet castled. The structure is now symmetrical and the position is not — one bishop is aimed at a target and the other is not.
notes.teaches: Offering a pawn trade to reopen your own bishop's diagonal is a fair bargain when the pawn comes straight back — count what the bishop is aiming at after the recapture rather than what the structure looks like.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5, taking d6 and f6 in hand and shutting the middle. Those are exactly the squares the earlier pawn move gave up, and there is now no pawn break that reclaims them.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that fianchettoes a bishop also gives away the squares of the other colour around it for good — against that, CLOSING the centre is not passive: it removes the counterplay that would distract you and leaves the weakened squares as the only thing happening on the board.

notes.explains: The pawn to f3 takes e4 in hand, which is the square the central advance needs. It breaks every rule about early development and it is the move that makes the advance possible at all.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that develops nothing and blocks your own knight's best square is worth playing when it buys the one square the position turns on — in a symmetrical structure whoever gets the big central advance in first is better, and preparing it with a pawn is slow, ugly, and the only way to get there.

notes.opening: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Main Line
notes.explains: The bishop settles on c5 looking down the diagonal at f2 and at g1 behind it. The knight already sitting in the centre now has a fork square that is covered, and the pawn move that opened the diagonal cannot be taken back.
notes.teaches: A pawn move in front of the king takes a square away from its own side — develop the bishop onto the diagonal that runs at that square, so it defends the square your own knight wants to land on and threatens to use it at the same time.

notes.opening: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Main Line
notes.explains: The bishop steps to b4 pinning the knight on c3 against the king behind it. The pawn move that chased it off the other diagonal is exactly what opened this one.
notes.teaches: A central advance that gains space with tempo also opens a diagonal behind it, and the piece it just chased is often the one that should use it — moving the same bishop twice breaks the rule about developing everything once, because here the rule is wrong: the second square pins the knight holding the centre.

notes.explains: The pawn has been offered on c5 and the centre pawn advances past it to d5, covering c6 and e6. Those are the squares the knight and the light-squared bishop want. The position locks, which suits the side whose bishop is already outside the pawn chain — the piece that could have been trapped is the one with the open diagonal.
notes.teaches: When the bishop comes out before the pawns are settled, a pawn push in the centre answers the challenge by closing it — judge the push by the two squares it covers rather than by the space it takes, because with both entry squares held the pieces opposite have nowhere to develop toward.

notes.explains: The pawn has come to e5 to hit the bishop, and the bishop drops back to g3 still looking at that same pawn. It also holds the pawns on f2 and h2 behind it. The advance gained space and created a target in the same move, and the bishop is now the piece asking the questions.
notes.teaches: A bishop attacked by a pawn advance should retreat along the diagonal rather than off it, if the square behind still bears on the pawn that just moved — the pawn cannot come back, so the retreat keeps the target and the tempo the opponent spent is gone.

notes.explains: The a-pawn steps to a3 and attacks the bishop on b4. It must either drop back, having achieved nothing, or take the knight, and after the recapture White owns the pair of bishops and a wide pawn centre, with only doubled c-pawns to show against it on the other side of the ledger.
notes.teaches: When an enemy bishop pins your knight, a rook-pawn poke asks it a hard question: retreat and lose time, or capture and hand you the bishop pair — against a defence built on that pin, forcing the trade early and taking the two bishops plus a broad centre is usually a fine bargain, even at the cost of a doubled pawn.

notes.explains: The pawn to e3 opens the light bishop's diagonal and supports the d4-pawn, and it is a step toward the one break this position is about: advancing the e-pawn to open lines for the two bishops. Kingside development and castling come first so that break can be prepared at full strength.
notes.teaches: Once a structure hands you the two bishops and a pawn centre, the whole game can narrow to a single break, and the discipline is to bend every move toward it — develop the pieces that clear the way and castle, so the central push comes under the best conditions instead of in a scramble.

notes.explains: The rook steps to e1 behind the pawn on e4. Until now, grabbing on c6 and taking the pawn in the centre lost the e-pawn straight back; with the file supported, that sequence is real and has to be answered.
notes.teaches: A capture that 'wins a pawn' is only a threat once the pawn behind it is covered — the same two-move trick can be harmless on one move and winning on the next, and the move that changes it is often a quiet rook step that touches nothing.

notes.explains: The pawn to b5 hits the bishop on a4 and takes c4 away from it at the same time, so the piece that made the capture work has to retreat. The queenside space is a bonus that the defensive alternative would never have collected.
notes.teaches: When a threat depends on one particular piece, the cleanest answer is often to attack that piece rather than to shore up what it is aiming at — defending the target is passive and permanent; hitting the attacker gains space and buys the move you were going to need anyway.

notes.explains: The pawn goes to d5 in one step, hitting the pawn on e4 and covering c4. The centre opens while every black piece is developed and the king is already castled; the pawn in the middle is the price of that.
notes.teaches: A gambit in a quiet position is not a wild bet; it is a purchase of TIME and OPEN LINES, and it is only sound if your pieces are already pointing at the king — push the central pawn in one move rather than two, because the tempo saved is the whole compensation.

notes.explains: The pawn to c6 holds the knight in the centre and props up the pawn on b5 behind it. The rook can no longer take the knight, and no piece has been diverted from the attack to babysit it.
notes.teaches: Given a choice of defenders, use the pawn — it holds a piece without being tied down itself, and nothing that attacks the defended piece is willing to trade into it, so the defence costs nothing and cannot be undermined by an exchange.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to d6 attacking the rook in the centre and connecting the rooks behind it. The rook has to leave, and the bishop is left on the diagonal that runs at the castled king.
notes.teaches: When an enemy piece is standing in your way, drive it off with a move that also belongs to your attack — a tempo-gaining move that leaves your pieces pointing somewhere useless has gained nothing; the test is where your army is aiming after the piece has run.

notes.explains: The queen drops into h3, holding the pawn on g3 and the pawn on h2 under attack and standing on squares no pawn can ever contest again. Nothing chases it: the defender has no light-squared piece left near its own king.
notes.teaches: A pawn move in front of the castled king answers one threat and creates a permanent one: the squares of the other colour around the king can never be covered by pawns again — so do not retreat the attacking piece when it is pushed, walk it INTO the holes, where nothing the defender still has can drive it away.

notes.explains: The queen checks from a5 at the king still on e1, and the routine stops: blocking commits a piece to a square it did not want, and the alternatives disturb the setup's order. The system player is out of their script on move six.
notes.teaches: A system opening's strength is its routine — the same setup in the same order every game — and the early queen check is the interruption: it arrives before the routine finishes, and every answer costs something the system wanted to keep.

notes.explains: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3 and pins it against the queen. The knight holds the centre together, and while it is stuck the development race is running in only one direction — the pawn-grabs on offer are worth less than the next developing move.
notes.teaches: In these solid setups one knight glues the position together — it holds the centre pawn and covers the squares the setup depends on — and the pin against the queen freezes that knight, so greed can wait: developing every piece against a tangled position wins more than any pawn on offer.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Anderssen Attack
notes.explains: The rook drops onto e1 behind the knight that has just taken in the centre. The knight is attacked and has no easy retreat, so the reply is dictated rather than chosen.
notes.teaches: When a piece takes a pawn in the centre, look at the FILE it is now standing on before deciding whether the pawn was worth anything — a rook swung behind it costs nothing, develops, and forces the intruder to be defended by a move the opponent did not want to make.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 hitting the pawn on c4 and taking e4 in hand, backed by the pawn that prepared it. The fianchettoed bishop is left looking at a wall it helped build.
notes.teaches: A flank opening only works while it argues about the centre — when the reply is a quiet fianchetto instead of a strike or a knight, the answer is the full central advance, and the side that was 'a tempo up' now finds itself playing the black side of its own system, a move behind.

notes.explains: The knight develops toward the centre, eyeing e5 and guarding the d4-pawn, while White simply prepares to clear the light bishop's road to c4. The extra pawn on c4 cannot be propped up for long, so it is regained a move later with every piece already in play.
notes.teaches: When an opponent gives a pawn back rather than trying to hold it, resist grabbing it at once — the value of the sequence is the lead in development you earn while collecting it, not the pawn itself, and recapturing straight away with the queen throws that lead away.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to e3 and unblocks the f1-bishop, whose diagonal now runs all the way to c4 to collect the pawn sitting there. It lends the d4-pawn extra support at the same time, and it does all of this without leaving a single weakness behind.
notes.teaches: A quiet pawn move that clears a path can be worth more than a natural developing move that commits you — opening the bishop's diagonal to reclaim the pawn keeps the position sound and the plans flexible, while a knight sortie into the centre first forces matters before you know which setup you need.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to c5 and strikes at White's d4-pawn. Once the central pawns come off, White's d-pawn will stand alone, with no pawn on the c-file or the e-file to shield it, and the isolated-pawn middlegame this line is known for is reached by a single freeing thrust.
notes.teaches: Learn the freeing break that defines a middlegame by its structure, not by memorizing the moves — the side with the lone central pawn plays for piece activity and outpost squares, the other blockades the pawn and trades down toward an endgame where it is weak, so know which side of that bargain you are on before the middlegame begins.

notes.explains: The knight leaps to e5, hitting the bishop on c4 and the queen on f3 at the same time. White cannot save the bishop, so Black walks away with the pair of bishops and shoves the queen onto a more exposed square. No fork needed — the double attack does the work.
notes.teaches: When an enemy bishop is planted on a square your knight can hit, jumping in to attack it can win the bishop pair even without a fork — forcing the trade and driving the piece behind it to an awkward square is a real gain in the opening.

notes.explains: After the swap Black holds the bishop pair, and look where the white queen sits — out in the open on c4. That is not a loss of the knight, it is a gain: Black's coming central expansion will hit the queen and gain time doing it.
notes.teaches: Trading a knight for a bishop is a clear gain when you come out with the two bishops and provoke the enemy queen onto an exposed square — a queen stuck in the open becomes a target your development can hit with tempo.

notes.explains: You could shut things in with d6 — but e6 is more flexible. It prepares the d5 break and leaves the light-squared bishop free to choose its diagonal later. Black expands while keeping every option open, rather than boxing his own pieces in.
notes.teaches: When you expand in the centre, choose the pawn move that prepares a break and keeps your pieces free over the passive one that blocks them in — flexibility is worth more than a solid but stodgy structure.

notes.explains: The pawn has advanced to e5 to chase the queen out of the centre. She steps to b4, where she hits the pawns on b7 and d6 and still holds the centre pawn and the knight behind her. The move that was meant to gain time has instead pointed her at the two pawns the pawn advance left behind.
notes.teaches: A queen driven off a central square should look for the diagonal that hits two pawns at once rather than the nearest safe square — when both targets are on squares a pawn can never defend, the defender has to answer with a piece, and the queen has kept the initiative she was supposed to lose.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Delayed Alapin Variation, with d6
notes.explains: The pawn to e5 attacks the knight on f6 and looks aggressive — but it is premature. The pawn on c3 is sitting idle, the e5-pawn itself has no proper support, so we just take it. Grab it and Black comes out a full tempo ahead in development.
notes.teaches: A central pawn push made before you can support it just loses time — when the advance can be met by a clean capture that leaves you ahead in development, welcome it. The space it grabbed evaporates and you are simply better for having let it come.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Delayed Alapin Variation, with d6
notes.explains: Rather than let the knight sit proudly on e5, the knight to d7 develops and attacks it, offering the swap. Whatever White chooses, Black comes out comfortably developed and a shade better — the intruder is challenged the moment it lands.
notes.teaches: Meet a centralised enemy knight by challenging it with a developing move that offers a trade on your terms — bringing a piece out while forcing the exchange beats tolerating the knight in your camp.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Delayed Alapin Variation, with d6
notes.explains: You could take back with the queen — but the bishop is better. Recapturing with it develops the piece and sets up a reroute to c6 on the long diagonal. The same capture, but it brings a man into the game instead of just restoring the count.
