notes.teaches: When you recapture, do it with the piece that also develops — a recapture that brings a man toward activity is two moves in one. Prefer the take that improves your position over the passive one.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Delayed Alapin Variation, with d6
notes.explains: The bishop swings to c6, seizing the long diagonal and hitting the g2-pawn, so White has to stop and deal with it. That bought tempo lets Black calmly finish with e6, the dark-squared bishop and castling — the bad piece is now the good one, and for free.
notes.teaches: An awkwardly placed bishop should be rerouted to its best diagonal, and doing it with a gain of tempo forces the opponent to react before you finish your own plan — move the bad piece to a good square while attacking something.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to e5 and asks the question directly, attacking d4 while nothing yet defends the position properly. Waiting one move to develop first would let that centre be reinforced, and then the same break arrives against a set-up that is ready for it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has spent moves building a broad centre with pawns, hit it before the pieces arrive to support it — a centre that has to be defended by pieces is a liability; the same centre given a free move to consolidate becomes a space advantage.

notes.explains: Taking on e5 here loses the pawn straight back: the queen checks from h4 and the pawn on e4 has no defender at all, so it drops with tempo. Developing the knight to f3 covers h4 instead, which does not make the queen sortie illegal but does make it cost a queen for a knight. Material can wait; the check square cannot.
notes.teaches: Before taking a pawn in the centre, look for the check that comes with it — a queen check on the edge of the board is easy to dismiss as a lunge, but if it arrives with tempo and collects a loose pawn on the way back, the capture was never free.

notes.explains: Black jumps the knight to d4 instead of defending, offering the trade in the centre and inviting the bishop to declare itself. Three replies branch here: taking on d4, retreating the bishop along the diagonal, and dropping it all the way home. The resulting pawn structures do not arise from any other line in this opening.
notes.teaches: Some sidelines are not shortcuts into the main lines — they build a structure that appears nowhere else in the opening, so general familiarity with the parent opening will not carry you, and the only preparation that helps is knowing this position specifically.

notes.explains: White has taken on d4 and castled, leaving Black a pawn on d4 and a choice. Two moves are genuinely playable: the bishop to c5, which is the most common, and the modest c6, taking the b5 square away. Anything else concedes more than the line can afford.
notes.teaches: An opening the books call dubious is only dubious against an accurate reply — that is exactly why strong players still pick one: the objective verdict matters less than whether the person opposite has looked at it recently.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to c4 and now eyes f7. Taking there with check drags the king out, and the queen arriving on h5 forces a pawn move — after which the undefended bishop on c5 falls. That is the tactical point behind the natural-looking bishop move, and it is why Black's replies here all have to reckon with it.
notes.teaches: A bishop aimed at f7 combines with a queen that can reach h5, and the two together are worth more than either alone — before developing a bishop where it can be hit by that pair, check whether it is defended, because the check on f7 is only the setup and the piece it wins is somewhere else entirely.

notes.explains: The knight has just come to f6, and pushing the e-pawn attacks it immediately. Black cannot meet it by striking back in the centre, because that opens lines toward the king while the pieces are still at home; the pawn has to come forward first, and only then can the position be held together.
notes.teaches: When a knight develops to its natural square in front of a pawn that can advance, the advance usually comes with tempo — and a tempo spent chasing a piece is a tempo you did not have to spend on development. Look for the pawn push before you look for a new piece to move.

notes.explains: The pawn on f4 attacks the pawn on e5 and puts the whole game's character on the table in one move. Accepting hands over the centre for a pawn; propping the pawn up with slow moves keeps the material and gives up the initiative instead.
notes.teaches: The f-pawn's early strike offers a pawn to seize the centre and the initiative — the knight developed to c3 first is what makes it sound, because the centre is covered, so whichever way the offer is answered the pawns and pieces come forward with tempo. Passive declines concede the centre without even winning the pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop on b5 attacks the knight on c6, the piece holding up the pawn on e5, and the king behind the knight makes the attack a pin. The strongpoint's defence is stretched one move after it was declared.
notes.teaches: When a pawn chain's strongpoint is held by a knight, the bishop's pin against that knight is pressure on the strongpoint itself — the defender is frozen, so every attacker you add counts double. Develop toward the pin rather than around it.

notes.explains: Both knights and the dark-squared bishop are developed and Black has struck at the centre from the side. The pawn advances to e4 hitting the pawn on d5 and covering f5. Taking it leads to a position where every white piece has a line and the extra pawn is on a square that cannot be held.
notes.teaches: A gambit is worth playing when the pawn buys development you were going to need anyway — pushing the second centre pawn while both minor pieces are already out hits the pawn holding the centre and opens the line for the pieces behind it, so the material comes back or it does not, but the position opens for the side that is ready.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 hitting the pawn on e4 and taking c4 in hand. Two pieces attack the square and two defend it, so the whole exchange resolves without loss and the centre opens while their pieces are still at home.
notes.teaches: A modest pawn move that declines to fight for the centre is an invitation — count the defenders of the square you want to break on: if the count is even, the break is sound, because every trade on it happens on your terms. Meeting slow play with a central strike is the standing answer, not a special case.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to e7, defending the queen behind it and leaving the king free to castle at once. The two more forward squares both walk into a knight jump that gains time.
notes.teaches: The main job of the last minor piece is usually to get the king to safety, not to find its most active square — a bishop planted aggressively where it can be chased by a knight costs a move and delays castling; the modest square finishes development this move. Ask what a piece is FOR before asking where it looks best.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to e5 instead of being propped up, attacking the bishop that came to pin it along with the pawns on c6 and f7. The bishop has to move again, and the knight is now the best-placed piece on the board.
notes.teaches: A bishop that comes out to pin a knight has committed itself to one diagonal — and if the knight can step FORWARD instead of being defended, the pin is answered by the piece it was aiming at. Before treating a pin as something to solve, check whether the pinned piece has a square in the middle where it hits more than it is worth.

notes.explains: The bishop drops back to e7, and the knight's leap to g5 — the move every attack in this structure begins with — now lands on a square the bishop already covers. The retreat looks like a concession and is actually a preparation: the attack's first move has been answered before it was played.
notes.teaches: Against a gambit you do not have to meet sharpness with sharpness — a modest retreat that pre-answers the standard attacking idea is a complete strategy. Slightly passive and completely solid beats theoretical and half-remembered, especially when the attacker is counting on you to know less than they do.

notes.explains: The pawn has advanced to d3, where it takes both c2 and e2 in hand — the queen's home diagonal square and the king's bishop's only developing square. Until it is dealt with, the pieces behind those squares are staring at a wall the opponent has to spend real moves dismantling.
notes.teaches: An extra gambit pawn is a bargaining chip, and sometimes its best move is to give itself back on the most annoying square available — pushed into the heart of their queenside, it sits on the squares their pieces need to develop through, so they spend moves removing it and you spend those moves developing.

notes.explains: The pawns have been traded in the centre and there are two ways to continue. Taking back restores material immediately and asks nothing. Jumping the knight to b5 instead hits the weak pawn the setup opposite created, and the pawn in the middle can be collected a move later.
notes.teaches: When the centre opens, recapturing is the move you play if nothing better exists — so look for the jump first. A knight that lands hitting several pawns at once cannot be answered by defending one of them, and the pawn in the middle is usually still there afterwards.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b4 pinning the knight on c3 against the king behind it. The pawn move that would normally chase this bishop away is unavailable, because the knight is standing on the square it needs.
notes.teaches: A system that develops the queen's knight before the c-pawn buys speed and pays for it with a pin — against any such setup, the bishop that comes out to pin that knight is the most annoying move available: it ties the piece the whole scheme rests on, and it cannot be answered by the pawn move the system has already given up.

notes.explains: The knight has come to f3 and the queen's landing on h4 is covered — the check that was the position's one forcing counter now walks into a defended square. One developing move turned the sting into a blunder, and everything the pawn sacrifice promised can be collected in peace.
notes.teaches: After giving up the f-pawn, the queen check on the h-file is the counter-blow every gambit player must respect — it is the difference between an attack and an accident, so the knight's developing move that covers the checking square is not optional or slow: it is the move that makes the whole gambit playable.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5 and attacks the knight on f6, the only piece the opponent has developed. The slow pawn move on the rim gave this advance for free, and the knight has to move again while the centre rolls forward.
notes.teaches: When your opponent spends moves on slow pawn gestures in a sharp position, open the game at once — their one developed piece becomes a target, and every tempo they spent on the flank is a tempo your centre uses now.

notes.explains: The pawn has eaten its way to g7 and now attacks the rook on f8, standing one square from the king with the shelter gone. Whatever happens to the pawn itself, the pawns that used to cover the king went with it, and the open lines remain.
notes.teaches: A pawn that reaches the sixth and seventh rank inside the king's shelter is worth more than the piece it may have cost along the way — each capture it makes strips another pawn off the king's cover, and by the time it stands next to the king, every heavy piece you own has a target to aim at.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3, where it holds the knight in the centre and covers the squares in front of it. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 is aimed down the long diagonal at that knight, and this quietly answers it — the knight is no longer loose, so the pawn breaks that would have won it are simply moves.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchetto the dark-squared bishop belongs where it both supports your own centre and contests the diagonal the enemy bishop was put on — a developing move that defends the piece already in the middle costs nothing and removes every tactic built on hitting it.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to f3, defending the pawn on e4 and covering g4 so no bishop or knight can land there. That single move is what makes the whole setup work: the centre cannot be undermined, the kingside pawns are free to advance, and the king has somewhere to go on the other wing.
notes.teaches: Before castling on the side you intend to attack, spend the pawn move that makes the attack legal — holding the centre pawn and covering the square an enemy piece would use to come forward is what lets the king go the other way and the pawns march.

notes.explains: The knights have come off in the centre and the bishop steps to d4, straight down the long diagonal at the bishop on g7. It hits the pawn on a7 on the way and holds the knight on c3 behind it. The defender must either accept the exchange of the king's best guard or spend moves avoiding it while the pawns are already coming.
notes.teaches: When attacking a fianchettoed king, the piece to remove is the bishop on the long diagonal — it is the only defender that covers the dark squares around the king, and getting your own bishop onto the same diagonal facing it forces the trade or forces the king's guard to stay home.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3 holding the pawn on d4 and covering the king's corner behind it. The king has stepped off the open file, the checks are finished, and the extra piece is still on the board.
notes.teaches: A king dragged out by a sacrifice is not in danger once it has a square to tuck into and the checks run out — walk it to safety by hand, then develop the piece that props up the centre, because the attacker who spent material on the exposure has to show a threat before you have finished.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Panov Attack, Modern Defense
notes.explains: The bishop steps to e6 holding the pawn on d5 and the pawn on f7 behind it. It does stand in front of the other bishop, which will come out the long way instead — a route that costs a move and gains a diagonal.
notes.teaches: A bishop that blocks its own colleague looks like a mistake and is not, provided the colleague has another route out — judge a developing move by what it HOLDS, because the pawn in the middle is the one both sides are about to fight over, and a piece defending it from the side is worth more than a tidy-looking diagonal.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Panov Attack, Modern Defense
notes.explains: The queen comes to a5 hitting the knight on c3 and adding a second defender to the pawn on d5, with the pawn on a2 in the same line. Nothing in the position can drive the queen off that square.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned to the defence of a central pawn, bringing the queen out on the same diagonal does two jobs in one move: it develops, and it adds pressure to the piece that is already busy — an early queen is only bad when it can be chased, and here nothing attacks the square.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Panov Attack, Modern Defense
notes.explains: Taking with the e-pawn doubles the f-pawns and clears e7, so the bishop still sitting at home now has the long dark diagonal to come out on. The alternative recapture keeps the pawns tidy and leaves that bishop with nowhere to go.
notes.teaches: When a capture can be answered two ways, pick the one that unlocks the piece you have not developed yet — doubling a pawn is a real cost, and it is the right price when the recapture opens the only diagonal your last minor piece has.

notes.opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Panov Attack, Modern Defense
notes.explains: The bishop comes to g4 pinning down the knight on f3, which is the main piece holding the pawn in the middle. Trade it off and the target has one fewer guard, with the rest of the black army already aimed that way.
notes.teaches: Against an isolated central pawn the plan is not to attack the pawn — it is to remove its DEFENDERS one by one and then attack it. The knight in front of the king is usually the busiest of them, so the bishop that can trade itself for that knight is worth more than the bishop pair.

notes.explains: The knight has taken on e4 and attacks two pieces from there: the bishop on g3 that was doing the pinning, and the knight on c3. The move looked forbidden while the pin stood; the pawn advances changed the geometry, and now it wins material or the initiative whichever way the opponent answers.
notes.teaches: A pin on your king's knight is only as strong as the tactics keeping it there — when the pawns have pushed the pinning bishop to a square where the knight's capture in the centre attacks it, the pin is over, so count everything the capture hits before dismissing it as impossible.

notes.explains: The king's knight goes to e2 rather than its natural square, so the knight on c3 is no longer the only thing holding the centre and the pin has nothing to win. The pawn move that would have chased the bishop was never needed.
notes.teaches: Facing a pin on the queen's knight, spending a pawn move to prevent it weakens the squares the pin was aiming at anyway — develop instead, and keep the modest square beside the king in reserve for the OTHER knight, so when the pin arrives that knight takes it, the pinned one is free, and no pawn has been touched.

notes.explains: The knight covers e4, so the pawn is ready to come there next and take the whole centre. That is the threat this move order lives on: an answer that ignores it lets the big centre appear and hands the opponent a game they chose rather than one you did. Meeting it in the centre keeps that push honest, because the pawn arriving on e4 can then simply be taken.
notes.teaches: When a knight develops before the centre pawns, look at which pawn break it has just made possible — a quiet-looking developing move can be the one that decides whether your opponent gets to choose their own opening or gets steered into yours.

notes.explains: Once the pawn arrives on h5 the white h-pawn has nowhere to go: its one square is occupied and it cannot capture, so the pawn storm stops without a piece being touched. That is why the attacking side treats this as the main line and starts looking at sacrificing on h5 instead — the pawn alone can no longer make progress.
notes.teaches: Against a rook pawn running at a fianchetto, meeting it head on is the move that ends the discussion — a pawn that has been blocked on an open file is not slow, it has no squares at all, and the attacker has to find a different plan or spend pieces.

notes.explains: Stepping the queen to d2 empties the last square between king and queen's rook, so castling long becomes available. That is the side the king belongs on here, because the h-pawn has already committed to the attack and going short would put the king behind it. The queen also connects to the bishop on f4, so the move does two jobs.
notes.teaches: A quiet queen move is often a castling move — before reading a developing move as slow, check which squares it empties, because the last piece to leave the back rank is what makes the king's journey to the other wing possible.

notes.explains: The bishop leaves the square the check pushed it to and comes to f5, where it does hit the pawn on c2 and cover the central light squares. It is a good square — reached one move late.
notes.teaches: Counting development means counting MOVES, not pieces — a piece that reaches its good square on the second try has cost two moves and delivered one developed piece, and that arithmetic is the whole reason a side stands slightly better out of a quiet opening. When you must move a piece twice, make the second square earn it.

notes.explains: The advance takes the centre but abandons d3, and the knight drops in on b4 eyeing that square and c2 while hitting the pawn on a2. There is no pawn left that can ever ask it to move.
notes.teaches: A pawn move that gains space also stops guarding the squares it has left behind — before playing the natural expanding move, look at which square in your own camp becomes permanently unavailable to your pawns, because a knight that lands there cannot be chased and cannot be ignored either.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Smith-Morra Declined
notes.explains: The knight develops and keeps an eye on the extra pawn on d4 while the big pawn on e5 stays defended. Black cannot prop the d4-pawn up, so White regains it at the moment that suits, having already brought a piece into play instead of spending the move on a recapture.
notes.teaches: When a pawn you could win back has nowhere to run, develop first and collect it later on your own terms — recapturing on the spot is the reflex, but the stronger move is often to bring a piece out and keep the tension, because every move you spend developing instead of grabbing is a move ahead.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Smith-Morra Declined
notes.explains: The knight comes to c3 and eyes d5, the square just in front of the isolated d-pawn. Pieces gather behind d4 so that the pawn can advance when the moment is right, opening lines for the bishops and rooks standing ready behind it.
notes.teaches: A lone central pawn is not just a weakness to be defended; its whole purpose is to advance — cluster your pieces behind it so the break can be made at the right moment, and the pawn that looked like a liability becomes the lever that rips the position open.

notes.explains: White has taken the pawn back and the gambit is over before it began — this is now a completely different opening, one where White has a broad centre and no attack. Grabbing the pawn instead is the principled test and it plays straight into the hands of someone who has studied the gambit for years. This road is far safer: less to memorise, and no way to lose in five moves to a line the opponent knows by heart.
notes.teaches: The best answer to a gambit is often not to take it or to refuse it, but to transpose it into an opening the gambiteer did not want to play — take the fun out of the setup rather than testing it head on.

notes.explains: Black hits the pawn on e5 at once rather than developing around it. That pawn is the one taking away squares — it denies f6 and d6 to the black pieces — and every move it survives is a move Black spends squeezed. White will have to spend time propping it up, and that is time not spent attacking.
notes.teaches: Against a broad pawn centre, attack the advanced pawn straight away — a centre only cramps you while it is intact, and the pawn furthest forward is always the one with the fewest defenders.

notes.explains: The knight comes out and props up the advanced pawn. Black now has a real choice: take on e5, which resolves the centre immediately, or bring the queen's knight out and add a second attacker instead. The knight move is the main and principled continuation, and it invites the bishop out to c4 — the position where the interesting theory really begins.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends a pawn you attacked, you get to choose between trading it off and adding a second attacker — trading clarifies; attacking again keeps the tension and the options.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the strongest diagonal it has, pointing at h7 and covering the light squares in front of the centre. The pawn in the middle can be taken; the position it is being traded for is a full move ahead in development.
notes.teaches: When your centre is attacked, defending it with a pawn is not the only answer — and it is often the worst one, because the propping move develops nothing and commits a square your pieces wanted. Give the pawn up and DEVELOP instead: a lead in development buys back more than one pawn is worth.

notes.explains: The rook comes to e1 straight behind the advanced pawn, holding it and holding the file behind it. If the pawn is captured now, a piece of ours arrives on that square rather than the position simply opening.
notes.teaches: When the opponent strikes at the pawn that anchors your whole position, capturing back is the move that throws the position away — the pawn is not the point, the square it sits on is, and taking removes your own occupant of it. Add a defender instead and make them do the trading.

notes.explains: The bishop settles on f4, defending the knight that occupies the key square. The pin one square further along looks more active and touches nothing that matters here; this is the square that keeps the knight where it is.
notes.teaches: A pin is attractive because it is concrete, and that is exactly why it distracts — if your position is built around holding one square, judge every developing move by whether it adds a guard to that square, because the flashier square that pins a knight but abandons the outpost is a worse move even though it looks like it does more.

notes.explains: The knight comes to d2, covering f3 — the square from which it will add another defender to the outpost — and holding e4 on the way. Nothing has been developed for its own sake.
notes.teaches: When a piece must be developed and a square must be reinforced, look for the move that does both — a knight has more than one route out, and the route that passes through a square from which it will defend your outpost is worth more than the one that merely looks central.

notes.explains: The modest pawn to e6 is the third option here, behind the two main central replies. Its interesting property is what it offers next move: once White builds the centre, Black can push the d-pawn and turn the game into a locked pawn chain where White's e-pawn has advanced past and both sides play on the wings. Some White players are delighted by that structure; others never play it at all, and this move makes them say which.
notes.teaches: A third-choice move can still be a good practical one when its point is to offer the opponent a transposition they may not want — choose by what it makes THEM decide, not by its ranking.

notes.explains: The pawn takes the centre alongside its neighbour, hitting c5. This is the obvious continuation and it hands the choice straight back: Black can push the d-pawn and steer toward the locked chain, or leave it and keep the open game. Either way White wants to know which reply is coming before playing this, because the answer to the d-pawn push is where the two roads separate.
notes.teaches: Occupy the centre when your opponent's last move invited it — a big centre is only a commitment if you have already decided how to answer the strike against it.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on d5 and White faces the fork in the road. Pushing past locks the chain and gives the game a completely different character. The alternative is simply to take, which is the recommended route for anyone who does not want that structure: White is reckoned slightly better in the position that follows, and after Black recaptures with the queen the game transposes into the well-worn lines where the queen comes out early and gets chased.
notes.teaches: When an advance would transpose into an opening you do not play, look for the capture that keeps the game in your own territory — trading is not passive when it steers the position toward theory you actually know.

notes.explains: The pawn on d6 attacks the pawn on e5, the one the opening's early moves lured forward. However the tension resolves, the bishop behind the pawn gets its diagonal and the centre stops belonging to one side.
notes.teaches: This whole defence provokes the centre forward in order to hit it, and the strike itself is not a subtle move — do not overthink it: the pawn challenges the advanced pawn, claims a share of the centre, and opens the bishop's diagonal in one routine gesture.

notes.explains: The bishop develops to g4 and attacks the knight on f3, which is all that stands between it and the bishop that recaptured on d1. One developing move, one threat, and the opponent's pieces — king in the centre, bishop home on d1 — must untangle under pressure.
notes.teaches: After a queen trade that denies castling, keep developing with hits — every piece that comes out attacking something extends the lead the trade created, and the piece that recaptured is usually the most tangled one.

notes.explains: The bishop on b2 takes the e5 square in hand down a completely open diagonal. The opponent's modest pawn move promised a central stake it has not yet made — until the pawn arrives on e5, the bishop owns the centre from the wing.
notes.teaches: This opening is one idea wearing a move order: the bishop on the long diagonal, fighting for the central dark squares with pieces instead of pawns — every reply that concedes that diagonal hands the bishop exactly the board it wanted.

notes.explains: The pawn on a4 has been taken, and the opponent's opening consists of pawn moves on both rims with no piece developed past the first rank. There is no trick to fear from pieces that have not moved; the material is simply banked and the game continues a pawn up with the better diagonal.
notes.teaches: Flank pawn gestures that are not backed by development are not threats — they are deposits. When the rim pawn offers itself, count what recapturing actually exposes; usually the answer is nothing, and the pawns your opponent marched forward are weaknesses you now own the squares beside.
notes.structural: a rim-pawn offer accepted after counting the undeveloped pieces behind it — gestures are not threats

notes.explains: The knight has landed on d6, checkmate. The pawn on e7 cannot take it because the queen on e2 stands behind the knight on the same file, and every flight square is covered. One automatic developing move earlier — the knight to d7, blocking the bishop that guarded d6's approach — is the whole story of the game.
notes.teaches: When a quiet-looking queen move appears in a position you know, stop and ask what changed — the move you always play may have just become a losing one. The queen stepping to the e-file turns the centralised knight into a discovered battery, and the standard developing move now allows mate on the spot.

notes.explains: The pawn on c3 invites the capture, and taking it opens the diagonals the whole attack is built on. The other try ignores the offer and strikes in the centre instead, returning the pawn on terms you choose rather than on terms your opponent has prepared for.
notes.teaches: A gambit pawn offered a second time is a question about time, not about greed — you can take everything and spend the next ten moves untangling, or hand one pawn straight back in the centre and reach a position where the extra material was never the point.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 and hits the pawn on e4, so the centre has to be resolved immediately rather than at leisure. It also covers c4, which is where the light-squared bishop wants to sit and stare at f7. Giving the pawn back here buys both of those, and the attack loses the square it was built around.
notes.teaches: The best way to decline a gambit is usually a pawn move that does two jobs at once — look for the push that hits something and takes away the square the attacking piece was heading for, because a defender that gains a move while removing a plan is worth more than a pawn.

notes.explains: Both bishops are now on their diagonals. The dark-squared one has taken on b2 and looks straight down at g7, and it covers f6 as well, so the natural developing square for the king's knight is contested before the knight has moved. Nothing is won yet; what has been bought is that every black piece must now come out with the attack already pointing at it.
notes.teaches: Count what a gambit buys in lines, not in pawns — two pawns given up for two bishops raking toward the same king is a real bargain when the defender still has pieces at home, because the moment the position opens, every tempo spent taking is a tempo not spent developing.

notes.explains: The bishop has come to b4 with check and it must be dealt with at once. Four answers are on the board: the king steps to f1, or one of three pieces interposes on the c3 and d2 squares — and each of them changes what the position is about. Blocking with the dark-squared bishop offers a trade of the piece doing the most work.
notes.teaches: When every way of answering a check gives something up, the choice is about which concession you can live with — blocking with a piece invites a trade you may not want, stepping the king aside forfeits castling, and the bishop that came to block is often the one the whole attack depended on. Pick the concession, do not stumble into it.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5 and hits the pawn on d6, so the centre cannot simply be left alone. What matters more is that it now covers f6, so the king's knight has lost its natural square while the position is still open. That is the shape of the whole gambit: not one big threat, but a series of small ones that each cost the defender a move.
notes.teaches: A pawn push in the centre earns its place when it hits a pawn and takes a square from a piece in the same move — before you push, look at what the pawn will cover once it has moved, because the square behind the target is often worth more than the target.

notes.explains: Black has stabilised with the pawn on d6 and the position is level in material after the pawn came back. Four tries come into consideration: two different queen placements, the natural knight development, and the central push. They lead to genuinely different games rather than to a single best line.
notes.teaches: With a lead in development and no forced win, the choice is which piece to commit and how early — a queen sortie asks a question immediately but can be answered by a queen move; a quiet developing move keeps every option and asks nothing. There is no refutation to find here, only a preference to have.

notes.explains: You are down two pawns and the hand itches to lunge at something — but there is nothing there yet. The knight to f3 finishes bringing the pieces out. You paid two pawns for the lead in development, so cash it in patiently; the initiative you bought is not going anywhere.
notes.teaches: In a gambit you have paid material for time, so spend that time on development, not premature threats — with only a couple of pieces out there is nothing real to attack yet.

notes.explains: The check comes, and you could just shuffle the king a square — but that throws away castling. Instead the knight blocks on d2 and develops in the same move. The check is answered and a piece comes into play, with king safety kept for later.
notes.teaches: Meet a check by blocking with a developing move wherever you can, rather than by moving the king out of its castling rights — the interposition that also brings a piece into play answers the check and improves your position at once.

notes.explains: Black's f6 loosens the light squares around the king — so we aim at them. The queen comes to b3, lining up behind the bishop on c4 and bearing down toward f7. Black's kingside knight has no easy way out, and the whole position leans on the squares that pawn move gave up.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens the shield in front of their king with a pawn move, aim pieces at the squares it exposed — a queen lined up behind a bishop on the same diagonal creates pressure toward the king a single piece never could.

notes.explains: Two pieces can take back here, and the choice matters. Recapturing with the knight keeps White's men coordinated toward the king — which still cannot castle with the bishops raking the long diagonals. It is the recapture that holds the bind, not the one that eases it.
notes.teaches: When two pieces can recapture, take with the one that keeps your force aimed at the target — preserving the pieces that restrict the enemy king matters more than a tidy-looking recapture with the other man.

notes.explains: The pawn has been offered on c5 and is taken. From there it covers b6 and d6, which are the two squares a knight or a bishop would use to win it back. Nothing recaptures immediately, so the extra pawn either survives or costs the defender a move to collect while the pieces opposite are still at home.
notes.teaches: Capturing toward the wing looks like it concedes the centre, and the question is what the pawn does from its new square — a pawn on the sixth file that covers both squares the opponent needs to recapture from is not a loose pawn, it is a wedge that has to be dealt with before anything else happens.

notes.explains: Capturing toward the centre doubles the f-pawns but opens the e-file that the rook will use once the king castles, and it leaves a solid block on f6, f7, g7 and h7 to shield the king. The structure looks damaged and is genuinely comfortable to play.
notes.teaches: When you recapture, taking toward the centre usually beats taking toward the edge, even at the cost of doubled pawns — doubled pawns that open a file for your pieces and build a wall in front of your king are a feature, not a flaw. Judge a pawn weakness by what it actually does, not by the name it carries.

notes.explains: The bishops have been traded and the pawn on f4 has committed the attack. The queen steps to e1, where she holds the pawn on e4, connects the pieces on the back rank, and can travel to the kingside along the third rank once the pawns advance. Nothing is attacked yet; the piece that will lead the attack has simply been put where it can join it.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack the queen usually belongs behind the pawns rather than in front of them. A move to the back rank that clears her original square, holds the centre pawn and opens the route toward the king does three jobs and threatens nothing — which is exactly why it is hard to meet.

notes.explains: The bishop completes its fianchetto on g2, aimed down the long diagonal. You could burn a move to stop the coming pin — but that would only soften the b4 square for nothing. Just develop, and let the opponent's little rook-pawn nudge be the wasted move.
notes.teaches: In a fianchetto system, answer a harmless flank pawn poke by simply continuing your development, not by reacting to it — spending a move to prevent a pin would weaken a key square for no real gain.

notes.explains: The natural move is d3 to prop the centre — but castling is stronger here. Once Black trades the bishop on c3, White recaptures toward the middle with a tempo and an open game, and there is even a tactic waiting if Black snatches the e4-pawn. Keep the pawn move in reserve.
notes.teaches: The instinctive supporting pawn move is not always best — castling first keeps a tempo in hand for when the pin is traded off, and leaves a tactical resource if the opponent gets greedy.

notes.explains: You could take back the tidy way and keep the pawns clean — but take with the d-pawn instead. It opens the dark-squared bishop's diagonal and tightens White's grip on the central squares. The doubled pawns are a small price for that activity.
notes.teaches: When you recapture, prefer the direction that opens a piece and grips the centre over the one that merely keeps the pawns tidy — a recapture toward the middle frees a bishop and stakes a bigger central claim.

notes.explains: If Black snatches the pawn on e4, don't scramble to defend — count it. The knight takes on e5, hitting the knight on c6, and White regains the material once the dust settles. A desperado counter-grab is nothing to fear when you have counted the line to the end.
notes.teaches: When the opponent grabs a pawn with a piece, look for the in-between capture that wins it straight back — and do not fear a desperado counter-grab. Counting the sequence out beats reflexively defending.

notes.explains: The pawn to c4 grabs a bit of space — but it hands over the d4 square for good, because White no longer has a c-pawn to ever support that break. Don't reach for fireworks to punish it; this is a sideline you answer with simple, sound positional chess.
notes.teaches: A surprising off-beat move is not the same as a mistake, but it rarely reflects deep preparation — meet it with calm, textbook play rather than trying to punish it at once. The refutation of a sideline is usually just sound development.

notes.explains: The bishop develops to g7 and rakes down the long diagonal, aimed right at the d4 square that White's early c-pawn push left soft for good. Nothing clever, just the natural move — the best piece pointed at the weakness.
notes.teaches: A fianchetto that rakes the long diagonal is a logical developing move whatever the specific opening — especially when it aims straight at a square the opponent has weakened. Point your best piece at the hole.

notes.explains: Pawn to d6 comes first. The natural knight to f6 would wall in the g7-bishop and loosen the grip on d4 — so we hold it back and route that knight to e7 instead. The pawn move is useful anyway and prepares a later central break.
notes.teaches: Order your developing moves to keep your best piece's diagonal open — delay the natural knight development that would block your own fianchettoed bishop, and play the useful pawn move first.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to g4, pinning the knight on f3 and preparing to trade it off. That knight guards the central d4 and e5 squares — the whole fight in this structure — so removing it is worth the bishop.
notes.teaches: There is more than one way to remove a key enemy defender — besides the usual pawn levers, simply pinning and trading it off with a bishop is an option players often overlook, and it is exactly the piece guarding the squares you want.

notes.explains: Yes, taking the knight hands over the bishop pair — the rule says keep it. But the rule bows to the position here: the centre is closed, so the two bishops matter little, and this trade removes a defender of the squares Black is fighting for. Development is untouched.
notes.teaches: General rules bow to a concrete priority — in a closed centre, giving up the bishop pair to remove a defender of the key squares is worth more than the abstract advantage of the two bishops. The position, not the maxim, decides.

notes.explains: The bishop stands on f5 with the diagonal toward b1 completely open — it attacks the knight sitting on its home square, so even the opponent's first developing moves are constrained. The pawn move to e6 can come next, closing the chain behind a bishop that is already at work.
notes.teaches: When the centre locks into a chain, get the light-squared bishop out before closing it in — and notice how much the freed bishop actually does. From its natural post outside the chain it sweeps the whole long diagonal into the opponent's queenside, and every piece that wants to develop on that side has to reckon with it.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on e6 and defends two pieces at once: the pawn on d5 in the centre and the bishop on f5 beside it. The chain is complete with the bishop on the right side of it, and every unit in the structure is now held by a pawn.
notes.teaches: The pawn move that completes a chain should be counted for everything it holds, not just the square it stands on. And a matching pair of pawns — one of theirs propping their centre, one of yours attacking it — cancel each other out: neither makes the pawn between them weaker or stronger by itself.

notes.explains: The knight has gone to h6 because the bishop sits on f5, the knight's usual home in this structure. The square e7 stays empty for the dark-squared bishop, so the kingside can finish developing without the pieces queuing behind one another, and the knight keeps g4 in view for its next hop.
notes.teaches: When your bishop already occupies the knight's favourite square, be deliberate about how the king's knight develops — the routes are not equal. The rim development that keeps the other bishop's square free is often the practical choice: the knight can re-route later, but a tangled queenside cannot untangle itself.
notes.structural: development order solved around an occupied square — the rim knight keeps e7 free and the pieces never queue

notes.explains: The queen stands on c7. From there she attacks the pawn on e5, the head of the chain. The knight's lunge to the rim asked her to move, and the retreat answered by hitting something — the opponent spent a move on the edge and got a new problem for it.
notes.teaches: Know the standard knight-traps by pattern, not by calculation — a queen on the knight's-edge square is a puzzle theme your opponent has drilled too. When the knight comes asking, step the queen to the square where she keeps working, and the retreat costs nothing.

notes.explains: The pawn strikes at e5, the head of the chain, with the king already castled and the rook standing behind the very file the capture will open. Every developed piece keeps its job while the pawn does the asking — this is the position the earlier quiet moves were for.
notes.teaches: Against a pawn chain there are two targets: the base and the head. Once your pieces are developed and castled, the strike at the head with the f-pawn opens your rook's file and asks the chain a question it cannot keep refusing. Before calculating any of the captures, list the enemy pieces that are undefended or defended only once — the piece that hangs at the end of a line is the most common thing a calculation forgets.

notes.explains: Both sides have made modest pawn moves and the position is still closed. The bishop goes to b2 on the long diagonal, where it hits the pawn on e5 and covers d4 — the square the centre would be contested from. It also holds the rook in the corner. Nothing has been risked, and the piece that will decide the game is pointing at the only fixed target on the board.
notes.teaches: A slow setup with pawns on the third rank is answered on its own terms: build the same shape, then develop the bishop onto the diagonal where the opponent's centre pawn already stands. The bishop arrives with a target rather than into empty space, which is the whole difference between a passive system and a patient one.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5 and attacks the knight on f6 — the one piece the opponent has developed — while their flank pawn move sits on the edge doing nothing for the fight. The knight must move again, and the pawn that chased it stands in the centre it was given for free.
notes.teaches: When your opponent spends their opening moves on flank gestures and repeat moves with the same piece, the centre push is the punishment. Every tempo they wasted is a tempo your pawns use to start asking questions their undeveloped pieces cannot answer.

notes.explains: The pawn steps into e6 attacking the knight on d7 and the pawn on f7 at once. There is no way to ignore it and no good way to take it — the capture opens the king's cover, and afterwards the pieces behind the broken pawns have nowhere sensible to stand.
notes.teaches: A pawn given away on the right square can be worth more than a pawn kept. The wedge thrown into the heart of an undeveloped position forks defenders, wrecks the pawn shelter whichever way it is taken, and leaves every enemy piece tripping over the wreckage for the rest of the game.

notes.explains: Two replies divide here. Developing the king's knight is the sound, mainstream choice. Jumping the queen's knight to d4 instead is the tricky one — it exists and is played, but it invites White to take on e5, and from there Black is relying on the opponent going wrong.
notes.teaches: A move can be playable, well known and still not good. Openings collect lines that survive because they set traps rather than because they equalise, and the way to meet one is to know the refutation rather than to avoid the whole position.

notes.explains: Grabbing the pawn on e4 with the knight loses a piece outright — White castles and the knight cannot be held, with the black queen and king sitting on the e-file behind it. The move that works instead is pushing the d-pawn, which cuts across the bishop's diagonal and the knight's path at the same time.
notes.teaches: A queen standing on the same file as her own king is a standing invitation, and it is worth noticing before you go pawn-grabbing rather than after. When the file between them can be opened, the tactics tend to appear on their own.

notes.explains: Taking the rook on h8 is the greedy try, and after Black recaptures the bishop on c4 the knight has just two squares to leave by, g6 and f7, and Black covers them both. The alternative is to take on d5 and keep the pieces in play; the position stays messy, but nothing is stranded.
notes.teaches: A rook in the corner is worth more than a knight only if the knight comes home. Before taking material with a piece that has to travel back through enemy territory, count its exit squares — a won exchange that costs the piece which won it is not won at all.

notes.explains: The knight can leap to c7 with check, hitting the king and the rook in the corner at once — but the queen on f7 travels along the seventh rank and takes it, and the whole idea comes to nothing. Retreating the knight to b6 keeps material, though it leaves the king alone in the centre, where the queen swings to g6 and hunts it down the light squares.
notes.teaches: When you calculate a discovered attack, check that the piece you intend to win cannot simply capture the piece doing the discovering. That single question is what separates a real double attack from one that evaporates, and it is the most common way these tricks are miscounted.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System
notes.explains: Taking on c5 reaches the structure the position was heading for, and the pawn now attacks the queen on b6, so the tempo comes back immediately. The gambit that this line usually concedes has simply not been paid.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is about to capture in the centre anyway, consider capturing FIRST. The structure that results is the same one they were aiming for — except you reach it without conceding the pawn, and the capture lands with tempo if their queen is standing where the pawn arrives.

notes.explains: The bishop takes on f7 with check, and the king has to recapture. The knight that follows arrives with check too, so there is never a move spare to save the bishop that is left hanging on the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: Before developing a piece to a natural square, count what is holding the square in front of your king. A bishop taken on f7 is only a sacrifice if the follow-up does not come back — when the king is dragged out with check and a knight fork or a loose piece waits behind it, the material returns and the king does not go home.

notes.explains: The knight now stands on g4, holding the piece the two checks made unsavable, and it bears down on the knight on f6 from there. The enemy king sits on g8 having lost the right to castle.
notes.teaches: A short forcing sequence is worth calculating to the END, not to the exciting move. The point of a check is rarely the check — it is that the opponent has no time to attend to the piece you are really going for. Count the material at the last quiet position, and if it comes out level with their king displaced, the sequence was sound.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b4 giving check, so the next move is not a free choice — it has to answer the king. The natural-looking square on the other diagonal invites a quiet pawn move instead, and quiet is exactly what a gambit cannot afford.
notes.teaches: Two developing squares can look equally natural and be worth completely different amounts. The one that comes with check forces the reply, and if the forced reply is the one you were hoping for, you have chosen your opponent's move for them. Prefer the developing move that asks a question over the one that merely occupies a good square.

notes.explains: The queen comes to e7 pointing straight down the file at the king, with a single pawn on e5 standing in between, and it defends the bishop out on b4 at the same time. Nothing is threatened yet, which is why it reads as a normal move.
notes.teaches: A piece aimed through a pawn at the enemy king is not doing nothing — it is a threat waiting for one square to empty. Set the alignment up FIRST, while it looks like ordinary development, and the tactic arrives later as a simple capture rather than as something that has to be found. The same move should also hold your loose pieces together.

notes.explains: The knight from g4 takes on e5, hitting the knight on f3 and the pawn on c4 and covering d3. The file behind it is now clear apart from one pawn, and the bishop on b4 is deliberately left to be taken.
notes.teaches: When two pieces can take the same pawn, the tie-break is what the square BEHIND the capture becomes. Recapture with the piece whose departure opens your own line, and the move does two jobs: it restores the material and it arms the alignment you built earlier. If the opponent now grabs the piece you left hanging, they are stepping into the idea.

notes.explains: The knight drops into d3 checking the king, and every square around it is filled by its own men. Nothing can capture the knight and nothing can interpose against a knight, so the game ends the move the bishop is taken.
notes.teaches: A king on its starting square with every piece still at home is not safe — it is enclosed. A knight that lands beside it gives a check no piece can block, and blocking is the only defence the surrounding men are able to offer. Count the king's real escape squares before deciding an uncastled king is merely undeveloped.

notes.explains: The knight comes out hitting the pawn on e4 and covering d5, the square the intended advance wants to control. Nothing has been committed and the slow plan already has a problem.
notes.teaches: A quiet pawn move that prepares a big centre is an announcement, and announcements should be answered before they are carried out. Develop the piece that attacks the pawn already standing in the middle: the opponent must now spend the move they wanted for the build-up on defending instead, and a plan interrupted one move early is usually a plan abandoned.

notes.explains: The knight goes to d5 rather than back, where it attacks the pawn on c3 and covers b4, e3 and f4. The pawn that would normally chase it from c4 is standing on c3 and cannot get there in one move.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advances to kick a knight, count which pawn would do the kicking NEXT before deciding where the knight goes. A knight that steps forward into the middle is only loose if a pawn can come and ask it to move — and if that pawn has already been spent on something else, the outpost is permanent. The move that prepared the centre is the move that gave the square away.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the diagonal aiming straight at f7, the one square a retreated-queen setup has not reinforced, with the centre already occupied behind it. Every move so far has been a piece coming out to a square it wants.
notes.teaches: Against a system whose whole point is solidity, there is nothing clever to find — occupy the centre, develop toward their weakest point, and let the extra space do the arguing. A setup that retreats the queen all the way home has conceded time, and time is only collected by moves that do something.

notes.explains: The bishop checks on b5, and however the check is met, the light-squared defenders start coming off the board — the pieces that would have guarded the squares the pawn advance abandoned in the centre. The holes are permanent; the defenders are not.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pawn advance leaves permanent holes, the bishop check that forces a trade is not a drawish gesture — it removes the one piece that could have covered those holes. Trade toward the weak squares: every exchange makes the holes harder to patch.

notes.explains: The knight has landed on f5, the square the pawn push to e5 gave away forever, and it attacks the pawn on d6 and the pawn on g7 at the same time. No pawn can ever ask it to leave — the hole has a tenant, and the rent is paid in defensive moves.
notes.teaches: A hole is only a weakness once a piece lives in it. The knight's jump to the square the pawn advance can never attack again is the follow-through — from there it hits in two directions at once, and evicting it costs a concession every time.

notes.explains: The knight has centralised on d5, attacking the pinned knight on f6 — pinned by the bishop against the rook behind it. Taking the intruder walks into the pin's point, and declining leaves a monster in the middle while the queen is away on b2 counting pawns.
notes.teaches: When your opponent goes pawn-grabbing with the queen while behind in development, answer in the centre, not on the wing she left. The knight's leap to the central square works because the pin behind it makes the capture unpalatable — and keep your eyes on the greater prize rather than the first material the tactic offers.

notes.explains: The pawn on d6 attacks the pawn on e5 directly. There is no way to keep the advanced pawn without committing more forces to it, so the opponent's second move is already a question they have to answer on their third.
notes.teaches: A pawn pushed forward this early has outrun its support, and the right response is to challenge it immediately rather than play around it. The pawn either trades itself off — giving back the space it grabbed — or its owner spends more moves propping it up while you simply develop.

notes.explains: The knight on e4 is supported by the pawn on d5, so the bishop is free to skip the defensive posting and come to g4, attacking the knight on f3 and pinning it against the queen behind it. One move, and it is the opponent who has to spend the next one.
notes.teaches: Before spending a move defending a piece, check whether it is already defended — a centralised knight held by a pawn needs nothing from you. Spend the move on a new problem for your opponent instead: the pin that ties their knight to the queen costs them a tempo however they resolve it.

notes.explains: The knight develops to d7 and takes the e5 square in hand, and behind it the pawn break with the f-pawn stays in reserve. Nothing here forces anything yet — but every piece now carries a small threat, and the opponent has to answer all of them at once.
notes.teaches: Positions are rarely won by one blow — they are won inch by inch, by creating enough small problems that they coalesce into a big one. Each developing move should carry a little annoyance: a square eyed, a pawn break held in reserve, a piece the opponent has to keep watching.

notes.explains: The modest pawn to d6 covers c5 and e5 and gets on with the position while the queen keeps eyeing the loose pawn. Nothing has been cashed in and the threat has not gone away.
notes.teaches: A queen sortie that eyes a loose pawn is strongest as a THREAT, not as a capture. Taking usually enters the one line the opponent has actually studied, where their development is the compensation. Leave the pawn hanging, make a useful move, and keep them solving the problem instead of following their preparation.

notes.opening: Alekhine Defense: Four Pawns Attack, Main Line
notes.explains: The bishop takes on f6, where it bears down the diagonal on the pawn on d4 and connects with the queen behind it. The chain that was cramping the position is gone and its remaining pawn is now the target.
notes.teaches: After a central break is resolved, recapture with the piece that ends up doing the most, not the one nearest to hand. A bishop that lands on the long diagonal turns the opened centre into pressure on the pawn that is left — the break was never about the pawn count.

notes.explains: Every white move so far has been a pawn, and the c-pawn takes still more ground while the knight on d5 is asked to move again. It is a real gain and a real risk at once: the knight drops back to b6 or c7 and White has to bring pieces out quickly, because a centre this wide with nothing developed behind it invites a counterstrike.
notes.teaches: Taking a large share of the centre with pawns is not the same as being ahead, and the danger grows with every further pawn move. Grabbing more space while none of your pieces are out is playable only if you can follow it immediately with accurate development — the space has to be defended by something.

notes.explains: Bringing the king's knight to f3 hands the light-squared bishop a job: it comes to g4 and pins the knight against the queen on d1, since e2 is empty. Developing the queen's knight to c3 first leaves f3 vacant, so that bishop has nothing to attack and has to choose a square on its own terms.
notes.teaches: When two knights both want to come out, the order is decided by which one can be given a target. Develop the piece that cannot be harassed first and leave the other at home a moment longer — the opponent then has to commit a piece without knowing what it will be aiming at.

notes.explains: The pawn on f3 supports the centre and blocks the king's knight from its natural square. Three replies come into consideration: capturing in the centre straight away, the modest pawn move that keeps the position closed, or bringing a knight out and leaving the tension for another move.
notes.teaches: When the centre is propped up by a pawn rather than a piece, you can take it, sidestep it, or develop and leave the tension. Taking resolves the position at once and hands over the centre. Sidestepping keeps everything closed and asks whether the prop was worth the move. Developing declines the argument entirely. All three are played here.

notes.explains: White has rebuilt the centre with the pawn on e4 and the f-file is open. Two tries come into consideration: the central pawn push that challenges the pawn head-on, or the king's knight developing onto it, which asks the same question without committing a pawn.
notes.teaches: Against a big centre held by pawns you can strike it or develop at it. The pawn break challenges immediately and accepts an open game; the knight comes out hitting the same pawn and keeps the tension for another move. Which you want depends on whether you are happy to open the position while your king is still at home.

notes.explains: The pawn has captured on c5 and from there attacks the pawn on d6 — a pawn won and a second one asked about, in one move. The tempting piece moves are still on the board and lose nothing by waiting; the pawn does not wait.
notes.teaches: When a clean capture wins a pawn and the tempting alternative merely looks clever, take the pawn. Material is the one advantage that does not evaporate while you work out the rest — the flashy move can be checked afterwards, from a position where you are already a pawn up.

notes.explains: The recapture has left doubled pawns on e6 and e7, the rook-pawn on a6 stands isolated with its b-file neighbour long gone, and the pawn cover in front of the castled king is torn where the f-pawn used to be. Three permanent debts on one ledger — the plan is to collect them.
notes.teaches: Pawn structure is a ledger, and sometimes the right plan is simply to read it. Doubled pawns, an isolated rook-pawn and a torn king's cover are not abstractions — each one is a target or an open line, and a position with several of them loses itself once you aim at them patiently.
notes.structural: the position judged by its pawn ledger — doubled e-pawns, isolated rook-pawn, torn king cover, all permanent

notes.explains: The queen's knight is out and Black has answered symmetrically. Several continuations come into consideration and they lead to genuinely different games: an immediate trade on the queenside, quiet development, a kingside fianchetto, or the pawn storm. There is nothing to refute here.
notes.teaches: Some positions have no best move, only a choice of what kind of game you want. A bishop out to the edge, a knight to its natural square, a fianchetto, a big pawn move on the f-file — each is sound, and each commits you to a different plan. Pick the one you understand rather than the one you half-remember.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to b5 and hits the knight on c6. Black can defend it, block, move it, or ignore the offer and let the trade happen, and each choice fixes something about the pawn structure for the rest of the game. From b5 the bishop also covers c4 and d3, so the light squares in the centre stay contested whatever happens.
notes.teaches: Offering to trade a bishop for a knight early is a structural decision made with a developing move. The knight is the piece holding the defender's centre together, so the offer must be answered — and however it is answered, something has been committed that was not committed a move ago.

notes.explains: The pawns have been traded and the knight takes back in the middle of the board. From there it covers b5, c6, e6 and f5 — the squares a bishop or knight would use to come forward — and holds the pawn on c2 behind it. Nothing is attacked; what has changed is that there is no comfortable square left for the pieces that have not developed yet.
notes.teaches: When you recapture in the centre with a knight, look at the squares it now covers rather than at the ground it occupies. A knight in the middle that holds b5, c6, e6 and f5 has taken over four entry points at once — the defender's pieces have nowhere to land, and that is what a central knight is really for.

notes.explains: The bishop takes the knight on f3. The pawn on h3 asked the question, and the pawn on g2 stands ready behind it. The bishop came out to make this trade — taking now does it on your terms.
notes.teaches: When the rook's pawn puts the question to your bishop, the retreat is not automatically the safe answer — count the pawn advances that follow before choosing it. Players are conditioned never to give a bishop for a knight, and that conditioning is exactly what walks the bishop into a cage two moves later. This bishop came out to take that knight; let it do its job.
notes.structural: the take-or-retreat decision answered by counting the pawn advances behind the retreat, not by habit

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The expansion with b5 is what this whole set-up is for, but played right now it simply drops a pawn: the c-pawn and the queen's knight both cover b5, and only the pawn on c6 guards it. The rook's pawn to a6 makes it two against two, and from here the break goes in whenever the moment is right rather than never.
notes.teaches: Before pushing a pawn into the opponent's half, count the pieces covering the square it lands on. A break that is one defender short is not a break, it is a donation — and the cheapest repair is almost always a quiet pawn move on the neighbouring file, which costs a tempo and buys the whole plan.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The knight arrives on b6 hitting the bishop and joining the pieces already trained on d5. Count where that bishop can go and the position speaks for itself — of its six squares, exactly two keep it guarding the pawn, and both of them are behind it on the same diagonal, further from the game rather than nearer to it.
notes.teaches: When a piece has been reduced to guarding a single pawn, push it further back before it can be re-routed. Time spent harassing a defender is not time lost: every square you take away from it is a square it can never help from again.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps to c4 and shuts the bishop off the long diagonal it was defending along. Three defenders become two, against three attackers, and the pawn on d5 cannot simply be guarded again: the one move that adds a defender without losing material is the central push, which is exactly the concession being played for.
notes.teaches: A pawn does not have to attack a square to win it. Pushing past a defender cuts the line that defender was working along, and a point held three times by pieces that can no longer see it is a point held twice. Removing a guard and adding an attacker are the same arithmetic from opposite ends.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The offer to trade on h6 is coming, and with the rook where it stands the retreat along the diagonal walks into a capture on the square the rook has just left, which means the trade cannot be declined. Stepping the rook to e8 empties that square and the retreat becomes free. It is a piece of technique worth keeping: the rook move looks like ordinary development and is really the answer to a threat one move ahead.
notes.teaches: When the whole character of your position rests on one bishop, look for the move that gives it a safe retreat before it is ever challenged. A fianchettoed bishop offered a trade has only one square to duck to, and whether ducking is possible depends on a rook standing a file away — so move the rook first, while it is still free.
notes.structural: prophylaxis one move ahead of a threat; one move, so no fork

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation, King's Knight Variation
notes.explains: The bishop stands on g7 aiming through the centre. One try puts a bishop opposite it on the same diagonal, so the piece the opponent built around has something to look at. The other develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, where it contests the squares in front of the fianchetto rather than facing it down.
notes.teaches: With both centre pawns out and the opponent fianchettoed, the choice is whether to answer on the long diagonal or on the dark squares. A fianchetto of your own blunts their best piece by facing it; the bishop developed outside the chain contests the squares that bishop wants to use instead. Both are mainstream and they ask different questions.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: The pawn on c3 says the plan is to build a broad centre next move. So Black hits e4 now, while it has only one defender's worth of help, rather than waiting for the pawn to arrive on d4 with everything behind it. This is the principled answer, and it is the one that avoids the cramped positions the other replies invite.
notes.teaches: When the opponent spends a move preparing a big centre, strike at it before the preparation finishes. The pawn that was going to be supported is worth attacking while it still stands alone.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: White takes, and now the question is which black piece takes back. The pawn on d5 is temporary either way: it holds c6 and e6 for a moment, and Black will remove it. What matters is which recapture leaves Black better placed for what comes after, and that is where the two roads split.
notes.teaches: A capture that is forced is still a choice about what comes next. Take when declining would hand the opponent the centre for free, then think about who recaptures.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: Rather than snatching the pawn immediately with the queen, the knight comes out and attacks it. The pawn is not running anywhere, so Black gets a developing move for free and avoids the queen being chased around the board with tempo. It is a small ordering decision that is worth a move.
notes.teaches: When a recapture is available to two pieces, prefer the one that develops. Bringing the queen out to grab a pawn invites the tempo moves that undo the grab.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: The pawn goes to d4 and hits c5, and the shape of the whole game is now settled: the pawns will come off and White will be left with a lone pawn on d4. That structure is a real weapon — it hands White the e5 and c5 squares and open files for the pieces — but only when the defender has no piece sitting in front of the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recognise the structure a move is aiming for, not just the move. An isolated queen's pawn is a plan — squares and initiative in exchange for a permanent weakness — and knowing which side of it you are on decides everything after.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: Black takes, and the pawn on d4 now touches c3. White will take back and the c-file opens for both sides. That is the deal being struck here: White accepts a pawn that no other pawn can ever protect, in return for space and open lines, and Black accepts the open lines in return for a permanent target.
notes.teaches: Trade into the structure you are happy to defend. Opening a file for the opponent is fine when the pawn you leave behind is the one that can never be defended by another pawn.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: White recaptures and there it is: a pawn on d4 with no neighbour on the c- or e-file, holding the squares in front of it and pointing at the black position. Whether it is an asset or a liability comes down to one square — the one directly ahead of it. If a black piece settles there for good, the pawn stops being a spearhead and becomes something to defend.
notes.teaches: An isolated pawn is strong exactly as long as it can advance. Judge the position by whether the square in front of it is available, not by the pawn count.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: The knight recaptures on d5 and, without spending a single extra move, it is standing exactly where a defender wants to be — directly in front of the isolated pawn, where no pawn can ever chase it away. From there it also contests c3, the square White's own knight wants. The structure still favours nobody outright: White develops the knight and the position steers into well-charted territory. But this is the comfortable side of it.
notes.teaches: Against an isolated pawn, the blockading square is the prize. Reaching it with a knight, and reaching it before the opponent is developed, is the version every defender is hoping for.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: The knight comes to f3, where it adds a defender to d4 while getting out. That is the pattern for the side with the isolated pawn: pieces first, and preferably pieces that touch the pawn on the way past, because the defender will be aiming everything at it. Trading pieces helps Black; keeping them on helps White.
notes.teaches: Develop the pieces that defend the weakness first. With an isolated pawn, every move that both develops and guards it is a move you did not have to spend later.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
notes.explains: The knight comes out and leans on d4 as it does so. That is the whole defensive method in one move: put the blockader in front of the pawn, then bring every other piece to bear on it, so each new attacker forces a new defender. Nobody has an advantage yet — but every piece Black develops has a job, and White's have to be arranged around one square.
notes.teaches: Against an isolated pawn, develop toward it. Attackers cost the opponent defenders, and a piece pinned to defensive duty has stopped playing.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps to d5 and hits the pawn on e4, so the tension has to be resolved at once. It also takes c4 in hand — the very square the bishop declined to stand on — so there is no retreat that re-argues the point.
notes.teaches: When the opponent develops a piece to a modest square instead of the argumentative one, the break they were declining to prevent becomes available — and a break that solves your opening is played the move it becomes sound, not later. The quiet developing move is not a mistake; it is a concession, and concessions are collected immediately.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: Taking with the b-pawn doubles on the c-file, but that pawn defends the knight sitting in the middle on d5 and covers b5, so neither enemy minor piece has a square in front of it.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the centre when the doubled pawn you accept has work to do. A pawn structure is not graded on its shape but on what it holds: a doubled pawn that defends a strong central piece and takes an outpost away from the opponent has already paid for itself, whatever it looks like.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The knight lands on c3 attacking the queen on d1 and the bishop on e2 at the same time, so it cannot be ignored for a move. Answering with the pawn is what damages the queenside, and that damage is chosen here, not stumbled into.
notes.teaches: Between two sound continuations, prefer the one that leaves your opponent no choice. A trade offered with a threat behind it is not really an offer — the recapture is forced, so you decide the structure that results rather than negotiating it.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps out to f5 and immediately hits the pawn on c2, so the next move is spent answering it rather than improving. It is developed and it is asking a question in the same breath.
notes.teaches: In a simplified position the last piece to come out should arrive on a target, not merely on a good square. Development that carries a threat buys the tempo you need to start a plan before the opponent starts theirs — the difference between an equal ending and a pressing one is usually one move of initiative.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The rook comes to c8 attacking the bishop on c6, and the damaged pawn on c3 stands behind it on the same file. The bishop must move, and the pawn it was shielding falls.
notes.teaches: When two enemy men stand on the same line, the piece you point down it wins one of them regardless of which moves. Look for the second target BEHIND the first before deciding a capture is only a capture — that is what turns an even trade into a won pawn.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to e5 and attacks the knight on f6, the defender in front of the castled king. Once it moves, the wedge stands permanently between the wings, and the standard kingside build-up unrolls behind it move by move.
notes.teaches: This whole setup plays the same middlegame every time, and it begins with the pawn wedge: the e-pawn advances, evicts the defender knight, and divides the board — your attack lives on the king's wing behind that pawn, their counterplay on the other. Learn the clockwork once and it plays itself for a lifetime.

notes.explains: The pawn on h4 covers g5, so the defence's freeing break there runs into a capture, and the same square is reserved for your own pieces to come through. Across the board the enemy pawn has reached b4 — both storms are declared, and the kingside one is the better prepared.
notes.teaches: In the standard attack a quiet rook-pawn move serves two purposes at once: it stops the freeing pawn break in front of the wedge, and it reserves the squares the pieces will use to lift toward the king.
