Their wing pawns will race meanwhile — that is the bargain of the position, and the side whose preparation is further along wins it.
notes.structural: the rook-pawn's two jobs — the g5 break covered and the lift squares reserved — while the wing race runs

notes.explains: The enemy pawns have marched all the way down the board while every one of your pawns on that wing still stands on its original square — no hooks, no holes, nothing for their pieces to use when they arrive. Meanwhile the pieces continue their regrouping toward the other king, where the game is actually being decided.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's counterplay is a pawn storm on the wing you have abandoned, the master's answer is to ignore it correctly: do not touch your pawns to meet theirs, because every pawn move on that wing creates the holes their pieces need. Pawns arriving alone win nothing — keep your own structure smooth and your pieces on the attacking wing.
notes.structural: the queenside storm met by not moving a single pawn — no hooks conceded, the race run only on one wing

notes.explains: The bishop settles on b7 with the long diagonal open through the centre, taking e4 in hand from a distance. The opponent's modest setup has no piece that argues for that square, so the central advance their position wants is already spoken against.
notes.teaches: Openings are conversations about specific squares, and when your opponent's quiet setup declines the sharp argument, pick the square their setup cannot fight for and own it. The fianchettoed bishop trained on the central light square decides what their pawns may ever do in the middle — a whole plan built from one diagonal.

notes.explains: The advanced pawn has been captured twice over, and the bishop finishes the sequence by retaking on c5, where it now attacks the pawn on e3 down the cleared diagonal. The count was knowable before the push: two captures against, one recapture for, and a bishop improved for free at the end of it.
notes.teaches: A pawn advance that looks like it gains space is a purchase, and the price is counted in captures: every pawn that can take it, and every recapture that follows. When the count comes out against the pusher, the space never existed — the pawn simply left. The modest pawn on b6 was insurance bought moves earlier for exactly this.

notes.explains: The bishop comes to e3 holding the pawn on d4 and the pawn on f4 at the same time. The trade on f3 is still available to them, and after it the centre is still propped up.
notes.teaches: When a bishop pins your knight, ask what the pin is FOR before you spend a move on it. If the plan behind it is to trade off the knight and leave a central pawn short of defenders, the answer is to add a defender to that pawn now — then the trade they were preparing simply happens and costs you nothing.

notes.explains: The queen settles on d2 holding the knight on c3, the pawn on d4 and the bishop on e3 all at once. Everything in the middle is now defended twice, and the king is ready to go long.
notes.teaches: A queen sortie against your queenside is answered by finishing your own development, not by defending the pawn it is eyeing. Bring the queen to the square that links your centre and your minor pieces together, and the pawn-grab becomes a line you WANT them to enter — they spend two moves on a pawn while your rook arrives with tempo.

notes.explains: Taking with the g-pawn doubles on the f-file, and the new pawn on f3 defends the pawn on e4 — so the big centre survives the trade intact. The file the pawn left is now open toward their kingside.
notes.teaches: Recapture toward the centre even when it doubles your pawns, if the doubled pawn is what holds your space. The structure looks damaged and the position is not: the pawn does a job, and the half-open file it leaves behind points at the wing the opponent is about to castle into.

notes.explains: White offers to swap the dark-squared bishops, and the reflex is to take back with a pawn and keep things tidy — but the queen does the job better. On d6 it sits on an open diagonal, active and looking both ways, and with the dark-squared bishops gone any cramp is gone with them. Black is already fully equal out of the opening.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers to trade your good bishop, recapture with the piece that lands on the best square, not just the nearest one — toward the centre, where the queen stays active and eyes both wings.

notes.explains: Here is the move you must not delay: the bishop to f5. Leave it home one move too long and your own pawns wall it in — but out here it grips the e4 square and stares down the whole diagonal, in play before White can challenge it with the bishop to d3. Out first, and your worst piece is suddenly a good one.
notes.teaches: In closed queen's-pawn structures, get the light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before your own moves lock it in — the piece that would be your worst becomes a good one simply by leaving early.

notes.explains: Which knight first? The one that takes something away. The knight to d7 clamps the e5 square, so White can never plant a piece on that central outpost — and only once e5 is denied do we bring the rest of the army out. Same pieces, right order, and the opponent's best square is gone for free.
notes.teaches: Order your developing moves by what they prevent — bring the knight that guards the key central square out first, and the same pieces played in the right order deny the opponent their best outpost for nothing.

notes.explains: The last knight comes to f6, and every black piece stands on a sensible square. There is no fancy stroke here to hunt for — the opening is simply solved, nothing hangs, and now it is White who has to find something to do. That burden is the whole point.
notes.teaches: A solid structure is not won by a clever stroke but by getting every piece to its natural square and leaving nothing loose — then the burden shifts to the other side to find a plan.

notes.explains: Black castles into a position with no weaknesses at all, and in a near-mirror structure that is exactly the achievement. White's only real try is the slow queenside roll with a3, b4 and b5 — but nothing is forced, and the burden of finding a plan is entirely White's. We finish the king and make them come to us.
notes.teaches: In a symmetrical, solid position, having no weaknesses is itself the achievement — it means the opponent must take the first committal step and hand you something to work against.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to e4, hitting the knight on c3 and offering the swap. It looks like a plain trade — but timed here the recapture works for you: when White takes and the d-pawn comes back, the d5 square opens for Black's other knight while White's knight loses its squares. This exchange is a lasting gain, not an even swap.
notes.teaches: Time a central knight jump for the moment the recapture improves your structure — trading a pair of knights can force a pawn recapture that opens a permanent square for your remaining knight.

notes.explains: Take back toward the centre, and this is not just rebuilding a chain — it is planting a thorn. The pawn lands on e4 attacking the knight on f3, shoving it to the passive h2 square, and the d5 hole is now permanent. White is left shuffling with nothing to do.
notes.teaches: Recapturing toward the centre can plant a thorn as much as rebuild a chain — a pawn that lands attacking an enemy knight drives it to a passive square and cramps the whole enemy camp.

notes.explains: No rush. The knight comes back to f6 with one square in mind — the d5 hole — and takes the roundabout route to reach it. There is no hurry at all, because the outpost is permanent and White has no way to cover it.
notes.teaches: Once you have an outpost, route a knight toward it patiently even if the path looks roundabout — a knight heading for a square no pawn can ever challenge is worth the two moves spent getting it there.

notes.explains: And there it is — the knight settles on d5, a square no enemy pawn can ever challenge. Planted in the heart of the board it blockades and dominates, and nothing can chase it off. Black's pieces are simply the better ones now, while White's shuffle with no plan.
notes.teaches: A knight on a square no enemy pawn can attack is worth far more than its material value — it blockades, it dominates, and it cannot be evicted. Plant it and the position plays itself.

notes.explains: White plays a3 to prepare b4 and roll the queenside — but meet it before it moves. The pawn to a5 clamps the b4 square and the whole advance is frozen dead. The queenside is shut, and White is left without a single constructive idea.
notes.teaches: Meet a wing pawn advance before it rolls — when the opponent prepares to gain queenside space, answering with your own rook-pawn one square up freezes the break and denies them the outpost the push was meant to create.

notes.explains: One wing is dead, so we shift the whole army to the other. The rook lifts to e6, planning to swing across to g6 and pile onto the king. A quiet edge is turning into a genuine attack — and White has no defenders coming the other way to meet it.
notes.teaches: When one wing is shut, shift your force to the other — a rook lifted along the rank can swing toward the enemy king, turning a quiet positional edge into a real attack the defender cannot answer.

notes.explains: Trades do not help both sides the same. The bishops come off and the knight recaptures on g4, back into the game — and what is left is knight against knight, where Black's, bound for its outpost, is plainly the better piece. Swapping is a win when what stays on the board is yours.
notes.teaches: Not every trade is equal — swapping pieces is good when what remains favours you. Trading light-squared bishops here leaves a knight-versus-knight middlegame where your knight is the far better piece.

notes.explains: One quiet restraining move before the storm: the pawn to f6 takes the e5 square away from White's knight and readies the plan of h5 and f5, rolling the kingside forward to tear open lines at the king. It is patient, not an immediate threat — but with the other wing dead, it is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: Prepare a pawn storm with a quiet restraining move first — a modest pawn advance can deny the enemy knight its central square and lay the groundwork for rolling the pawns forward to open lines at the king.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Maróczy Bind, Gurgenidze Variation
notes.explains: The queen steps out to b6 and takes aim at the pawn on b2, which is the obvious half of the move. The half that makes it work is that the bishop on e3 has no defender, and it is one of the two pieces holding the knight on d4 together. Grabbing material immediately would let the position be defended; asking a second question first is what makes the loose bishop start to matter.
notes.teaches: Before playing the capture you can see, look for the piece that is not defended. A tactic usually fails or succeeds on one loose piece somewhere else on the board, and the strongest move is often the quiet one that adds a second problem while that piece stays loose.

notes.explains: The pawn strikes at c5 and attacks the pawn on d4, which the early bishop sortie left underdefended by pieces. The system now has to answer a concrete question in a position its move order never wanted to discuss.
notes.teaches: A system that develops its bishop before minding the centre has left the centre to be minded by you. The immediate c-pawn strike attacks the base while the system's pieces are still filing into their usual seats — the setup's comfort is exactly one tempo of neglect, and this move collects it.

notes.explains: The pawn on c3 now defends the pawn on b4 — a second pawn committed to holding the first. The capture on b4 opens the rook's file whenever you choose, and the chain of props stays behind on squares the rook will visit one by one.
notes.teaches: When your lever hits their wing pawn and they answer by propping it with another pawn, the exchange is yours to take: capturing opens the file your rook already stands on, and every prop they added becomes another target hanging on it. Props do not defend a file — they furnish it.

notes.explains: The bishop steps outside the chain to f5, hitting the pawn on c2 down the open diagonal. Once the e-pawn advances behind it, this bishop is already on the good side of everything.
notes.teaches: When a closed centre is coming and you will need a pawn on e6, develop the light-squared bishop FIRST. That one move is the difference between an active piece and the bad bishop that defines every version of this structure — and it is available for exactly one move, before the pawn goes.

notes.explains: The queen steps to b6 defending the knight on c6, so the exchange on that square is answered by the queen rather than by a pawn. The structure stays whole and the queen is developed to an active square in the same move.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is lining up to trade itself for your knight and wreck your pawns, the answer is not to move the knight — it is to arrange a recapture by a PIECE. The trade then still happens, and it costs you nothing: they have spent a bishop to develop your queen.

notes.explains: Castling has put the rook on f1, on the half-open file the pawn trade left behind, and the bishop on c4 already looks at f7 from the other side. The pieces now converge on one square from two directions, which is what makes the coming ideas real rather than hopeful.
notes.teaches: When your f-pawn has already been traded away, castling short is an attacking move: the rook arrives on the half-open file pointed straight at the weakest square in the enemy camp. Do it before starting anything violent — the sacrifice ideas only work with the whole army signed in.
notes.structural: castling as an attacking move — the rook lands on the half-open file the pawn trade prepared

notes.explains: The bishop has taken on f7 with check, so the king must deal with it at once and loses the right to castle whatever it chooses. Every developed piece joins the chase from its current square — the sacrifice spends one bishop to make all of them stronger.
notes.teaches: A king out in the open is easier to checkmate than a king behind pawns — that arithmetic is what piece sacrifices on the weakest square are buying. When your pieces already converge there and the defender is short of developed pieces, giving the bishop to drag the king forward is a typical idea, not a stunt.

notes.explains: The knight develops to d2 and defends the pawn on e4 in the same motion — the last undeveloped piece joins the game and a target comes off the opponent's list at once. Nothing about the material edge made this optional; converting is just development continued.
notes.teaches: Even in a winning position, the rule does not change: develop the last piece, and pick the developing square that also does a job. A knight that comes out defending a pawn asks nothing of the pieces already working, and a position with every piece playing needs no heroics to convert.

notes.explains: The queen checks from a5 and attacks the bishop on b5 in the same breath. The reply that covers the check and defends the bishop at once looks perfect — and it steps directly into the pawn advance that wins the blocking piece. The check chose the opponent's move for them.
notes.teaches: A check that also attacks a piece narrows your opponent's world to a handful of replies — and when the most natural of those replies walks into the next blow, the check is really a two-move combination wearing a modest face. Look one move past the block before deciding a check achieves nothing.

notes.explains: The pawn advances to d4 and attacks the knight on c3 — the piece the check just compelled to that square, now pinned against its own queen's defence of the bishop. The knight was placed by force and is collected by a pawn.
notes.teaches: A piece forced to a square by a check is a piece whose next address you already know. The quiet pawn advance that attacks the compelled blocker is the harvest: it cannot step away without abandoning the job the check gave it, and the pin against the queen behind it seals the trap.

notes.explains: The bishop captures on d2 with check, so the recapture is forced before the opponent can take anything back elsewhere. The rook on offer was louder; the capture with check was correct, and the whole exchange resolves a piece ahead with no counting required.
notes.teaches: In a sequence of mutual captures, take with check whenever you can — the check fixes the move order, because your opponent must answer it before collecting anything of yours. Getting waylaid by the biggest piece on offer instead of the forcing capture is how won sequences come apart.

notes.explains: The queen steps to e3, still holding the pawn on e4 and now covering the dark squares in front of it. The trade is refused without giving the opponent the recapture that would have brought a piece out.
notes.teaches: When a queen trade is offered, the choice is not just yes or no — it is which square you decline ONTO. Taking would develop their knight for them with the recapture; stepping aside is only better if the new square keeps everything defended and stays out of the way of your own development. Decline onto a working square or take on your own terms; never just move.

notes.opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
notes.explains: The pawn to c3 holds d4 against the challenge, which is only possible because the knight went to the other square and left the c-pawn its move. The centre stays intact and the second knight will take over the defence.
notes.teaches: Developing a knight to the square that blocks your own bishop looks like a beginner's error and is a deliberate trade: it keeps the c-pawn free, so when the centre is challenged you can prop it with a pawn instead of dissolving it. You give up a diagonal for a move or two and keep the whole centre — decide which of the two the position is about.

notes.explains: The bishop comes out to c4 aiming at the pawn on f7, the only pawn near the king with no pawn defending it. From the same square it covers d5, which is where the defender's freeing pawn break wants to land, and b5. Nothing is threatened yet; what has happened is that the natural ways to free the position are all a little harder.
notes.teaches: A bishop on c4 is doing more than staring at f7. From that square it also covers d5 and b5 — the two squares the defender needs for a knight or a freeing pawn — so it restrains as much as it attacks. Judge the piece by the whole diagonal, not by the one square at the end of it.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to d3 and defends the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4 at the same time. Both were the loose points in the position: the bishop could be hit by a pawn coming to d5, and the centre pawn had nothing behind it. One quiet move removes both problems and the position becomes simply solid.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is committed early, spend the modest pawn move that supports it. A single pawn holding both the bishop and the centre pawn means neither can be won by a pawn advance, and the position stops having a tactical answer — which is exactly what an early bishop needs.

notes.explains: The pawn has come to d5 and the bishop must move. Going to b5 hits the knight on c6, which is the piece supporting the centre, so the move that looked forced arrives with a threat. The bishop also holds the pawn on d3 from there, so nothing is left loose behind it.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advance chases your bishop, look for the retreat square that attacks something rather than the one that keeps the old diagonal. A bishop driven backwards has lost time; a bishop driven sideways onto the piece holding the centre has gained it back.

notes.explains: The knight jumps to e5 where it hits the knight on c6 — already attacked by the bishop — and the pawn on f7 at the same time. Defending c6 does nothing about f7 and vice versa, so the defender has to give something up or accept a trade on terms they did not choose. The knight also holds the pawn on d3 behind it.
notes.teaches: Two pieces attacking the same piece is the ordinary way to win it; two pieces attacking two different things is better. Look for the square where the knight joins the bishop against one target and picks up a second one on its own.

notes.explains: Both knights are out and the centre is still unresolved. Three continuations come into consideration here: taking on the centre at once, the bishop to b5 hitting the knight that holds it, or the bishop to c4 aiming at the weakest square near the enemy king. They lead to genuinely different games rather than to a single best line.
notes.teaches: Three sound third moves with little between them objectively, and a real difference in what you are signing up for. Opening the centre leads to the positions both sides have studied hardest. Offering the bishop for the knight trades a piece for a permanent change in the pawn structure. Putting the bishop out toward f7 keeps everything flexible and takes the game somewhere far less familiar — which at club level is most of its value.

notes.explains: The bishop develops to e3 and attacks the pawn on c5. The quiet move is not passive — it completes development, connects the heavy pieces, and puts a question to the queenside pawn in the same motion. The sharper pawn sacrifice was available; simplicity outranked it.
notes.teaches: Part of having a positional style is knowing when simplicity is required. When the position is rich with sharp tries, the developing move that completes your setup is often stronger than any of them — a trade that ruins your pawns a little while opening a file for your rook is a price worth agreeing to in advance.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on f5 attacking the bishop on e6 and the knight on g6 at the same time — two pieces, one pawn, and only one of them can step away. The capture on e6 a move earlier is what put the bishop there, so the whole sequence was one idea: pull the piece in, then hit it and its neighbour together.
notes.teaches: A pawn storm earns its keep when each step lands with tempo. Trade in the centre to pull a piece onto the square your pawn wants to hit, and the advance stops being a loosening gesture and becomes a forcing sequence — every move of it answered on your opponent's clock.

notes.explains: The queen on d6 has taken the backward pawn. The rook on d1 defends the queen along a completely open file. The whole line aimed at this pawn, and the rook move converts the raid into control of the only open file on the board.
notes.teaches: When a backward pawn falls, the file it lived on is the real prize. Bring the rook to that file at once — the piece that captured is strong there but exposed, and the rook behind it turns a one-move raid into permanent occupation.

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: The knight comes out to hit e4 and, in doing so, allows the most famous sacrifice in this opening. That is a real choice, not an oversight: the resulting positions are fine for Black, but only for a Black who knows them. There is a quieter sideline too, the immediate central push, which is the other thing to have seen before it appears on the board.
notes.teaches: If your reply allows a famous sacrifice, the sacrifice is not optional homework — it is the first thing to know. Playing a move because it looks natural, without the line behind it, is how a good move loses a game.

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: White strikes at e5 instead of going for the sacrifice. The pieces have not moved anywhere unusual, but the game has left the bishop-on-c4 lines and is heading somewhere with a different name and different theory. This is the sideline that a player who only prepared the sacrifice will be improvising against.
notes.teaches: A pawn break can change which opening you are in without changing a single piece placement. Recognise the transposition and you are already in known territory rather than thinking from scratch.

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: Black takes in the centre. The pawn on d4 is not going to be held for the rest of the game and it does not need to be — it costs White a move to regain, and that is a move Black spends developing. What matters is which structure appears when White finally takes it back.
notes.teaches: Accept the pawn when declining costs you the centre anyway. A gambit pawn you can give back on your own terms is a bargaining chip, not a debt.

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: The pawn drives at the knight on f6 and this is the gambit proper — White has given a pawn and is now using the tempo. Moving the knight is legal and playable, but there is one move here that is considered far more reputable than any of them: hitting back in the centre and letting the knight look after itself.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advance both gains space and attacks a piece, expect the reply to be a counter-strike rather than a retreat. Look for the move that hits back before you look for a square to run to.

forkOf.lineName: Italian Game / Italian: Two Knights with d4

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: Instead of moving the attacked knight, the pawn goes to d5 and hits the bishop on c4. Both pieces are now under fire and it is White to choose, which is a far better version of the position for Black than any retreat. The idea is worth remembering beyond this exact opening — the central counter-push is the standard answer whenever a wing attack asks a question in the middle.
notes.teaches: Counter-attack beats retreat when the counter-attack hits something of equal value. Ignoring a threat is sound whenever your own threat is at least as fast.

notes.opening: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
notes.explains: The bishop steps aside to b5, pinning the knight on c6 against the king — that knight cannot legally move at all right now. Two roads out. The traditional one, considered for a long time to be essentially forced, jumps the other knight forward. The newer one retreats it to d7 instead, which looks like it does nothing and in fact blocks the pinning line, so the knight on c6 is free again and the capture on d4 no longer wins anything.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, count how many ways there are to break the pin before assuming the traditional one is best. Blocking the line is a move that also develops.

notes.explains: The knight on b5 wants to land on c7, where it would check the king and hit the rook in the corner at the same time. Three replies deal with it: a bishop check on b4 that answers the threat by making one of its own, a knight to a6 covering the square from the edge, and a bishop to d6 blocking the square directly. All three address c7; they are not equally good.
notes.teaches: When one square is the whole problem, list every way of dealing with it before choosing — guard it, occupy it, or hit something bigger elsewhere. The move that comes to mind first is usually the one that defends most obviously, and obvious defence and best defence are different things.

notes.explains: Black has just recaptured on d6 with the c-pawn, accepting doubled pawns on the d-file in exchange for the half-open c-file. From here the queen sortie to b6 is the critical try, while castling is the move most players reach for.
notes.teaches: The reply you will actually meet is not always the sharpest one. Preparing only for the critical try leaves you improvising in the position that turns up most often, so it is worth knowing the ordinary continuation at least as well as the forcing one.

notes.explains: The g- and h-pawns are marching at the bishop on g6, and the threat of pushing the h-pawn again is the reason Black is uncomfortable. Stopping it with the h-pawn does not solve the problem either: the knight on e5 simply takes the bishop, and recapturing with the f-pawn wrecks the pawns in front of the king, leaving the pawn on g6 as the next target.
notes.teaches: A bishop developed outside its own pawn chain can be chased by pawns, and the chase costs nothing when your king has not committed to that side. Before placing a bishop where pawns can reach it, look at whether the opponent's kingside pawns are still free to advance.

notes.explains: The queen recaptures on d4 in the centre, holding the pawn on e4 and the knight on c3 while eyeing the knight on f6 and the pawn on a7. The trade removed a defender and gave the queen the best square on the board.
notes.teaches: Trading a knight in the centre because it is 'just a trade' is how a position quietly goes wrong. Count what stands there afterwards: if the recapture puts their queen in the middle where nothing can chase her, you have spent a developed piece to improve the strongest piece they own. A trade is only equal when the square it leaves behind is.

notes.explains: The pawn move to c3 propped up the knight but took the c3 square away from the queenside knight — the natural defender of the pawn on e4. The knight comes to f6 attacking that pawn, and there is no longer a clean way to add a defender.
notes.teaches: When your opponent reinforces one piece with a pawn move that steals a square from another, count the defenders of their centre again — the pawn move often costs more than it saves. A move that neither develops nor defends the pawn that matters is an invitation to attack that pawn one more time.

notes.explains: Taking with the d-pawn opens the queen's file: the path from d8 down to the knight on d4 is clear where a pawn stood a move ago, and the bishop on c8 has its diagonal too. The alternative capture kept the prettier pawns and left both of those pieces staring at their own pawn.
notes.teaches: When several recaptures are possible, prioritise piece placement and activity over pawn structure. The recapture that opens lines for your unmoved pieces is usually worth a small structural concession — pieces win games while structure is being admired.

notes.explains: The knight stands back on f6 rather than traded off, and from there it looks at two forward posts at once — d5 in the centre and g4 beside the enemy king's position, both empty and both reachable in one hop. The opponent's own knight wanders the queenside meanwhile; the redeployment race has a leader.
notes.teaches: A retreat that begins a redeployment is a retreat in name only. When trading would relieve your opponent's cramped pieces, step back instead and point the piece at its next post — keeping the pieces on is itself a way of making a passive position hard to breathe in.
notes.structural: a retreat chosen over a relieving trade — the piece keeps two forward posts and the cramp stays theirs

notes.explains: From c7 the queen attacks the pawn on h2 down a completely open diagonal, and the same square supports the knight's leap toward g4 next. Nothing attacks the queen on c7, and everything she looks at has to be minded.
notes.teaches: Look for the queen move that does two jobs from one square: eye a distant weakness and support the pieces' next jumps. The best queen squares early in the middlegame are usually the quiet ones a knight cannot reach, where the queen pressures without being pressured.

notes.explains: The pawn steps to e5 and attacks the knight on d4 directly, so the central advance begins on the opponent's clock. It also takes f4 in hand for the pawn behind it — the plan is e5, then f5, then the further push, and this first step pays for itself.
notes.teaches: Keep the tension until your pieces are placed, then let the central pawns roll. A pawn push that arrives hitting a piece starts the whole advance with a gained move, and each pawn that follows walks into space the first one cleared.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Bc4 Variation
notes.explains: From c4 the bishop looks down at d5, the square the central break needs, and the same diagonal reaches the pawn on f7. Both jobs come from one move, but only the first explains why this square is chosen over the quieter one behind it.
notes.teaches: A developing move can be aimed at a SQUARE rather than at a piece, and when it is, the square is the reason — not the diagonal it happens to open. Black's whole opening rests on one freeing break; the bishop is placed where it argues against that break before it is ever played. Ask what a developing move is DENYING, not only what it is doing.

forkOf.lineName: Sicilian: Dragon / Accelerated Dragon: quiet Be2 and the ...d5 break

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The bishop comes to c4 and hits the knight on d5. Black's knight will drop back and the bishop will be nudged again, so on a tempo count White appears to be losing the argument. That is the appearance the line trades on: what White is really doing is inviting Black to grab the centre with a pawn, which is exactly the position White wants to meet.
notes.teaches: Judge a developing move by what it invites, not by the tempo count. This one looks careless: the bishop attacks a knight that is happy to step aside, and White will end up moving the same bishop twice. Play it anyway when the retreat it provokes is a move you want played — a 'lost' tempo that buys the position you are aiming for is not lost at all.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: Black pushes the d-pawn two squares and it looks frightening — the centre is suddenly Black's and the pawn arrives untouched. But White's pawn already stands on e5, so the push can be met in passing this move and only this move. The scary-looking advance is the move White was fishing for.
notes.teaches: Before you fear a pawn arriving beside yours, check whether your own advanced pawn can take it in passing. A two-square push that sails past a pawn on the fifth rank is answerable for exactly one move, and that single-move window is the whole reason the advanced pawn was worth keeping there.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: White takes in passing. Declining would leave the centre closed in Black's favour and let the light-squared bishop come to g4, where it lands on the knight guarding f3 with the queen sitting behind it — Black's most awkward piece solved with tempo. Taking keeps the tension on White's terms.
notes.teaches: When a capture in passing is available and the alternative hands the opponent an easy developing move, take. The cost of declining is rarely the pawn — it is that the opponent's last problem piece walks out to a good square with a threat attached, and the position you were provoking never appears.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: Black recaptures on d6 and White's natural instinct is to hit the centre at once. That is not what this line is for. The bishop's diagonal is open, the pieces come out first, and the play is aimed at the queenside knight rather than at a pawn break that would only release the tension early.
notes.teaches: A pawn break being available does not make it the plan. In this system the centre push is the move you keep in reserve while the pieces come out, because the target is not the centre at all — it is the knight sitting on the rim, and pieces get at it faster than pawns do.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: White castles rather than beginning the queenside plan immediately. The king leaves the centre, the rook joins, and only then does the work start; the alternative is beginning an operation on one wing with the king still sitting where a file could open.
notes.teaches: Castle before you start something. A plan that needs several moves on one wing is only safe once the king is off the file it started on — the tempo spent tucking it away is what lets every later move be about the attack instead of about defence.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: White takes on e6 rather than avoiding the trade. The recapture is forced, and the square it fills is precisely the one Black's game depends on.
notes.teaches: Trade into the square your opponent's own development needs. A capture that forces a recapture onto a square their pawn was going to use is worth more than the bishop pair — you are not winning material, you are taking away the move order that would have solved their position.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The queen must retake on e6, and the square stays shut either way: White's bishop stood there, and now Black's own queen does. The pawn on e7 still has nowhere to go, so the dark-squared bishop is stuck at home and the king stays in the centre. Black has to move the queen again before anything opens, and that is the time White uses to go after the knight on b6.
notes.teaches: Count development by what the opponent CAN do next, not by pieces out. If the square their kingside needs is occupied first by your piece and then by theirs, the bishop behind it never comes out and the king never castles — and every move they spend untangling is a move you spend attacking.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The traditional move here is d4, breaking in the centre at once. Instead the pawn steps to a4, heading for a5 and the knight on b6. Taken on its own that threat is nothing — the knight will have c8, d5 and c4 to run to — and that is exactly the point: a5 is not about the knight, it is the first step of a march to a6. Worth naming what not to play too. A rook to e1 is the move most players reach for, and it helps Black: the queen on e6 is the thing keeping his kingside shut in, so driving it away does his work for him.
notes.teaches: A wing push is worth playing even when its immediate threat is easy to answer, provided the pawn is going somewhere. And never chase an enemy piece that is standing in its own army's way — the tempo you win is a tempo you hand straight back.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The queen leaves e6 of its own accord, and Black is right to move it: while it stood there the e-pawn could not go anywhere and the dark-squared bishop was stuck at home. From d7 it holds the knight on c6 and the kingside is finally free to come out. So the free time is over — whatever White is doing on the queenside has to happen now, not later.
notes.teaches: When the opponent solves the problem you were profiting from, that is the moment to commit. A plan that was optional one move ago is urgent now.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The pawn arrives on a5 and asks the knight on b6 where it would like to go. Every retreat is still there, so nothing has been won — the move is played because the queenside has to keep moving while Black is busy untangling on the other side of the board. The break with d4 has not been abandoned; it is being held back for the moment it costs Black the most.
notes.teaches: Two plans at once is not indecision. Push on the wing while their pieces are looking the other way, and keep the central break in reserve until the position is already stretched.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The knight steps into the middle instead of shuffling back to c8, and from d5 it leans on the pawn on c3. The urgent point, though, is what Black has not played. If his own a-pawn reaches a6 first, White's pawn on a5 stops dead — it can never advance again, the knight on c6 leans on it, and a spearhead turns into something that needs guarding.
notes.teaches: A wing pawn is a weapon while it can still advance and a liability the moment it cannot. Whoever fixes the structure decides which of the two it turns into.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The pawn goes to a6 first, before Black's can. It hits b7, and it nails the pawn on a7 down for good — that pawn now has no move at all, and whatever ends up guarding it is a piece that is not guarding the king. It also settles b5 permanently: the only black pawns that could ever have covered that square are the c-pawn, long past it, and the a-pawn, which is now frozen.
notes.teaches: Freeze the structure on your terms. A pawn planted deep in their camp costs them a defender for the rest of the game, while the same pawn one square further back costs them a single tempo.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: Black shuts the door rather than let the pawn crash into b7. Leaving it one move longer loses the queenside outright, and taking the other way, with the b-pawn, only invites a rook to a6 with a permanent look at the pawn on a7. So this is the least bad reply, and it still costs: the light squares behind the pawn chain now have nothing that can ever cover them. White has no light-squared bishop — that one was traded on e6 — but a queen travels the same diagonals, and that is the piece those squares are being saved for.
notes.teaches: A pawn thrust has done its job when every reply is a permanent concession. And when the piece that naturally works a colour of squares has been traded off, ask which OTHER piece moves the same way — a queen covers a bishop's diagonals.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: Now the centre, because a move from now it will be too late — Black is one move from freeing the bishop, and the moment the kingside is out the queenside squares stop mattering. The pawn hits c5 and opens the middle without forcing anything. If Black takes, the knight recaptures; if Black takes again, the queen lands on d4 propped up by the pawn on c3 and looking straight down the long diagonal at g7, which is exactly the square the bishop on f8 needs freed.
notes.teaches: A central break is only strong while the opponent is still tangled. Once their pieces come out it stops being a break and starts being a trade, so take the moment when it exists rather than the moment that feels tidy.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The pawn steps to e6, propping up the knight on d5 and clearing the way for the bishop. The obvious reply is to shove the c-pawn and kick that knight, and it is the wrong move: the knight simply goes to b4, a square no white pawn covers, and from there it hits the pawn on a6 the whole queenside plan is built around while the chain that was holding the centre together comes apart behind it.
notes.teaches: Before kicking a piece, check where it lands. A square your pawns can never attack is not a retreat, it is a new home — and the pawn you moved to do the kicking is usually the one that ends up loose.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The knight jumps to e5, touching the queen on d7, the knight on c6 and the pawn on f7 all at once — which is really an invitation. The point is not the knight, it is what replaces it: once the pieces come off, a pawn stands on e5 instead, and the position stops being a possible isolated-pawn middlegame and becomes the structure this whole line is aiming for.
notes.teaches: Offer a trade when the recapture improves your pawns. The piece that comes off is worth less than the structure the exchange leaves behind.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: Taking with the pawn rather than a piece is the whole idea. The pawn on e5 now sits on top of the position and holds f6 and d6 for the rest of the game — and those are precisely the two squares Black wants: f6 for the dark-squared bishop, and f6 again for a knight if the c-pawn ever comes forward. The d-file opens at the same time, and it opens pointing at the knight on d5, for the side with the extra space.
notes.teaches: Recapture with the pawn when the pawn does more standing there than the piece would. A pawn that holds two squares the opponent needs is worth more than the file it gives up.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
notes.explains: The bishop comes out to e7 and the king is one move from safety, which makes the queen move the obvious one: from g4 it hits the pawn on g7 behind the bishop and the pawn on e6 in front of it, and the bishop on c1 can follow it to h6. The pawn on e5 is what makes that plan work — the natural defence of putting the bishop on f6 simply gets taken. Meanwhile the knight has come round to a3 for one reason: b5 is a square no black pawn can ever cover, and the only thing guarding it is the queen on the seventh rank. The moment that queen steps away, the knight drops in.
notes.teaches: A piece parked on an odd square is developed if it is waiting for one specific entry point. Put it where it can arrive the instant the single defender leaves, then make the defender want to leave.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: Both sides are developed and the tension in the centre still stands. One try is a modest pawn move on the edge that removes a square before it is used. The other takes on c6 immediately, doubling the pawns there and opening a file, which changes what both sides are playing for.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed bishop you can either spend a quiet move keeping the position intact, or resolve the centre at once and accept a structural change in return. The quiet move looks like it does nothing and is preventing something; the exchange gives the defender doubled pawns and gives up the tension. Both are real; they are not the same game.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The pawn steps to a3 and covers b4, which is the square the queen and the dark-squared bishop both eye when they want to hit the knight on c3 with something behind it. Nothing is threatened and nothing is developed; what has changed is that a whole family of annoying moves is off the board before it appears.
notes.teaches: A pawn move on the edge that develops nothing and attacks nothing can still be the best move on the board. Judge it by the square it takes away: if the piece that wanted that square was going to arrive with tempo, the quiet move has saved the move it would have cost you.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The bishop comes to c4 and stares at the pawn on f7, which is the only pawn near the king not defended by another pawn. From the same square it covers d5, so the freeing pawn break in the centre is contested before it is played. That double duty is why this square, rather than a more modest one, is the one to aim for. It also answers the tempting grab in the centre: the pawn there is defended once and attacked once, so taking it is not winning a pawn — it is a trade that banks on the pawn push which would fork the recapturing knight and this bishop, and the bishop on c4 is the piece that break has to get past.
notes.teaches: A bishop aimed at f7 is doing two jobs whenever the defender has castled: it hits the pawn in front of the king, and it covers the square in the centre that the defender's pieces most want. Before you decide the bishop is only an attacking piece, look at what it holds behind the attack.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: The knight has taken on e4 and there are two ways to answer. Recapturing the knight straight away keeps everything simple. Taking on f7 with check first is the move: the king has to choose between stepping out and letting the rook come to f7, and only then does the knight come off. Material ends up level — what has changed is where the black king lives.
notes.teaches: Given a chance to win back a piece or to take a pawn with check, look at what the check does to the defender's position before assuming the recapture is better. A capture that forces the king to move or drags a rook onto an awkward square buys more than the exchange of pieces it costs.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Accelerated Dragon, Modern Variation
notes.explains: Black's pawn stands on c6 with b7 and c7 empty behind it. The pawn advances to e5, hitting the knight on f6, and it covers d6 as well, so the knight cannot drop back into the middle of the position. It has to go somewhere awkward, and every move it spends finding a square is a move the attacker spends developing.
notes.teaches: After trading in the centre, the follow-up push earns its place if it hits a piece and takes a square in one move. The knight it attacks is usually the piece holding the defender's position together, and the square behind the pawn is where the attack wants to land next.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defense
notes.explains: The queen takes back in the centre, one of the two main answers. Most players do find this far, and then run out of preparation — because the point of the position is what happens next. The queen stands on the square White's d-pawn wants, so it will be advanced with gain of time, and the knight coming to c3 will hit the queen again. Two free developing moves for White. That is not a refutation, but it does mean Black has to know exactly where the queen is going before playing it out.
notes.teaches: Knowing the right first move is not the same as knowing the line. The tempo losses come two and three moves later, so learn the follow-up or the move you memorised will not help you.

notes.explains: The bishop on b5 pins the knight on c6, but the pawn on b7 defends that knight, so there is nothing to pile up on. Meanwhile the bishop from c8 has come to g4 and attacks the knight on f3 — the one developing move that also puts a question to the defender of the centre.
notes.teaches: Before avoiding a pin, ask what the pin actually threatens. A pinned piece that is already defended by a pawn cannot be won by piling up, so the pin is a picture, not a problem — and you are free to spend the move on the piece that genuinely needs a job.

notes.explains: The light-squared bishop has already been exchanged for the knight, and only now does the pawn step to e6 — the chain closes behind a bishop that is no longer inside it. Every remaining piece has a natural square, which is the whole point of the trade's timing.
notes.teaches: In this pawn structure the light-squared bishop is the piece with no future, so give it away for a knight before the pawn chain closes over it. Once the trade is made, the rest of the development is peaceful — there is no bad piece left to apologise for.
notes.structural: trade the bishop the structure condemns, then close the chain — order, not material, is the lesson

notes.explains: The knight on b3 is aiming at c5, and it can only sit there for good if the dark-squared bishops come off. The queen on c7 stands behind the bishop on d6, defending it, and the bishop covers f4 — so the trade offer on f4 that would enable the outpost has no square to land on.
notes.teaches: A knight eyeing an outpost usually needs one more thing to happen before the outpost is real — most often a trade of the piece that could evict it. Find that enabling trade and deny it, and the whole plan stays theoretical.

notes.explains: The pawn on g7 is the only defender of the pawn on h6, and it is also the only defender of the knight on f6 — one pawn, two jobs. The diagonal from c1 to h6 is open, so the capture on h6 is available right now, and answering it with the g-pawn leaves the knight behind it loose.
notes.teaches: Before castling, count the defenders on the squares in front of your king and check whether one pawn is doing two jobs. A capture on the square an overloaded pawn guards forces it to choose, and whatever it stops guarding falls next. Improving the position first costs one move; castling into the capture costs a piece.
notes.structural: an overloaded pawn counted before castling; the capture it invites is read off the open diagonal, not guessed

notes.explains: The pawn stands on a5, taking b4 away from the pieces behind it, and the knight on b3 now has to reckon with the pawn coming one square further and hitting it directly. Whatever the knight chooses, the choice was forced by a pawn move that cost nothing.
notes.teaches: A knight parked on the edge is asked the question with the rook's pawn. The pawn move is healthy on its own — it gains space and takes a square away — and the threat of running one square further forces the knight to declare where it is actually going.

notes.explains: The knight has landed on e4 and attacks three pawns at once — the pawn on c3, the pawn on g3, and the pawn on c5. No pawn can ever evict it from this square, so every one of those targets has to be watched for as long as the knight chooses to stay.
notes.teaches: Outposts run both ways. The same central square you spent moves denying to their knight is usually available to yours, and a knight that lands there with several targets in reach is worth more than any of the pieces it is annoying.

notes.explains: The pawn arrives on f5 and defends the knight on e4, so the knight is now held by a pawn on a square no enemy pawn can ever attack. The sharper queen moves were available, but each of them left the knight's future to be negotiated; this settles it first.
notes.teaches: When a knight has found a great central square, the move that guarantees it stays there outranks the sharper tries. Cement first — the attacking ideas do not run away, and every later plan is stronger with the knight permanent than with it evictable.

notes.opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Kasparov Attack
notes.explains: Black has recaptured on f6 and the knights are off, leaving a symmetrical-looking centre where Black is solid but short of space. Several setups are available: a kingside fianchetto with the g-pawn, the classical bishop to d3, and the modest c-pawn move, which is easy to read as pure consolidation and is well regarded precisely because it is not.
notes.teaches: Against a defence that is solid rather than sharp, there is nothing to refute — so the opening question stops being which line wins and becomes which setup you want to play. Choose by the kind of position you want on the board, because all of the reasonable tries here are sound and they lead to different games.

notes.opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Kasparov Attack
notes.explains: White's knight stands on e4, recaptured and so far unchallenged. Two different pieces can head for d7, and the choice is which one goes: the queen's knight, which offers a trade in the centre straight away, or the light-squared bishop, which leaves the knights on and challenges with pieces instead.
notes.teaches: Two developing moves onto neighbouring squares, and the difference is which piece you are willing to trade. Bringing the knight out offers an exchange in the centre and simplifies toward a solid game; developing the bishop keeps the knights on and prepares to challenge with pieces rather than by trading.

notes.explains: The bishop already stands on f5, outside the pawns, and only now does the pawn come to e6, defending the pawn on d5 and completing the chain behind a bishop that escaped in time. Compare the two pictures: identical pawns, and the difference is one move of ordering.
notes.teaches: When the centre gets locked with a pawn chain, the light-squared bishop's whole life depends on which side of the chain it stands on. Bring it out first and only then close the chain behind it — the same structure with the bishop inside is a well-known headache, and with the bishop outside it is simply comfortable.

notes.explains: The queen on b6 attacks the pawn on b2 down the open path, and together with the pawn on c5 it leans on the chain's base. If the pawn on d4 ever takes on c5, the chain is theirs no longer — the recapture comes with a gain of time and the centre stops being a wall.
notes.teaches: Against a pawn chain, pressure beats haste: aim pieces at the chain's base and keep the tension. Capturing in the centre yourself releases it — trade on the base pawn only when something concrete is won by it. If they capture toward you instead, their own chain breaks up and your pieces come in through the gap.

notes.explains: The bishop stands on a3 after taking the pawn. The king on e8 sits on a light square. The remaining attacking bishop runs on dark squares, so it can never check that king. No discovery exists, and the pawn count decides who came out ahead.
notes.teaches: Before playing a sequence that leaves pieces hanging for a move, check for discovered checks the way a strong player does — by colour complex, not by staring. A king on a light square can never be checked by a dark-squared bishop, so whole families of discoveries can be ruled out in one glance.
notes.structural: a grab verified by colour complex — light-squared king, dark-squared bishop, so no discovered check exists

notes.explains: The bishop returns from its pawn-grab by way of b4, and the move is check — the king on e1 has to be dealt with before anything else happens. The retreat costs nothing because the opponent spends the move answering it.
notes.teaches: A piece that has grabbed material deep in enemy territory should come home with tempo whenever the board offers it. Every forcing move on the way back is a whole move your opponent cannot use to punish the raid.

notes.explains: The knight on g6 cuts the bishop's diagonal from d3 toward h7, so the standard attacking picture against the castled king is switched off by a piece rather than a weakening pawn move. From g6 the knight also takes f4 under control, a square right next to the queen's diagonal, which is exactly the kind of option that makes an opponent spend moves on guard duty.
notes.teaches: A repositioned knight can be worth playing for what it stops and what it might do, not what it does today. Blocking a dangerous diagonal with a knight rather than a pawn keeps the pawn shield intact, and the knight sits loaded — potential energy the opponent has to keep accounting for.

notes.explains: The pawn to a6 covers b5, so the bishop has no check there and no outpost either, and it prepares the pawn behind it to advance and take space. Nothing is threatened; both jobs are about the next ten moves.
notes.teaches: The most-played quiet move in a whole family of openings usually earns its place twice over. Here it takes a check square away from a bishop AND prepares the pawn advance that claims the queenside — one is defensive, the other is the plan, and the move that does both is why it appears in system after system.

notes.explains: Black has answered in the sharpest way, and you might be bracing for a big theoretical brawl — but I would rather sidestep all of that. The little pawn to c3 simply prepares to build the centre with d4, and it steers us into a calm, sound structure we actually understand instead of a memory contest.
notes.teaches: Against a sharp defence, the setup you know cold usually beats the one that is objectively critical but unfamiliar — especially while you are still learning.

notes.explains: Black strikes at the centre with d5, and here you could shove past with e5 and lock things up — but I will take instead. Capturing on d5 steers us into the isolated-pawn structure, and that is a game where both sides' plans are laid out from the very first move.
notes.teaches: When a position offers you a choice of structures, pick the one whose plans you know cold.

notes.explains: So we are steering toward an isolated pawn, and the whole fight will be about the square directly in front of it. Our job is to clamp down on that square, blockade the pawn, and trade pieces until it is nothing but a weakness — and that plan is set before the pawn is even isolated.
notes.teaches: The way to fight an isolated pawn is to own the square in front of it: blockade it, pile up on it, and trade down until it is simply weak.

notes.explains: There is no rush to grab anything back; the pawn is not going anywhere. So we develop — the knight comes out eyeing e5 and guarding d4 — and we keep the trade on c5 in reserve for the moment it also costs Black a tempo.
notes.teaches: When the plan is to win a slow structural battle, develop first — the timing of the key trade matters more than making it now.

notes.explains: The bishop comes out with check — a free tempo. We develop a piece while Black has to stop and deal with it, and any trade that follows costs him time, not us.
notes.teaches: Prefer the developing move that also asks a question; a check that develops is a move for nothing.

notes.explains: We are a shade better, so let us keep it simple and trade the bishop off rather than shuffle it back. We swap a pair of minor pieces, keep a clean structure, and get on with castling — no heroics needed when you already hold the pull.
notes.teaches: With a small, safe edge, simplicity is a weapon — fewer pieces mean fewer ways to go wrong.

notes.explains: King to safety first. We castle, everything is developed, and only now do we turn to the pawn tension. The whole edge is the pressure coming against that isolated pawn, and that pressure is cashed in by patience, not by rushing.
notes.teaches: In a quiet structural edge, castle and finish development before you act — a small advantage is converted slowly.

notes.explains: Now the trade. Black has just committed the bishop to e7, so taking on c5 forces him to recapture and lose a move — the very same swap, timed to cost him a tempo. And he is left holding the isolated d-pawn we have been eyeing all along.
notes.teaches: Time your trades for when they also gain something — the same capture, made a move later, can cost the opponent a tempo.

notes.explains: Here is the moment. Black took back with the bishop, the natural move — but it left his king sitting on the open e-file, and we pounce with the rook check. That innocent-looking recapture is the real mistake: the check is the first move of a forcing line that wins material.
notes.teaches: Before a natural recapture, check what it opens — an open file at your own king can turn a routine move into a losing one.

notes.explains: Black blocks with the knight — but look: it has stopped guarding d5. So we do not take the knight, we snap the pawn with the queen first. Count the loose pieces before grabbing, and the whole sequence nets two pieces for a rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent blocks a check by pulling a piece off a defence, look for the in-between capture — count what is suddenly loose.

notes.explains: The dust settles: two minor pieces against a rook, and in material value we are a clear piece up. Now do not rush — bring the king out, finish developing, and let the two pieces work together. Coordinated, they simply outgun the rook.
notes.teaches: Two minor pieces usually beat a rook — keep the pieces on, coordinate them, and do not hurry the conversion.

notes.explains: The bishop steps to e3 to take the c5 square away from his knight. Walking into the pin against our king looks risky — but it is not: if the king moves off, we just answer with King-to-f2, unpinning and defending the bishop in one stroke. A pin you can break by force was never really a pin.
notes.teaches: Calculate a pin before you fear it; if a simple move next turn breaks it, the pin is an illusion.

notes.explains: King to f2 — it breaks the pin and defends the bishop at the same time, and now the knight is free to reroute toward the centre. In an endgame the king marches up and joins the fight, and with an extra piece that walk is half the technique.
notes.teaches: In the endgame the king is a fighting piece — centralising it is half of converting an advantage.

notes.explains: One more improving move: the pawn to b4 takes queenside space and, backed by the pawn on c3, takes the c5 square away from Black's rook. The bishop on e3, the knight on f3 and the rook on e1 all coordinate, and against two rooks that extra minor piece decides it — from here it is just a matter of technique.
notes.teaches: A pawn push should serve a plan — take space and a key square, rather than sit back and defend.

notes.explains: The centre is locked with pawns on e4 and e5 and neither side is breaking through quickly. The pawn goes to h3 and covers g4, which is the square the light-squared bishop uses to come out and offer itself for the knight. With that square gone, the bishop has no active post and the fight moves to the wings.
notes.teaches: A rook's pawn moved one square in a closed position is almost never about air for the king. Ask which piece wanted the square it just covered: if a bishop or knight was coming there to trade off your best piece, the quiet pawn move has prevented a plan rather than made a hole.

notes.explains: The pawns have come off in the centre and the bishop recaptures on d4. From there it hits the knight on f6 and the pawn on a7, and it looks down the long diagonal at the bishop on g7 — the piece guarding the dark squares near the king. It also holds the knight on c3 behind it, so nothing is left hanging while the pressure builds.
notes.teaches: When the centre is released, take back with the piece that lands on the diagonal facing the enemy king. A bishop that arrives hitting a knight and staring past it at the fianchetto has answered the exchange with a threat, so the defender never gets the free move the trade was meant to buy.

notes.explains: The pawn's advance means c5 can no longer be challenged by a pawn, so the bishop settles there and looks straight down the diagonal at f2. It is a home nobody can take away.
notes.teaches: A pawn that advances past a square can never guard it again. When the centre pawn steps forward, ask which square in front of it just became permanent property — then put a piece there. The developing move that occupies it is doing two jobs: it develops, and it collects the concession.

notes.explains: The pawn to d6 defends the bishop on c5 and props up the pawn on e5 behind it, and the other bishop's diagonal is opened in the same move.
notes.teaches: A piece on a strong square still needs holding. The quiet pawn move that supports it costs one tempo and buys permanence — and it usually opens a line for the next piece at the same time, which is what makes it worth playing before anything more ambitious.

notes.explains: The knight hops to g4 hitting the pawn on f2 alongside the bishop, and the only way to hold it puts the other knight on the rim. Once the knight has left the centre, the f-pawn behind it is free to advance.
notes.teaches: A knight leap that looks superficial is worth calculating when the only defence forces a piece to the edge. You are not counting on the threat landing; you are counting on the answer being ugly. Provoking a defender onto a bad square is a real gain even when nothing is won by force.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: Taking on c6 hits the bishop on b4 and the queen behind it while it removes the knight, so the capture cannot simply be ignored. With that knight gone the central pawn can be reinforced next move without the pin costing anything.
notes.teaches: When a pin threatens to win your central pawn, do not look for a way to hold the pawn — look for the piece whose capture the pin is aiming at, and trade the piece that supports the threat. Removing one attacker from the equation is worth more than adding a defender, because it also gains time if the trade comes with hits of its own.

notes.opening: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
notes.explains: The bishop comes to d3 holding the pawn on e4 and the pawn on c2 behind it. It has no open diagonal today, and it is the reason the centre stands.
notes.teaches: A bishop blocked by its own pawn is not automatically misplaced. If the pawn it stares at is the one holding your space, the bishop is doing the most valuable job on the board — bad bishops defend good pawns — and the moment that pawn advances, the same bishop becomes the best piece you own. Judge a piece by the job, not by the diagonal.

notes.explains: The pawn stands on e5 holding d4 and f4, claimed for free the moment the knight stepped back to b3, and the reply mixes systems — the modest pawn move belongs to a setup whose knight is supposed to still be in the centre. The opening argument is already won on move six.
notes.teaches: When the centralised knight retreats, the central pawn advance it was preventing becomes available at full value — no tricks left to fall into, a full share of the centre gained. An opponent mixing two systems usually pays exactly here: each half-system allows the resource the other one was built to prevent.
notes.structural: the central stake collected the move the knight retreated — mixed systems each allowing the other's antidote

notes.explains: Black offers a second pawn to open the f-file and get the pieces out fast. Capturing on f6 does win it, but Black recaptures with the knight and emerges developed with the file already open in front of the white king. Pushing the e-pawn to e4 instead holds the extra pawn without opening anything, and leaves Black to prove the compensation.
notes.teaches: Against a gambit, the pawn is not the prize — the question is what the opponent gets for it. Taking everything offered often hands back exactly what was being paid for: quick development and an open file. Declining once, and keeping the extra pawn on your own terms, is usually the better bargain.

notes.explains: The pawn on e5 looks loose, but taking it opens the line to the black king: the queen comes to h5 with check the moment the f-pawn captures. So the pawn defends itself, and White has spent the move building a centre instead of babysitting it.
notes.teaches: A pawn can be defended by consequences rather than by defenders. When capturing it exposes the enemy king along a diagonal, the pawn is guarded by the check that follows — and a defence like that costs no piece and no time.

notes.explains: Black eyes the pawn on e5 and White wants to hold it. Developing the bishop to f4 is the instinctive way, and it runs into the queen coming to b4: the fourth rank is empty after the capture on e5, so the check on the king and the attack on the bishop arrive together. The piece cannot be saved by parrying the check.
notes.teaches: Before defending a pawn with a piece, check the ranks and diagonals the defender will stand on. The most natural-looking guard is worth nothing if the enemy queen can check and attack it in the same move — and a fourth rank swept clear by an early exchange is exactly where that happens.

notes.explains: Black has developed the bishop actively instead of regaining the pawn, and three continuations branch from here: bringing out the queen's knight, supporting with the d-pawn, or the knight to e7. White's job in all of them is the same — finish development without giving the f-file or the long diagonal away.
notes.teaches: In a gambit that has already lost its pawn, the defender's tries fan out quickly and none of them is forced. Meeting them is a matter of knowing the one idea that answers the whole family — usually to develop, keep the extra pawn, and refuse open lines — rather than memorising a reply to each.

notes.explains: The knight takes on e5, forking the knight on c6 and leaning on d7 and f7. The bishop that just developed is not defending anything it left behind, so the pawn was simply available.
notes.teaches: A developing move that looks natural can still drop a pawn, and the way to find it is to ask which defender left. When a piece comes out to an active square without adding anything to the centre, count the guards on the central pawn again before assuming the position is symmetrical — and take, rather than fearing the counter-check that comes with it.

notes.explains: The pawn to d4 attacks the knight that has just recaptured and takes c5 away from it, so the material comes straight back. The king on f2 is inconvenienced, and inconvenience is not compensation.
notes.teaches: A sacrifice that drags the king out is only worth a piece if you can name what comes NEXT. A check the king simply accepts, followed by a central pawn move that regains the material with tempo, leaves the sacrificing side a piece down and the exposed king perfectly safe. Take the piece and hand it back on your own terms.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Main Line
notes.explains: The pawn steps to c3 and props up d4, the joint the opponent is attacking with the c-pawn and the pieces massing behind it. With the base secured by a pawn, the pieces are free to develop toward the real plan instead of babysitting the centre.
notes.teaches: A pawn chain has a base, and the base is where the whole structure is held or lost. When the opponent piles pressure onto the point at the head of your chain, the calm reply is to reinforce it from behind with a pawn rather than tie pieces to its defence. One quiet supporting move frees your pieces for the plan the position actually calls for.

notes.opening: French Defense: Advance Variation, Main Line
notes.explains: The a-pawn steps to a3 to prepare pushing the b-pawn to b4, claiming room on the queenside and shoring up the very tension the opponent leans on. It also denies b4 to the enemy pieces, so nothing lands there with tempo.
notes.teaches: When the opponent throws their weight against one wing, answering the pressure with expansion of your own often beats passive defence. A modest rook-pawn move that prepares to gain space changes the question: instead of holding a point under fire, you claim room and put the opponent on the back foot where they meant to press. Meet an attack by seizing space, not by hunkering down.

notes.explains: The bishop develops to c4 and attacks the pawn on f7 down an open diagonal, while the enemy knight sits on e4 with its position still unpaid for. Development and threat arrive in one move — the punishment for the wrong order is simply that your normal moves now come with teeth.
notes.teaches: Move orders inside one opening are not interchangeable — the same developing move can be fine after one sequence and dubious after another. When your opponent picks the order that grabs in the centre too early, the bishop's natural developing square becomes a refutation: it aims at the weakest pawn while their advanced piece still has to justify itself.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: The knight lands on f7 forking the queen and the rook in the corner, which is exactly why it is tempting. What follows is a long series of checks that must each be met exactly, and at the end of them White is no better — so the risk buys no advantage, only an obligation to remember a great deal of theory correctly under pressure.
notes.teaches: A line can be objectively playable and still be the wrong practical choice. When every continuation is forcing and one slip ends the game, the recall a line demands is part of its price, and a verdict of "balanced" does not repay that price.

forkOf.lineName: Two Knights Defence / Traxler: 5.Bxf7+ Declined Sacrifice

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Pushing the d-pawn opens the queen’s bishop and strikes at the centre while Black’s pieces are still committed to a kingside attack that has not started. Black’s position is defensible, but only by a reply most players never consider.
notes.teaches: Against a gambit whose whole value is preparation, the strongest practical reply is often the one your opponent has not studied. A move that is merely good but unexpected can outperform a move that is best and famous, because the opponent’s preparation is part of the position too.

forkOf.lineName: Two Knights Defence / Two Knights: Traxler Counterattack

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Advancing the d-pawn ignores the threat and challenges the bishop that aims at f7. Because it interferes with the most dangerous attacking piece rather than fleeing, Black gains the time a defensive move would have spent.
notes.teaches: When a defender’s instinct is to protect the attacked point, the saving move is often to hit something of equal value instead. Counting who is attacking what, rather than rescuing the piece under fire, is what finds these.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: Taking with the bishop comes with check, and the king has exactly two squares — neither of them a capture, because the knight covers f7 — so Black spends the move walking and loses the right to castle on the way. The lines that make this whole variation dangerous never begin, and White is simply a pawn up with a safe king.
notes.teaches: Against an aggressive gambit, prefer the capture that removes the opponent’s attacking chances over the one that wins the most material. The best practical answer often leaves the fewest enemy pieces pointing at your king.

forkOf.lineName: Two Knights Defence / Two Knights: Traxler Counterattack

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: The king has six legal squares here. Stepping forward keeps everything defended and walks into a forced mate; stepping back concedes a pawn and survives. The difference is not calculation depth, it is which question was asked first.
notes.teaches: A king dragged into the open has to choose between holding on to material and getting out of the way, and the instinct to hold on is usually the losing one. Count the checks available to the attacker before deciding where to step, not after.

notes.opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Counterattack
notes.explains: The knight is attacking f7 and instead of defending it the bishop has come out. Three tries come into consideration here: taking on f7 with the knight, the bishop check on f7 first, or the central pawn push that ignores the offer and opens the position while the defender's pieces are committed.
notes.teaches: When the defender ignores your threat and develops into it, stop and count before grabbing. The capture that looks like it wins material invites the whole point of their move; the check first changes the order; and the central push declines the argument altogether and plays chess. Knowing which one you want is the difference between walking into preparation and setting your own.

forkOf.lineName: Two Knights Defence / Two Knights: Fried Liver Defence 5...Na5

notes.opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
notes.explains: The centre pawns have come off and the knight has recaptured on d5, standing on the long diagonal. The bishop develops to g2 hitting it immediately, so the knight must be defended or moved before anything else happens. The bishop also covers e4 and holds the rook in the corner, which is why this setup is solid as well as active.
notes.teaches: The point of a fianchetto is not that the bishop is safe there — it is that the diagonal already contains a target.
